additional_notes: Literally “to open (the) mouth.” Used both literally and figuratively. Very common in negative expressions like “non aprire bocca” (“don’t say a word / don’t speak”). It can also imply finally speaking, especially after being silent (“ha aperto bocca” = “he finally spoke up”).
target_language_example: Non aprire bocca: è un segreto.
native_language_example: Don’t say a word: it’s a secret.

meaning: to open your eyes; (figuratively) to realize/see the truth.
additional_notes: Literal meaning: physically open your eyes. Very common figurative use means “wake up to reality,” “become aware,” or “recognize the truth,” often after being fooled or not noticing something. You can also say “aprire gli occhi a qualcuno” = “to open someone’s eyes (to something).”
target_language_example: Mi ha mentito per anni, ma finalmente ho aperto gli occhi.
native_language_example: He lied to me for years, but I finally opened my eyes.

additional_notes: Used mainly in military/police/news contexts to mean beginning to shoot with weapons. Figuratively, it can also mean to start a strong verbal attack or criticism (e.g., in a debate).
target_language_example: I soldati hanno aperto il fuoco contro i ribelli.
native_language_example: The soldiers opened fire against the rebels.

meaning: to open the doors; to open up (welcome/allow access).
additional_notes: Often used literally (opening actual doors) and figuratively to mean welcoming someone, giving access, or creating opportunities. Common with "a" + person/group ("aprire le porte a qualcuno") or "al/alla" + place/event ("aprire le porte al pubblico").
target_language_example: Il museo apre le porte al pubblico alle dieci.
native_language_example: The museum opens its doors to the public at ten.

additional_notes: A formal/neutral term for weapons that shoot using an explosion (e.g., pistole, fucili). Often used in news, police, and legal contexts. Plural: "armi da fuoco".
target_language_example: È vietato entrare con un’arma da fuoco.
native_language_example: It’s forbidden to enter with a firearm.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something is accompanied by someone/something else. The standard spelling in Italian is usually "insieme a" (same meaning). It’s followed by a noun or pronoun: "insieme a Maria" (together with Maria), "insieme a me" (together with me).
target_language_example: Vengo assieme a te al supermercato.
native_language_example: I’m coming to the supermarket together with you.

additional_notes: Used as a preposition meaning (1) physically around/surrounding something: "attorno alla casa" = around the house; or (2) approximately with times, dates, and quantities: "attorno alle 5" = around 5 o’clock, "attorno a cento" = about 100. It often combines with articles: a + il/lo/la/i/gli/le → al/allo/alla/ai/agli/alle (e.g., "attorno al tavolo").
target_language_example: Ci sediamo attorno al tavolo attorno alle otto.
native_language_example: We sit around the table around eight o’clock.

meaning: back and forth; to and fro.
additional_notes: Used to describe repeated movement or switching between two directions/places (walking, traveling, moving objects, etc.). Often follows verbs like andare/fare/camminare/correre: “andare avanti e indietro” = “to go back and forth.” It can also be used more generally for repeated back-and-forth action.
target_language_example: Ho fatto avanti e indietro tra casa e l’ufficio tutto il giorno.
native_language_example: I went back and forth between home and the office all day.

additional_notes: Formal/legal-sounding phrase used to indicate that someone qualifies for a benefit, service, discount, refund, etc. Often followed by "a" + noun/infinitive: "avente diritto a uno sconto" (entitled to a discount), "avente diritto a votare" (eligible/entitled to vote). It agrees in number: "aventi diritto" (plural). Often seen in notices: "Riservato agli aventi diritto" = "Reserved for those entitled/eligible."
target_language_example: Lo sconto è riservato agli aventi diritto.
native_language_example: The discount is reserved for those who are entitled to it.

meaning: to have to do with; to be involved with.
additional_notes: Used to say something is related to something else (“This has to do with…”), or that someone deals/has contact with someone/something (“I don’t want to have anything to do with…”). Often appears as: "Che c’entra?" (related idea) or "Non ho niente a che fare con..." (I have nothing to do with...).
target_language_example: Questo problema ha a che fare con il lavoro.
native_language_example: This problem has to do with work.

meaning: to take care (of); to be careful (to).
additional_notes: Common in the forms “avere cura di + noun/pronoun” (to take care of something/someone) and “abbi/abbia cura di + infinitive” (please make sure to...). Similar to “prendersi cura di,” but “avere cura” can sound a bit more formal or used in instructions.
target_language_example: Abbi cura di chiudere la porta quando esci.
native_language_example: Make sure to close the door when you leave.

meaning: to take effect; to have an effect.
additional_notes: Used for medicines, rules/laws, decisions, or actions that start working ("take effect") or produce a result ("have an effect"). Common in formal and everyday contexts. Often followed by “su” + person/thing affected: “avere effetto su…”.
target_language_example: Il farmaco non ha ancora avuto effetto.
native_language_example: The medicine hasn’t taken effect yet.

additional_notes: Common way to express hunger in Italian: you say you “have” hunger, not that you “are” hungry. Often used as "Ho fame" (I’m hungry). You can intensify it with "Ho molta/tanta fame" (I’m very hungry), or talk about someone else: "Hai fame?" (Are you hungry?), "Lui/Lei ha fame" (He/She is hungry).
target_language_example: Ho fame, mangiamo qualcosa.
native_language_example: I’m hungry, let’s eat something.

additional_notes: Literally “to have cold.” Used with a subject pronoun: “Ho freddo” = “I’m cold.” You can add “molto” (very) or specify a place: “Ho freddo qui.”
target_language_example: Ho freddo, puoi chiudere la finestra?
native_language_example: I’m cold, can you close the window?

meaning: to begin; to start (to take place).
additional_notes: Formal/common in announcements, schedules, and writing. Used with an event as the subject (e.g., the concert, the meeting). Similar to "iniziare/cominciare" but slightly more formal. Often followed by a time or place: "alle...", "a...".
target_language_example: La riunione avrà inizio alle 9:00.
native_language_example: The meeting will begin at 9:00.

additional_notes: Used mainly in formal or written Italian (news, announcements, official contexts) to say an event happens at a certain time/place. Often followed by a time or location: "La riunione avrà luogo domani" / "avrà luogo a Roma". In everyday speech, Italians often use "succedere" or "avvenire" instead.
target_language_example: La cerimonia avrà luogo alle 18:00 in Piazza Duomo.
native_language_example: The ceremony will take place at 6:00 pm in Duomo Square.

meaning: to be afraid; to be scared.
additional_notes: Common way to express fear in Italian (literally “to have fear”). Often followed by di + infinitive (“I’m afraid to do…”) or che + clause (“I’m afraid that…”). You can also specify what you’re afraid of with di + noun (e.g., paura dei cani = fear of dogs).
target_language_example: Ho paura di perdere il treno.
native_language_example: I’m afraid of missing the train.

meaning: to keep in mind; to be aware of; to remember.
additional_notes: Used when you want to say you’re aware of something, you remember it, or you’re considering it (often in practical situations). Common in phrases like “Tieni/abbia presente che…” (“Keep in mind that…”). It’s more about being mindful/aware than memorizing.
target_language_example: Tieni presente che domani il negozio è chiuso.
native_language_example: Keep in mind that the shop is closed tomorrow.

meaning: to be right; to be correct.
additional_notes: Used to agree that someone’s opinion or statement is correct. Often appears as a response: “Hai ragione” (You’re right). You can also use it to admit someone else is right: “Hai ragione, scusa.”
target_language_example: Hai ragione: il treno parte alle otto.
native_language_example: You’re right: the train leaves at eight.

meaning: to make sense; to be meaningful.
additional_notes: Used to say something is logical or reasonable (or not). Often used in questions and negatives: "Ha senso?" (Does it make sense?), "Non ha senso" (It doesn’t make sense). You can also use it for purpose/meaning: "La vita ha senso" (Life has meaning).
target_language_example: Quello che dici non ha senso.
native_language_example: What you’re saying doesn’t make sense.

meaning: to be thirsty; to feel thirsty.
additional_notes: Literally “to have thirst.” Used with the verb avere (to have) in Italian (not *essere*). Common everyday phrase; you can also say "Ho tanta sete" (I’m very thirsty) or "Ho un po’ di sete" (I’m a little thirsty).
target_language_example: Ho sete. Possiamo comprare dell’acqua?
native_language_example: I’m thirsty. Can we buy some water?

meaning: to be sleepy; to feel like sleeping.
additional_notes: Literally “to have sleep,” but it’s the normal Italian way to say you’re sleepy (not *essere sonno*). Often used in the present tense: *Ho sonno* (“I’m sleepy”). You can intensify it with *molto*: *Ho molto sonno* (“I’m very sleepy”).
target_language_example: Ho sonno, vado a dormire presto stasera.
native_language_example: I’m sleepy, I’m going to bed early tonight.

additional_notes: Used with the verb avere (“to have”) + successo (“success”). It’s common for talking about people, projects, events, or products that do well or become popular. Often followed by con (“with”) to say who/what it’s popular with (e.g., con il pubblico = with the public/audience).
target_language_example: Il film ha avuto successo in Italia.
native_language_example: The movie was successful in Italy.

meaning: to be wrong (not to be in the right).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is incorrect in an argument or situation. Often contrasted with "avere ragione" (to be right). Common patterns: "Hai torto" (You’re wrong), "Ho torto" (I’m wrong), "Avere torto su qualcosa" (to be wrong about something).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, hai torto: il treno parte alle otto.
native_language_example: Sorry, you’re wrong: the train leaves at eight.

meaning: rowboat; a boat powered by oars.
additional_notes: Used to describe a small boat you move with oars (remi). It’s common when talking about lakes, rivers, rentals, or boat trips. You may also hear the singular form in context: “una barca a remi”.
target_language_example: Abbiamo noleggiato una barca a remi sul lago.
native_language_example: We rented a rowboat on the lake.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition that is sufficient for something to be OK or to happen. It’s often followed by the subjunctive (especially in more careful Italian): "Basta che tu venga" (= as long as you come). In casual speech you may also hear the indicative, but learners should aim for the subjunctive after "basta che".
target_language_example: Puoi uscire, basta che torni entro mezzanotte.
native_language_example: You can go out, as long as you come back by midnight.

additional_notes: Used to talk about applauding after a performance, to show approval, or to get someone’s attention. It’s a common, neutral expression. Also used in the imperative: “Batti le mani!” (Clap your hands!).
target_language_example: Alla fine dello spettacolo, tutti hanno battuto le mani.
native_language_example: At the end of the show, everyone clapped.

additional_notes: In Italian, this English loan phrase is commonly used for the sport played on sand (usually teams of 2). You may also see or hear the Italian form "pallavolo sulla spiaggia" (less common in everyday speech). Often used when talking about sports, summer activities, or tournaments.
target_language_example: D’estate gioco a beach volley con gli amici.
native_language_example: In the summer I play beach volleyball with my friends.

additional_notes: Used to praise someone for a well-executed action—often a shot or hit in sports/games (tennis, soccer, billiards), but also figuratively for a clever idea or smart decision. Literally 'nice hit/blow,' but in English you usually say 'nice shot' or 'good one.'
target_language_example: Bel colpo! Hai preso il bersaglio al primo tentativo.
native_language_example: Nice shot! You hit the target on the first try.

meaning: Making a good impression; looking good (socially).
additional_notes: Common in Italian culture: fare bella figura means to appear well-mannered, well-dressed, and appropriate to the situation (not just physically attractive). The opposite is fare brutta figura (“to make a bad impression,” to embarrass yourself). Often used about behavior at events, meeting people, or representing your family/company.
target_language_example: A quella cena voglio fare bella figura, quindi mi vesto elegante.
native_language_example: At that dinner I want to make a good impression, so I’ll dress elegantly.

additional_notes: Used to praise someone for a good job or good result. Often said as an exclamation: “Ben fatto!” You may also hear “Hai fatto un buon lavoro” (more neutral/explicit) or “Bravo/Brava!” (very common, agrees with the person’s gender).
target_language_example: Ben fatto! Hai risolto il problema in pochi minuti.
native_language_example: Well done! You solved the problem in a few minutes.

additional_notes: Most often used to talk about illegal trade, especially of things like tickets, currency, or scarce goods (e.g., selling something “on the black market”). In other contexts it can also literally mean a “black bag/handbag,” so the surrounding words usually make the meaning clear.
target_language_example: Hanno comprato i biglietti in borsa nera.
native_language_example: They bought the tickets on the black market.

meaning: a right-hand man; a trusted main assistant.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s closest helper or second-in-command (at work, in politics, in an organization, etc.). Literally means “right arm,” and it’s often used with "essere" or "diventare": "È il mio braccio destro" (He/She is my right-hand person). Can also appear as "la mia braccio destro" depending on the person referred to, though "il braccio destro" is also commonly kept.
target_language_example: Giulia è il braccio destro del direttore.
native_language_example: Giulia is the director’s right-hand woman.

additional_notes: A common Christmas greeting, used in person, in messages, and on cards. You can also say “Buon Natale!” as an exclamation. Often paired with “e felice anno nuovo” (“and Happy New Year”).
target_language_example: Buon Natale a te e alla tua famiglia!
native_language_example: Merry Christmas to you and your family!

additional_notes: A common New Year’s greeting. You can say it on or around New Year’s Day, often with “Auguri!” (Best wishes). Also used in the fuller phrase “Buon anno nuovo” (“Happy New Year”).
target_language_example: Buon anno! Ti auguro tanta felicità.
native_language_example: Happy New Year! I wish you lots of happiness.

additional_notes: Used before starting to eat (or when someone else is about to eat). You can say it to your table, to someone you’re serving, or to friends in a casual setting; it also works in polite situations. Often shortened to just “Appetito!” in very informal speech, but “Buon appetito” is the standard.
target_language_example: Buon appetito! La cena è pronta.
native_language_example: Enjoy your meal! Dinner is ready.

additional_notes: Used as a birthday greeting. You can say it directly to the person, write it on a card/message, or use it as a toast. Common variants: “Tanti auguri!” (best wishes/happy birthday) and “Auguri!” (congratulations/best wishes—often used for birthdays too).
target_language_example: Buon compleanno, Giulia!
native_language_example: Happy birthday, Giulia!

additional_notes: Common polite greeting used from morning through early afternoon. In standard spelling it’s usually written as one word: “buongiorno”. You can also use it to greet someone when entering a shop or starting a conversation.
target_language_example: Buongiorno, come sta?
native_language_example: Good morning, how are you?

meaning: “Good work” or “have a good day at work.”
additional_notes: Used as a friendly wish when someone is about to start working or is at work (like saying “have a good shift”). It can also praise someone’s performance (“good job”). Often said when you’re leaving someone who is working (e.g., a shop assistant).
target_language_example: Allora ci vediamo dopo: buon lavoro!
native_language_example: See you later: have a good day at work!

meaning: “good for you” (often meaning “good for you, then”).
additional_notes: Used to react to someone’s good news, success, or choice. It can sound genuinely supportive, but depending on tone/context it can also be sarcastic or dismissive (similar to English “good for you”). Often said as a standalone phrase.
target_language_example: Hai trovato un lavoro nuovo? Buon per te!
native_language_example: You found a new job? Good for you!

meaning: 'good afternoon' (also used as a polite greeting in the late afternoon).
additional_notes: Used as a greeting or farewell from early afternoon until early evening (roughly after lunch until around dinner time). It’s more formal/polite than 'ciao' and works well with strangers, in shops, or in professional settings. Similar to 'buongiorno' (morning/early afternoon) and 'buonasera' (evening).
target_language_example: Buon pomeriggio, come posso aiutarla?
native_language_example: Good afternoon, how can I help you?

additional_notes: Used to talk about practical, reasonable thinking in everyday situations. Often appears with articles ("il buon senso") or in expressions like "avere buon senso" (to have common sense) and "con buon senso" (sensibly).
target_language_example: Serve un po’ di buon senso per risolvere questo problema.
native_language_example: We need a bit of common sense to solve this problem.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s mood or general cheerfulness. Often appears with the verb “essere” (to be) or in phrases like “di buon umore” (in a good mood).
target_language_example: Oggi sono di buon umore.
native_language_example: Today I’m in a good mood.

additional_notes: Common wish said before an exam, performance, trip, interview, etc. You can also use it as a noun phrase (“good luck”) in sentences like: “Ti auguro buona fortuna” (I wish you good luck). Often paired with the reply “Grazie!” or “Crepi!”/“Crepi il lupo!” when someone says “In bocca al lupo!” (a different way to say “good luck”).
target_language_example: Buona fortuna per l’esame di domani!
native_language_example: Good luck for tomorrow’s exam!

additional_notes: A polite, common greeting used when saying goodbye (in person, on the phone, or in emails). Similar to "buona giornata" = "good day" and "buona giornata a lei" is more formal. Often said to someone you won’t see again until later the same day; for evening, you’d use "buona serata" or "buona notte" depending on context.
target_language_example: Grazie, buona giornata!
native_language_example: Thanks, have a good day!

meaning: “Good night.” (said when going to bed or saying goodbye late at night)
additional_notes: Used as a nighttime farewell, especially when someone is going to sleep. It’s more “goodnight” than a general evening greeting (for that, use “buona sera”). You can also say “Buonanotte” as one word; both are common.
target_language_example: Sono stanco, vado a letto: buona notte!
native_language_example: I’m tired, I’m going to bed: good night!

meaning: 'good evening' (a greeting, often from late afternoon onward).
additional_notes: Used as a greeting when you meet someone in the evening, and sometimes as a polite sign-off. Commonly written as one word in standard Italian: "buonasera".
target_language_example: Buona sera, come sta?
native_language_example: Good evening, how are you?

additional_notes: Used to talk about polite behavior and etiquette (often in general, or how someone was brought up). Common in phrases like "avere buone maniere" (to have good manners) and "insegnare le buone maniere" (to teach good manners). Often with the article: "le buone maniere".
target_language_example: A tavola bisogna avere buone maniere.
native_language_example: At the table you need to have good manners.

meaning: a good-for-nothing person; a useless person.
additional_notes: An insulting label used to criticize someone as lazy or incompetent. Often used as a noun ("È un buono a nulla") or after "essere" ("sei un buono a nulla"). Use with caution because it’s offensive.
target_language_example: Non ascoltarlo: è solo un buono a nulla.
native_language_example: Don’t listen to him: he’s just a good-for-nothing.

additional_notes: Common food item. Literally “butter of peanuts.” You’ll see it on ingredient lists (es. “con burro di arachidi”) and in shops or cafés when talking about what a product contains or what you want to buy.
target_language_example: Vorrei un panino con burro di arachidi e marmellata.
native_language_example: I’d like a sandwich with peanut butter and jam.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase for asking for entry or getting someone’s attention before entering. Uses the verb “bussare” (to knock) with “a + la” → “alla”. You can also say “Bussa!” (“Knock!”) or “Ho bussato alla porta” (“I knocked on the door”).
target_language_example: Scusa, posso bussare alla porta prima di entrare?
native_language_example: Sorry, can I knock on the door before coming in?

meaning: to throw/knock (someone or something) to the ground; to drop on the floor.
additional_notes: Used for causing something/someone to fall onto the ground, either intentionally (throwing) or by force (knocking down). In everyday contexts it can also mean simply dropping something on the floor (often accidentally). Related: "buttare giù" can also mean "to knock down" or "to take down" depending on context.
target_language_example: L’ha spinto e l’ha buttato a terra.
native_language_example: He pushed him and knocked him to the ground.

additional_notes: Commonly used to mean forcing someone or something to leave a place (e.g., a bar, a house, a club), often because they’re not allowed to stay or they’re causing trouble. It can also mean removing or discarding something (like throwing out trash), but for objects Italian often uses "buttare via". In the past tense: "hanno buttato fuori" = "they threw/kicked (someone) out".
target_language_example: Il buttafuori l’ha buttato fuori dal locale perché urlava.
native_language_example: The bouncer kicked him out of the place because he was shouting.

meaning: to throw down; also: to jot down (quickly), to knock down/demolish, or to swallow/drink (quickly).
additional_notes: The meaning depends on context. With notes/ideas it often means “to jot down” (Butta giù due righe = Jot down a couple of lines). With buildings/walls it can mean “to knock down/demolish”. With food/drink it can mean “to swallow/drink quickly”. Literally it’s “to throw down.”
target_language_example: Butta giù l’indirizzo, per favore.
native_language_example: Jot down the address, please.

additional_notes: Common with objects you don’t want anymore. Often used with pronouns placed before the verb: "Lo butto via" (I throw it away), "Li hai buttati via?" (Did you throw them away?). Similar to "gettare via".
target_language_example: Non buttare via questa bottiglia: la riciclo.
native_language_example: Don’t throw away this bottle: I recycle it.

additional_notes: Used for a public place where you can make phone calls (often a small booth). In Italy today it’s less common than in the past; you may also hear "cabina del telefono". Plural: "cabine telefoniche".
target_language_example: C’è una cabina telefonica vicino alla stazione?
native_language_example: Is there a phone booth near the station?

additional_notes: Used for someone who tracks down fugitives for a reward (a “taglia”). Common in Western/crime contexts and in movies/TV. Literally “hunter of bounties,” but in English the natural term is “bounty hunter.”
target_language_example: Nel film, il cacciatore di taglie dà la caccia a un criminale per la ricompensa.
native_language_example: In the movie, the bounty hunter hunts a criminal for the reward.

additional_notes: Common formal term used in news, science, and everyday discussion about long-term changes in Earth’s climate (especially global warming and its effects). Often used with verbs like “combattere” (to fight), “affrontare” (to address), or “ridurre” (to reduce) and phrases like “gli effetti del cambiamento climatico” (the effects of climate change).
target_language_example: Dobbiamo agire subito contro il cambiamento climatico.
native_language_example: We need to act immediately against climate change.

meaning: to change the subject / change the topic.
additional_notes: Used when you want to move the conversation to a different topic (sometimes to avoid an uncomfortable subject). Often appears as an imperative: “Cambiamo argomento” (Let’s change the subject) or “Cambia argomento” (Change the subject).
target_language_example: Possiamo cambiare argomento?
native_language_example: Can we change the subject?

additional_notes: Used when someone decides differently from what they previously intended or believed. Very common in everyday speech. You can specify what you changed your mind about with "su" (e.g., "cambiare idea su qualcosa") or express a change of plan with "cambiare idea e + verb".
target_language_example: Ho cambiato idea: non vengo più.
native_language_example: I changed my mind: I’m not coming anymore.

additional_notes: Literally “room for sleeping.” Common in housing/hotel contexts. Often used with articles and prepositions: "la camera da letto" (the bedroom), "in camera da letto" (in the bedroom). Not to be confused with "camera" meaning "room" in general (or "camera" as in a camera in English).
target_language_example: La camera da letto è al primo piano.
native_language_example: The bedroom is on the first floor.

additional_notes: Commonly used for a military tank. Plural: "carri armati". Literally "armored cart/wagon," but the natural English translation is "tank."
target_language_example: Durante la guerra, un carro armato attraversò il ponte.
native_language_example: During the war, a tank crossed the bridge.

additional_notes: Used when you need roadside assistance or a vehicle has to be removed (e.g., after a breakdown or accident). Common with the verb "chiamare": "Ho chiamato il carro attrezzi" = "I called a tow truck."
target_language_example: La macchina non parte: devo chiamare il carro attrezzi.
native_language_example: The car won’t start: I need to call a tow truck.

additional_notes: Used for paying in shops/restaurants or online. Often said with the article: "la carta di credito". In Italy you may also hear "carta" alone when the context is clear, and "pagare con la carta" = "to pay by card".
target_language_example: Posso pagare con la carta di credito?
native_language_example: Can I pay with a credit card?

additional_notes: Common everyday item; you’ll see it on shopping lists and in bathrooms. Also said as “carta da bagno” or “carta toilette” in some contexts. In a store you might ask: “Dov’è la carta igienica?” (“Where is the toilet paper?”).
target_language_example: Scusi, dov’è la carta igienica?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the toilet paper?

additional_notes: Common everyday term for an animated TV show, film, or cartoon in general. Plural: "cartoni animati". Often used with "guardare" (to watch): "Guardo i cartoni animati" = "I watch cartoons."
target_language_example: Da bambino guardavo spesso i cartoni animati in TV.
native_language_example: As a child I often watched cartoons on TV.

meaning: a very vulgar intensifier meaning “fucking / damn” (used like “that fucking …”).
additional_notes: Very common in spoken Italian but highly offensive/vulgar (literally refers to “dick”). Used before a noun to show anger, annoyance, or emphasis: “quel cazzo di …” = “that fucking …”. Avoid in polite situations; a milder alternative is “accidenti” or “quel maledetto …”.
target_language_example: Non trovo le chiavi di quel cazzo di motorino!
native_language_example: I can’t find the keys to that fucking scooter!

additional_notes: Used in construction/engineering to refer to concrete strengthened with steel (rebar). In Italian you’ll often see it abbreviated as “c.a.” in building plans or descriptions (e.g., “struttura in c.a.”).
target_language_example: Il palazzo è costruito in cemento armato.
native_language_example: The building is made of reinforced concrete.

additional_notes: Common term for a large indoor/outdoor complex with many stores (often with restaurants and a supermarket). You can use it with articles: "il centro commerciale" (the mall) or "un centro commerciale" (a mall). Often used with "andare al" (to go to the): "andare al centro commerciale".
target_language_example: Sabato andiamo al centro commerciale a comprare un regalo.
native_language_example: On Saturday we’re going to the mall to buy a gift.

meaning: “what’s wrong?” / “what’s the matter?”; also “what is there?”
additional_notes: Common in speech. Often short for “Che cosa c’è?” or “Cosa c’è?”. Used to ask what the problem is (Che c’è? = What’s up/What’s wrong?) or what is present/available (Che c’è in frigo? = What’s in the fridge?). Can also appear in phrases like “Che c’è da fare?” (What is there to do?) and “Che c’è di nuovo?” (What’s new?).
target_language_example: Che c’è? Ti vedo preoccupato.
native_language_example: What’s wrong? You look worried.

additional_notes: A very strong, vulgar exclamation used to show anger, shock, or frustration. Often said as a standalone reaction (“Che cazzo!”) or in questions like “Che cazzo fai?” (“What the fuck are you doing?”). Avoid in polite conversation; use milder alternatives like “che diavolo…?”, “che cavolo…?”, or “ma che…?” instead.
target_language_example: Che cazzo fai?
native_language_example: What the fuck are you doing?

additional_notes: Used to say something doesn’t take much effort, often to reassure someone or downplay how hard a task is. It can sound a bit dismissive depending on tone. Literally “what does it take (to do it)?”; often said as a rhetorical question. You may also hear: “Che ci vuole a…?” + infinitive (e.g., “Che ci vuole a farlo?” = “How hard can it be to do it?”).
target_language_example: Dai, che ci vuole: in dieci minuti è pronto!
native_language_example: Come on, it’s easy— it’ll be ready in ten minutes.

additional_notes: Used to ask “what?” in direct questions (Che cosa vuoi?) and indirect questions (Non so che cosa dire.). It’s slightly more explicit than just “che?” or “cosa?” and can sound a bit more emphatic depending on tone. Often followed by a verb: “Che cosa fai?” = “What are you doing?”
target_language_example: Che cosa vuoi mangiare?
native_language_example: What do you want to eat?

additional_notes: An exclamation used to show surprise, annoyance, or impatience, often in questions. Stronger than plain “che…?” but generally less vulgar than “che cazzo…?”. Can be used alone (“Che diavolo!”) or before a question word/verb (“Che diavolo fai?”).
target_language_example: Che diavolo stai facendo?
native_language_example: What the hell are you doing?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the fate or whereabouts of someone or something that’s disappeared, been lost, or hasn’t been seen/heard about in a while. Often followed by a noun or name: “Che fine ha fatto Marco?” or by “il/la/lo …”: “Che fine ha fatto il mio libro?”. You can also use it alone if the context is clear.
target_language_example: Che fine ha fatto il mio cellulare? Non lo trovo più.
native_language_example: What happened to my phone? I can’t find it anymore.

additional_notes: Common question to ask for the current time. Often used as "Che ore sono?" as well (very common and sometimes preferred). You can add "Scusa" or "Mi scusi" to be more polite: "Scusa, che ora è?" / "Mi scusi, che ora è?".
target_language_example: Scusa, che ora è?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what time is it?

additional_notes: A common way to ask for the current time. Literally “what hours are (they),” so it uses plural "sono" even though English uses singular. Often followed by "Sono le..." (for most times) or "È l’una" (for 1:00). You can add "Scusa" or "Mi scusi" to be more polite.
target_language_example: Scusa, che ore sono?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what time is it?

additional_notes: Very informal and mildly vulgar expression used to complain that something is boring, annoying, or a hassle. Literally refers to “balls” (testicles), so avoid in formal settings or with strangers. You can also hear it as just “Palle!” or “Che palle!” as a standalone reaction.
target_language_example: Che palle, dobbiamo aspettare ancora mezz’ora!
native_language_example: What a pain, we have to wait another half hour!

meaning: “what a thing!” / “what stuff!” (expresses surprise, disapproval, or disbelief).
additional_notes: Common in spoken Italian as an exclamation reacting to a situation, story, or object (often with a negative or puzzled tone, but it can also be amused). It’s similar to “what a mess/what the heck” depending on tone. Can be followed by a clause: “Che roba che…”.
target_language_example: Che roba! Non mi aspettavo una cosa del genere.
native_language_example: What a thing! I wasn’t expecting something like that.

additional_notes: Colloquial/regional way of saying standard Italian “che faresti?” or “che cosa faresti?”. Here “te” is an informal/regional form of “ti” (“you”), and “farebbi” is a regional variant of the conditional “faresti” (“you would do”). Used to ask what someone would do in a hypothetical situation.
target_language_example: Se vincessi alla lotteria, che te farebbi?
native_language_example: If you won the lottery, what would you do?

meaning: “What’s gotten into you?” / “What’s wrong with you?”
additional_notes: Used (often as a question: “Che ti prende?”) to express surprise or annoyance at someone’s sudden behavior or mood change. It’s fairly colloquial and can sound a bit confrontational depending on tone. Also common: “Che ti prende oggi?” (“What’s gotten into you today?”).
target_language_example: Che ti prende? Sei nervoso da stamattina.
native_language_example: What’s gotten into you? You’ve been nervous since this morning.

additional_notes: Used to ask about an event or problem affecting someone. The verb is in the past (“è successo” = “happened”), but in conversation it often means “What happened?” or “What’s the matter?” depending on context. More informal variants: “Che è successo?” (What happened?) or “Che ti è preso?” (What’s gotten into you?).
target_language_example: Ti vedo preoccupato: che ti è successo?
native_language_example: You look worried: what happened to you?

meaning: check-in (registration for a flight or at a hotel).
additional_notes: Used as an English loanword in Italian, especially for travel. Common patterns: "fare il check-in" (to check in) and "il check-in" (the check-in). In more formal contexts you may also see "registrazione" (registration/check-in).
target_language_example: Dobbiamo fare il check-in online prima del volo.
native_language_example: We have to check in online before the flight.

additional_notes: A strong, confrontational question used to scold someone who is acting arrogant, rude, or overstepping boundaries. It’s usually said in anger or disbelief. Often followed by a complaint, e.g., “Chi ti credi di essere per parlarmi così?”
target_language_example: Chi ti credi di essere per dirmi cosa devo fare?
native_language_example: Who do you think you are to tell me what I have to do?

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unspecified person or people in a general way (like English “whoever…” or “those who…”). Often appears in sayings/proverbs, e.g., “Chi vive vedrà” (“Time will tell,” literally “Who lives will see”).
target_language_example: Chi vive vedrà.
native_language_example: Time will tell.

meaning: to ask for someone’s hand (to ask to marry them / to propose).
additional_notes: A fixed expression used when someone asks a person (or traditionally their family/parents) for permission to marry. It’s formal/traditional in tone. Often used with “a qualcuno” (to someone) and “di qualcuno” (of someone): “chiedere la mano a Maria” or “chiedere la mano di Maria (ai suoi genitori)”.
target_language_example: Ha chiesto la mano di Giulia ai suoi genitori.
native_language_example: He asked Giulia’s parents for her hand in marriage.

additional_notes: Used for doors, windows, cars, etc. You’ll often hear it in the imperative (Chiudi a chiave!) or with an object pronoun: Chiudila a chiave. The opposite is aprire (a chiave) = to unlock/open (with a key).
target_language_example: Prima di uscire, chiudi la porta a chiave.
native_language_example: Before going out, lock the door.

meaning: to shut up (telling someone to stop talking).
additional_notes: Informal and rude/insulting. Literally means “to close the beak,” comparing someone to a bird. Used to order someone to be quiet; in polite situations, prefer “stai zitto/a” (still informal) or “per favore, puoi fare silenzio?”.
target_language_example: Chiudi il becco e ascolta un attimo!
native_language_example: Shut up and listen for a moment!

meaning: "Of course!" / "Sure!" (to strongly agree or say something is obvious).
additional_notes: Used mainly in spoken Italian to respond politely and emphatically, often meaning “certainly” or “no problem.” You’ll also hear the longer form “ci mancherebbe altro,” which is even stronger. It can answer requests (“Can you help?”) or confirm statements (“You’re coming, right?”).
target_language_example: Mi dai una mano? — Ci mancherebbe!
native_language_example: Can you give me a hand? — Of course!

meaning: “I’ll take care of it.” / “I’ll handle it.”
additional_notes: Used to offer to deal with a task or problem yourself, often to reassure someone. Literally “I’ll think about it,” but in everyday Italian it usually means you’ll take responsibility and sort it out. You can stress the subject with “io” (as here) to mean “I’ll do it (not you).”
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: ci penso io a chiamare il taxi.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’ll take care of calling the taxi.

additional_notes: Used when a problem or annoying situation is happening again, often with frustration or irony. Common in spoken Italian; you can also add a colon after it to introduce what’s happening again (e.g., “Ci risiamo: …”).
target_language_example: Ci risiamo: hai perso di nuovo il telefono.
native_language_example: Here we go again: you’ve lost your phone again.

meaning: "See you" / "we’ll see each other" (said when saying goodbye).
additional_notes: Common, friendly way to end a conversation. Literally means “we see each other” (ci = “each other/us,” vediamo = “we see”). Often used on its own, or with a time/place: "Ci vediamo domani" (see you tomorrow), "Ci vediamo alle 8" (see you at 8).
target_language_example: Ok, grazie! Ci vediamo domani.
native_language_example: OK, thanks! See you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to talk about duration or time. Very common in phrases like “tra cinque minuti” (in five minutes), “fra cinque minuti” (same), “ancora cinque minuti” (five more minutes), and “solo cinque minuti” (just five minutes).
target_language_example: Arrivo tra cinque minuti.
native_language_example: I’ll be there in five minutes.

additional_notes: Used for the seat belt in a car (and sometimes other vehicles). You’ll often hear it in safety instructions or reminders: "Metti la cintura di sicurezza" / "Allaccia la cintura". Plural: "cinture di sicurezza".
target_language_example: Prima di partire, metti la cintura di sicurezza.
native_language_example: Before leaving, put on your seat belt.

additional_notes: Common drink ordered at a bar/café, especially in winter. Often thicker than American hot chocolate. You may also see it as "cioccolata calda densa" (thick) or "una cioccolata calda, per favore" when ordering.
target_language_example: Vorrei una cioccolata calda, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a hot chocolate, please.

meaning: a vicious circle (a self-reinforcing negative cycle).
additional_notes: Used to describe a situation where a problem causes more of the same problem, making it hard to break the cycle. Common in everyday speech and in more formal contexts (news, psychology, economics). Often used with verbs like "entrare in" (to get into) and "uscire da" (to get out of).
target_language_example: È un circolo vizioso: più mi stressavo, meno dormivo, e più ero stressato.
native_language_example: It’s a vicious circle: the more I stressed, the less I slept, and the more stressed I was.

additional_notes: Very vulgar slang (literally refers to “dick”); use only with close friends or in very informal contexts, and avoid in polite/company/work situations. Often used alone as an exclamation (“Col cazzo!”) or in the structure “E col cazzo che + verb…” to mean “There’s no way that…” / “As if I’m going to…”.
target_language_example: —Mi presti la macchina stasera? —Col cazzo!
native_language_example: “Will you lend me the car tonight?” “No fucking way!”

meaning: “with time”; “over time / as time goes by.”
additional_notes: Contraction of "con il tempo" ("with the time"). Used to say that something changes or becomes true gradually as time passes. Common with verbs like "migliorare" (to improve), "cambiare" (to change), "capire" (to understand).
target_language_example: Col tempo, tutto diventa più facile.
native_language_example: Over time, everything becomes easier.

meaning: a stroke of luck; a lucky break.
additional_notes: Used to talk about an unexpected piece of good luck that helps you. Often with verbs like "avere" (to have) or "essere" (to be): "Ho avuto un colpo di fortuna" = "I had a lucky break."
target_language_example: Ho trovato l’ultimo biglietto: che colpo di fortuna!
native_language_example: I found the last ticket: what a stroke of luck!

meaning: coup d’état (a sudden overthrow of a government).
additional_notes: Used in politics/news to describe an illegal or forceful seizure of power, often by the military or a group within the state. Very common in headlines: "tentato colpo di stato" (attempted coup), "fare un colpo di stato" (to stage a coup).
target_language_example: Il governo ha denunciato un tentato colpo di stato.
native_language_example: The government denounced an attempted coup d’état.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase for the general-purpose knife used for preparing food in the kitchen. Literally “knife for kitchen” (coltello = knife; da = for/for use in; cucina = kitchen). You can use it with articles and adjectives: un coltello da cucina, il coltello da cucina, un buon coltello da cucina.
target_language_example: Mi serve un coltello da cucina per tagliare le verdure.
native_language_example: I need a kitchen knife to cut the vegetables.

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason for something, often with surprise or curiosity. It’s common in conversation and usually sounds a bit more natural/less formal than "perché?". You can also use it inside a longer question (e.g., "Come mai non vieni?").
target_language_example: Come mai sei in ritardo?
native_language_example: How come you’re late?

additional_notes: Common in spoken Italian as an emphatic way to agree. Tone is crucial: said warmly it means genuine agreement (“of course”); said with irony or a certain intonation it can mean disbelief (“yeah, right/as if”). You may also see it as a question: “Come no?” = “Why not?” / “How could it be otherwise?”.
target_language_example: —Mi dai una mano? —Come no!
native_language_example: —Can you give me a hand? —Of course!

additional_notes: Used to express strong shock, disapproval, or anger at what someone did or said. It’s addressed directly to someone (singular “tu”). You may also hear it as a question or exclamation: “Come osi?” / “Come osi!”. Often followed by an infinitive: “Come osi parlare così?” (“How dare you talk like that?”).
target_language_example: Come osi parlarmi così?
native_language_example: How dare you speak to me like that?

meaning: like before; as it was before.
additional_notes: Used to say something is the same as it was previously, or to ask/hope that things return to their previous state. Common after a change or problem: "Tutto è tornato come prima" (everything went back to normal). It can also be used in requests: "Facciamo come prima" (let’s do it the way we did before).
target_language_example: Dopo l’aggiornamento, il telefono funziona come prima.
native_language_example: After the update, the phone works like before.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an unreal, hypothetical, or doubtful situation, often followed by the imperfect subjunctive (congiuntivo imperfetto): "come se fossi..." (as if I were...). It can also be used more neutrally for comparisons that aren’t necessarily unreal, depending on context.
target_language_example: Mi parla come se non mi conoscesse.
native_language_example: He talks to me as if he didn’t know me.

additional_notes: From the verb chiamarsi (“to be called”). Used to ask someone’s name (often followed by “Lei” for formal or “tu” for informal: Come si chiama Lei? / Come ti chiami?) or to ask the name of something: Come si chiama questa cosa?
target_language_example: Scusi, come si chiama?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what’s your name?

additional_notes: Used to say something is done correctly, in a proper way, often implying a standard or expectation (e.g., a meal, job, greeting, apology). It can describe an action (“fare qualcosa come si deve”) or a person/thing (“una cena come si deve” = a proper meal). Sometimes used with a mildly critical tone if something was not done well.
target_language_example: Voglio una cena come si deve, non un panino al volo.
native_language_example: I want a proper dinner, not a quick sandwich.

meaning: “How are you?” (formal/polite; literally “How are you doing?”).
additional_notes: Used with Lei (formal “you”) when speaking politely to someone you don’t know well, someone older, or in professional settings. In informal speech with friends you usually say come stai. Common replies: Bene, grazie. / Così così. / Non c’è male.
target_language_example: Buongiorno, signora. Come sta?
native_language_example: Good morning, ma’am. How are you?

meaning: How are you? (informal; to one person).
additional_notes: Common greeting using the verb "stare" (to be/feel). Use with friends, family, or people you’re on first-name terms with. More formal/polite: "Come sta?" (to one person) or "Come state?" (to more than one person). Common replies: "Bene, grazie" (Good, thanks), "Così così" (So-so), "Non c’è male" (Not bad), "Male" (Bad).
target_language_example: Ciao! Come stai?
native_language_example: Hi! How are you?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s name when speaking to one person you address with tu (friends, peers, kids). Literally “how do you call yourself.” For a more formal/polite version use: “Come si chiama?” You can answer with: “Mi chiamo …” (My name is …).
target_language_example: Ciao! Come ti chiami?
native_language_example: Hi! What’s your name?

additional_notes: Used to leave the choice to the other person (“it’s up to you”). It can sound neutral and polite, but depending on tone it may also sound dismissive (similar to “whatever you want” or “suit yourself”). Common with verbs like fare/decidere: “Fai/decidi come ti pare.”
target_language_example: Andiamo al cinema o a cena? Come ti pare.
native_language_example: Shall we go to the movies or to dinner? Whatever you prefer.

additional_notes: Very common, informal-friendly greeting. Often followed by “bene” (good), “così così” (so-so), or “non c’è male” (not bad). You can also add “Come va?” as a quick check-in with friends, colleagues, or people you’ve just met.
target_language_example: Ciao! Come va?
native_language_example: Hi! How’s it going?

additional_notes: Used for a male roommate; for a female roommate you’ll often hear "compagna di stanza" or "coinquilina" (f.). You can also use it for someone you share a room with temporarily (e.g., in a dorm, hospital, or on a trip), not only in an apartment. Plural: "compagni di stanza".
target_language_example: Il mio compagno di stanza russa, quindi dormo male.
native_language_example: My roommate snores, so I sleep badly.

additional_notes: Used to express sincere feelings (thanks, apologies, good wishes, affection). It often refers to the speaker’s feelings, but you can also say it generally (e.g., "Ti auguro... con tutto il cuore"). In English it’s close to “from the bottom of my heart.”
target_language_example: Ti ringrazio con tutto il cuore per il tuo aiuto.
native_language_example: I thank you with all my heart for your help.

additional_notes: Common in everyday banking. In Italy, a conto corrente is the standard account used for daily transactions (deposits, payments, direct debits, salary). Often shortened to "conto" in context. You may see related phrases like "aprire un conto corrente" (open an account) and "numero di conto" (account number).
target_language_example: Vorrei aprire un conto corrente.
native_language_example: I’d like to open a bank account.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the money account you have at a bank. More commonly you’ll hear "conto in banca" without the preposition: "conto in banca" or simply "conto" in context; and especially "conto in banca" is less common than "conto corrente" (current/checking account).
target_language_example: Ho un conto in banca, ma non ho ancora un conto corrente qui in Italia.
native_language_example: I have a bank account, but I don’t have a checking account here in Italy yet.

meaning: to have someone’s back; to cover for someone.
additional_notes: Used figuratively to mean protecting or supporting someone, especially in a risky situation, or helping them by taking responsibility/blame. Often appears with an indirect object pronoun: “coprirmi le spalle” (have my back), “coprirti le spalle” (have your back), “coprirgli/le le spalle” (have his/her back).
target_language_example: Tranquillo, ti copro le spalle io.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ve got your back.

additional_notes: A standard, polite closing in formal emails and letters. Very common in Italian business and professional writing. You can also see variants like “Distinti saluti” (more formal) or “Un cordiale saluto” (singular, slightly less formal).
target_language_example: La ringrazio per la Sua disponibilità. Cordiali saluti, Marco Rossi
native_language_example: Thank you for your availability. Kind regards, Marco Rossi

meaning: to run after; to chase; (figuratively) to pursue someone/something.
additional_notes: Often used with a direct object (correre dietro a qualcuno/qualcosa). Literally it’s “to run behind,” but in everyday Italian it usually means “to chase after” or “to go after,” both physically and in a figurative sense (e.g., pursuing a goal or trying to get someone’s attention).
target_language_example: Non correre dietro ai soldi: pensa a quello che ti rende felice.
native_language_example: Don’t chase money: think about what makes you happy.

meaning: to run the risk (of); to risk (doing something).
additional_notes: Used to say there is a danger or possibility of a bad outcome. Commonly followed by "di" + infinitive: "correre il rischio di perdere...". You can also specify what you risk with "di" + noun: "correre il rischio di un incidente". Often used in warnings or advice.
target_language_example: Se esci senza ombrello, corri il rischio di bagnarti.
native_language_example: If you go out without an umbrella, you run the risk of getting wet.

additional_notes: Used to express surprise, frustration, or disbelief, often in questions: “Cosa diavolo fai?” It’s informal and can sound rude, especially with strangers or in formal situations. A milder alternative is “che diavolo” or more neutral “che cosa…?”
target_language_example: Cosa diavolo stai facendo?
native_language_example: What the hell are you doing?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a purpose or intended result. Common with the subjunctive when the subject changes or the meaning is purpose/necessity (e.g., "così che tu possa..."); it can also be used with the indicative to express a result/consequence (often like "so... that"). Similar to "in modo che".
target_language_example: Parlo lentamente così che tu possa capire.
native_language_example: I speak slowly so that you can understand.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re feeling or doing only okay/average, often as a brief answer to “Come stai?” or “Com’è andata?”. It can also describe something that’s mediocre (e.g., a movie or meal). Tone is casual but not rude.
target_language_example: —Come stai? —Così così, oggi sono un po’ stanco.
native_language_example: —How are you? —So-so, today I’m a bit tired.

meaning: 'so-called' (used to indicate a name/label is not exact, is disputed, or is used ironically).
additional_notes: Often written as one word: "cosiddetto". It usually comes before a noun ("il cosiddetto esperto" = "the so-called expert"). It agrees in gender and number: cosiddetto/cosiddetta/cosiddetti/cosiddette. Can be neutral (a commonly used label) or skeptical/ironic depending on tone/context.
target_language_example: Non mi fido del così detto esperto che hanno chiamato.
native_language_example: I don’t trust the so-called expert they called.

additional_notes: A formal/solemn expression meaning “let it be so,” often used at the end of a statement, agreement, or wish. Common in religious or ceremonial contexts; in everyday speech, Italians more often say “va bene” (“okay”) or “amen” in explicitly religious contexts.
target_language_example: Hai deciso di partire domani? Così sia.
native_language_example: Have you decided to leave tomorrow? So be it.

additional_notes: Common term for lotion/cream you put on your skin to protect from the sun. You’ll often see it in beach or pharmacy contexts. You can also say “protezione solare”; on bottles you may see “SPF” as “SPF” or “fattore di protezione (solare)”.
target_language_example: Hai messo la crema solare?
native_language_example: Did you put on sunscreen?

additional_notes: Used for a small cube of ice, especially in drinks. You’ll often hear it in bars/restaurants when asking for ice in a beverage. Plural: "cubetti di ghiaccio".
target_language_example: Mi può portare un bicchiere d’acqua con due cubetti di ghiaccio, per favore?
native_language_example: Could you bring me a glass of water with two ice cubes, please?

meaning: 'to throw away' / 'to be thrown away' (for something to discard).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean it should be discarded because it’s useless, broken, or expired: “cose da buttare” (things to throw away). Common in everyday contexts (trash, old items, spoiled food). Similar structure to “da + infinitive” = “to be + past participle / to + verb” in English.
target_language_example: Questi yogurt sono scaduti: sono da buttare.
native_language_example: These yogurts are expired: they should be thrown away.

additional_notes: Colloquial expression used after a noun or after phrases like “fa”/“è” to say something is done in a very poor way. Often implies something is sloppy or unacceptable: “un lavoro da cani” (a lousy job), “guidare da cani” (to drive terribly). Literally “of dogs,” but used figuratively.
target_language_example: Ho fatto un lavoro da cani e devo rifarlo.
native_language_example: I did a terrible job and I have to do it again.

meaning: from the beginning; again from the start.
additional_notes: Common in music and performance directions (often written “D.C.”) meaning to repeat from the start. In everyday Italian it can also mean restarting or starting over: “ricominciare da capo.”
target_language_example: Se non ti è chiaro, te lo spiego da capo.
native_language_example: If it isn’t clear to you, I’ll explain it again from the beginning.

additional_notes: Colloquial intensifier used after verbs/adjectives to emphasize a strong degree: e.g., “mi piace da dio” = “I like it a lot / it’s awesome,” “sto da dio” = “I feel great.” It’s informal and not usually translated word-for-word (literally it contains “God,” but it’s mainly used as emphasis).
target_language_example: Questo gelato è da dio!
native_language_example: This ice cream is awesome!

meaning: “Where does it come from?” / “Where is it from?”
additional_notes: Used to ask the origin or source of something. Literally “from where (it) comes.” With people, you’ll usually ask “Da dove vieni?” (informal) or “Da dove viene?” (formal, to one person using Lei). You can also specify the subject: “Da dove viene questo?” (Where does this come from?).
target_language_example: Scusi, da dove viene questo formaggio?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where does this cheese come from?

meaning: “Where are you from?” / “Where do you come from?”
additional_notes: Common question when meeting someone. Literally “from where you come”; uses informal singular “tu” (vieni). Polite form: “Da dove viene?” (Lei). You can answer with “Vengo da…” (I’m from…).
target_language_example: Ciao! Da dove vieni?
native_language_example: Hi! Where are you from?

meaning: 'to do' / 'to be done' (something that needs doing).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean it needs to be done (e.g., "cose da fare" = "things to do"). Often appears in lists, plans, and reminders. With "avere" it can express obligations: "Ho molto da fare" = "I have a lot to do". With "essere" it can mean "to be done": "C'è ancora molto da fare" = "There's still a lot to do."
target_language_example: Oggi ho tante cose da fare.
native_language_example: Today I have lots of things to do.

meaning: when I grow up; as an adult.
additional_notes: Used to talk about what you will do in the future when you are older, or to refer to yourself/others in adulthood. Common with the verb "fare" to say what job you want ("Da grande farò..."). You can also use it more generally to mean "as an adult" (e.g., "Da grande ho capito...").
target_language_example: Da grande voglio fare il medico.
native_language_example: When I grow up, I want to be a doctor.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something as extremely unpleasant, stressful, chaotic, or scary (e.g., una giornata/una situazione/una fila da incubo). Literally “from (a) nightmare,” but in English you usually say “a nightmare” or “nightmarish.”
target_language_example: Ho avuto una giornata da incubo al lavoro.
native_language_example: I had a nightmare of a day at work.

additional_notes: Used after adjectives or verbs to mean “extremely/very” or “a lot,” often in casual speech. Common with feelings or reactions: stanco da morire (dead tired), annoiarsi da morire (be bored to death), ridere da morire (laugh a lot), paura da morire (terrified).
target_language_example: Sono stanco da morire.
native_language_example: I’m dead tired.

meaning: nowhere; from nowhere (not from any place).
additional_notes: Used to say something/someone is in no place, is going to no place, or comes from no known place. Often appears with verbs like andare (to go), essere (to be), trovare (to find), venire (to come): “Non vado da nessuna parte” = “I’m not going anywhere.”
target_language_example: Non riesco a trovare le chiavi da nessuna parte.
native_language_example: I can’t find the keys anywhere.

meaning: aside; on one side; set aside (often in phrases like mettere/lasciare da parte).
additional_notes: Commonly used to mean "aside" in everyday situations: putting something to the side (physically) or saving/reserving something (money, time, an object). Very often appears with verbs like "mettere da parte" (to put aside/save) and "lasciare da parte" (to leave aside/put aside, also figuratively: to drop a topic). Can also mean "from" someone/somewhere in expressions like "da parte di" (by/on the part of).
target_language_example: Metti da parte un po' di soldi per le vacanze.
native_language_example: Put aside/save a bit of money for the vacation.

additional_notes: Used to show who does something or who a message/feeling/action comes from. Often follows a noun: "un messaggio da parte di..." (a message from...). Similar in meaning to "da" in many cases, but "da parte di" is a bit more explicit/formal about the source/agent. Not typically translated word-for-word as "from part of" in English.
target_language_example: Ho ricevuto una chiamata da parte di Marco.
native_language_example: I received a call from Marco.

meaning: when I was little / as a child.
additional_notes: Used to talk about what someone was like or used to do in childhood. It can change for gender/number: da piccolo (male, singular), da piccola (female, singular), da piccoli/da piccole (plural). Often used at the start of a sentence or after the subject: “Io, da piccolo, …”.
target_language_example: Da piccolo andavo spesso al mare con i miei nonni.
native_language_example: When I was little, I often went to the seaside with my grandparents.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened not long ago (often with the present tense): "Sono qui da poco" = "I’ve only been here a short time." Can also be used with "è/era" to mean someone/something is "of little value/poor quality" (more judgmental): "È una persona da poco".
target_language_example: Sono arrivato da poco.
native_language_example: I arrived recently.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to dismiss it as not worth much (e.g., "un film da quattro soldi"). Literally "of four coins," but it’s an idiomatic way to say something is lousy or second-rate; it can sound insulting depending on tone.
target_language_example: Non voglio comprare un telefono da quattro soldi.
native_language_example: I don’t want to buy a cheap, low-quality phone.

meaning: always; for as long as I can remember.
additional_notes: Used to say something has been true from a very long time ago up to now. It often appears with the present tense (or present perfect) and works like “since always.” You can also use it for habits/preferences ("L'ho sempre fatto" / "Lo faccio da sempre").
target_language_example: Vivo qui da sempre.
native_language_example: I've lived here forever / as long as I can remember.

meaning: evening; for the evening (e.g., evening wear).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something meant for the evening, especially in set phrases like "abito da sera" (evening dress) or "scarpe da sera" (evening shoes). It can also contrast with "da giorno" (daytime). Often implies something more elegant/formal.
target_language_example: Per la cena di gala serve un abito da sera.
native_language_example: For the gala dinner you need an evening dress.

additional_notes: Used to say you are doing something alone or independently. It agrees with the subject: **da solo** (male), **da sola** (female), **da soli/da sole** (plural). Often comes after the verb: *Vado da solo*, *L’ho fatto da solo* (“I did it myself”).
target_language_example: Vado al cinema da solo.
native_language_example: I’m going to the movies alone.

additional_notes: Used to indicate the direction or position an action comes from (e.g., looking, pulling, coming) beneath something. Often paired with verbs like guardare (to look), prendere/tirare (to take/pull), or sbucare (to pop out). Can also be used in phrases like "di sotto" (downstairs/below) and "da sotto in su" (from the bottom up), but "da sotto" specifically emphasizes the source/direction.
target_language_example: Guarda da sotto il tavolo: le chiavi sono lì.
native_language_example: Look under the table: the keys are there.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does something alone/independently. Common with verbs like stare/essere (to be), fare (to do), andare (to go), rimanere (to stay). It can also mean “to oneself” in expressions like parlare da sé (“to talk to oneself”).
target_language_example: Preferisco andare da sé.
native_language_example: I prefer to go by myself.

meaning: pocket-sized; for carrying in your pocket.
additional_notes: Used after a noun (or in phrases like “versione da tasca”) to describe something small, portable, or a travel/pocket edition. Common with books, dictionaries, notebooks, tools, and guides. Similar to “tascabile” (pocket-sized).
target_language_example: Hai una guida da tasca di Roma?
native_language_example: Do you have a pocket guide to Rome?

meaning: for a long time; for some time (already).
additional_notes: Used to say something has been true or happening for a while, often with the present tense: "Lo conosco da tempo" = "I’ve known him for a long time." It can also mean "already" in the sense of "for some time now": "È da tempo che..." = "It’s been a long time/some time that..." Often contrasts with "da poco" (recently).
target_language_example: Vivo qui da tempo.
native_language_example: I’ve been living here for a long time.

meaning: for ages; for a long time (lit. “for a lifetime”).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something has been happening (or hasn’t happened) for a very long time. Often with the present tense for ongoing situations (e.g., “Non lo vedo da una vita”) or with the passato prossimo to mean “it’s been ages since…” in English. Common in everyday speech; not rude.
target_language_example: Non ci vediamo da una vita!
native_language_example: We haven’t seen each other in ages!

additional_notes: Used to say you are physically near something/someone to see, observe, or experience it better. Often follows verbs like vedere (to see), guardare (to look at), osservare (to observe), conoscere (to get to know): “vedere/guardare da vicino.”
target_language_example: Vorrei vedere il quadro da vicino.
native_language_example: I’d like to see the painting up close.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re beginning at the starting point, with no previous progress or knowledge. Common with verbs like partire, cominciare, iniziare, ricominciare, and also in learning contexts (e.g., livello da zero). Often paired with a destination or goal: “da zero a …”.
target_language_example: Ho iniziato a studiare l’italiano da zero.
native_language_example: I started studying Italian from zero (from scratch).

meaning: Go for it! / Give it your all!
additional_notes: Informal encouragement to do something with energy or intensity (work, studying, sports, dancing, etc.). It’s the imperative of “darci dentro” and is often said to a friend: “Come on, push harder!”
target_language_example: Dai, dacci dentro: dobbiamo finire entro stasera!
native_language_example: Come on, give it your all: we have to finish by tonight!

additional_notes: Used to say something appears/happens suddenly or unexpectedly. Often comes after verbs like "apparire" (to appear), "spuntare" (to pop up), "uscire" (to come out), "arrivare" (to arrive), or "venire" (to come). It’s also used in a more literal sense meaning “from nothing,” especially in phrases like "creare dal nulla" (to create from nothing).
target_language_example: È spuntato dal nulla e mi ha spaventato.
native_language_example: He popped up out of nowhere and scared me.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens with a real audience or face-to-face, rather than recorded, streamed, or virtual. Common with events and performances: "concerto dal vivo" (live concert), "musica dal vivo" (live music). You can also use it about meeting someone: "vederti dal vivo" = to see you in person.
target_language_example: Preferisco vedere il concerto dal vivo.
native_language_example: I prefer to see the concert live (in person).

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to mean that something comes from someone’s own perspective/experience/side: e.g. dalla propria esperienza (“from one’s own experience”), dalla propria vita (“from one’s own life”). It’s made of da + la (= dalla) + propria (possessive adjective). The possessive agrees with the noun that follows (proprio/propria/propri/proprie).
target_language_example: Ognuno parla dalla propria esperienza.
native_language_example: Everyone speaks from their own experience.

meaning: to go for it; to put a lot of effort in (give it your all).
additional_notes: Informal, encouraging expression. Often used as an imperative: "Dacci dentro!" = “Come on, go for it!” / “Put your back into it!” The "ci" refers to what you’re working on (studying, training, a project), and "dentro" adds the idea of really getting into it. Common with "con" + activity: "darci dentro con lo studio / con gli allenamenti".
target_language_example: Dai, dacci dentro con lo studio se vuoi passare l’esame.
native_language_example: Come on, really put effort into studying if you want to pass the exam.

meaning: to go to someone’s head (e.g., alcohol, success).
additional_notes: Used when something affects your head/mind and makes you feel dizzy, drunk, or behave differently (often more arrogant or overconfident). Common with alcohol: "L’alcol mi dà alla testa" = "Alcohol goes to my head." Can also refer to fame/success: "Il successo gli ha dato alla testa" = "Success has gone to his head."
target_language_example: Basta un bicchiere di vino e mi dà alla testa.
native_language_example: Just one glass of wine and it goes to my head.

meaning: 'to listen to' (to pay attention to someone/something).
additional_notes: Used to mean listening seriously or taking someone’s advice/words into account. Often followed by "a" + person/thing: "dare ascolto a qualcuno/qualcosa". Common in phrases like "Non dare ascolto" (= don’t listen to / don’t pay attention to).
target_language_example: Non dare ascolto a quello che dice: non è vero.
native_language_example: Don’t listen to what he says: it isn’t true.

additional_notes: Informal. Literally “to give five.” Used when you want to celebrate, congratulate, or agree with someone by slapping palms (a “high five”). You can also say: “Dammi cinque!” (“Give me five!”).
target_language_example: Ce l’abbiamo fatta: dai cinque!
native_language_example: We did it: high five!

meaning: to go crazy; to freak out; to lose it.
additional_notes: Common idiom used when someone suddenly loses control, panics, or behaves irrationally. Often used in the past tense (ha dato di matto) or with "sto per" to say you’re about to lose it. Not literal in English (it doesn’t mean “to give as crazy”).
target_language_example: Quando ho visto il conto, ho dato di matto.
native_language_example: When I saw the bill, I freaked out.

meaning: to set fire (to); to burn down.
additional_notes: Used with a direct object, often introduced by "a" ("dare fuoco a + noun"). Common in news/crime contexts for arson. Literal idea is “to give fire,” but in English you normally say “set fire to.”
target_language_example: Hanno dato fuoco alla macchina.
native_language_example: They set the car on fire.

meaning: to be out of your mind; to talk nonsense.
additional_notes: Informal idiom used to say someone is acting crazy, exaggerating, or saying things that don’t make sense (often in frustration: “Ma dai, stai dando i numeri!”). It can refer to temporary behavior rather than a serious mental condition.
target_language_example: Con tutto questo stress sto dando i numeri.
native_language_example: With all this stress I’m going out of my mind.

meaning: to do your best; to give your best.
additional_notes: Used to say you will try as hard as you can, or that someone performed at their highest level. Often appears with “di sé” (dare il meglio di sé = to give your best) and can be conjugated: do/dai/dà il meglio; ho dato il meglio.
target_language_example: Domani darò il meglio di me all’esame.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’ll do my best on the exam.

additional_notes: Often used with the preposition "a": "dare la caccia a qualcuno/qualcosa" = to hunt/chase someone or something (literally “to give the hunt”). Can describe literal hunting (animals) or a figurative pursuit (criminals, an idea, success). Similar to "cacciare" in meaning, but this phrase emphasizes the pursuit.
target_language_example: La polizia sta dando la caccia al ladro.
native_language_example: The police are hunting/chasing the thief.

meaning: to give someone a hand; to help.
additional_notes: Common in everyday Italian. It can mean literally offering your hand (e.g., to greet, to help someone stand up), and more generally helping someone with a task. Often used with an indirect object pronoun: "dammi una mano" = "give me a hand".
target_language_example: Mi dai una mano con queste valigie?
native_language_example: Can you give me a hand with these suitcases?

additional_notes: Used with an adjective or noun to mean you consider/assume something is true (often without proof, sometimes mistakenly). Common patterns: “dare per scontato” (to take for granted), “dare per morto” (to assume dead), “dare per perso” (to assume lost). Takes a direct object: “Davo la partita per finita.”
target_language_example: L’avevo dato per perso, ma alla fine l’ho ritrovato.
native_language_example: I had assumed it was lost, but in the end I found it again.

meaning: to take for granted; to assume (as obvious/true).
additional_notes: Used when you assume something is true or will happen without checking or appreciating it. Often followed by a clause with che (e.g., "Do per scontato che...") or by a noun/pronoun (e.g., "Non darlo per scontato").
target_language_example: Do per scontato che tu abbia capito, ma se vuoi te lo rispiego.
native_language_example: I’m assuming you understood, but if you want I’ll explain it again.

meaning: to listen to; to pay attention to; to heed.
additional_notes: Usually used with "a" + person/thing: "dare retta a qualcuno/qualcosa". It means taking someone’s advice or paying attention to what they say (often used in negatives or imperatives: "Non dargli retta!", "Dammi retta").
target_language_example: Dammi retta: non uscire senza ombrello.
native_language_example: Listen to me: don’t go out without an umbrella.

meaning: to get on someone’s nerves; to annoy (a lot).
additional_notes: Commonly used with an indirect object pronoun: "mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli dà sui nervi" = "it gets on my/your/his/her/our/your/their nerves." Often used in the present tense to describe an ongoing annoyance. Similar in meaning to "dare fastidio," but "dare sui nervi" is stronger (more like "drive someone crazy").
target_language_example: Mi dai sui nervi quando mastichi con la bocca aperta.
native_language_example: You get on my nerves when you chew with your mouth open.

meaning: to hit/strike; to give a knock.
additional_notes: Literally “to give a blow.” It’s used for a single impact or quick action, often followed by a preposition: **dare un colpo a** + thing/person (e.g., a punch, a hit) or **dare un colpo alla porta** (“to knock on the door”). In everyday speech it can also suggest doing something quickly/once (e.g., giving something a quick hit or knock).
target_language_example: Ha dato un colpo alla porta.
native_language_example: He knocked on the door.

meaning: to take a look; to have a quick look.
additional_notes: Common, everyday way to ask someone to look at something briefly (a message, a document, a shop window, a problem). Often used with "a" + thing/person ("dare un’occhiata a...") or with an object pronoun ("darci un’occhiata" = take a look at it/there; "dargli un’occhiata" = take a look at it/him). You can also use it as a polite request: "Puoi dare un’occhiata...?"
target_language_example: Puoi dare un’occhiata a questo messaggio, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you take a look at this message, please?

meaning: to teach someone a lesson (often: to punish or show someone they were wrong).
additional_notes: Used both literally (a teacher giving a lesson/class) and more commonly as an idiom meaning to “teach someone a lesson” after bad behavior or arrogance. The “lesson” can be moral, practical, or a punishment. Often followed by “a qualcuno” (to someone): “dare una lezione a qualcuno”.
target_language_example: Se continua così, qualcuno gli darà una lezione.
native_language_example: If he keeps it up like this, someone will teach him a lesson.

meaning: to help; to lend a hand.
additional_notes: Common, friendly way to offer or ask for help. Often used with "a" + person ("dare una mano a Marco") or with "con" + task ("dare una mano con i bagagli"). You can also say "Mi dai una mano?" for "Can you help me?".
target_language_example: Mi dai una mano con queste valigie?
native_language_example: Can you give me a hand with these suitcases?

meaning: to get rid of; to give away (often by selling or donating).
additional_notes: Commonly used when you don’t want something anymore and you pass it to someone else (sell, donate, or give for free). It can also mean to hand out/distribute in some contexts (e.g., flyers), but the most frequent beginner use is “to give away/get rid of.” In the past it’s often used as a set phrase: “ho dato via…”
target_language_example: Ho dato via i vestiti che non mettevo più.
native_language_example: I got rid of / gave away the clothes I didn’t wear anymore.

meaning: to give life to; to create/bring about.
additional_notes: Most often used as "dare vita a + noun" meaning to create something new or make something happen (a project, an organization, an initiative, an idea). More formal than "creare" in everyday speech, and can also mean "to give rise to" (cause) in contexts like events or problems.
target_language_example: Hanno dato vita a un’associazione per aiutare i senzatetto.
native_language_example: They created an association to help homeless people.

additional_notes: Used on forms, in official contexts, and when giving personal information. Often appears as “Data di nascita:” followed by a date, commonly written in Italy as day/month/year (e.g., 14/03/1995).
target_language_example: Qual è la tua data di nascita?
native_language_example: What is your date of birth?

meaning: employer (the person or company you work for).
additional_notes: Used in work, contracts, and official contexts. Often appears in forms and documents: “dati del datore di lavoro” (employer details). Literally “giver of work,” but in English you normally say “employer,” not “work giver.”
target_language_example: Devo comunicare il cambio di indirizzo al mio datore di lavoro.
native_language_example: I have to tell my employer about my change of address.

meaning: in front of; before (in position or time).
additional_notes: Common preposition phrase used to indicate location (something is facing or positioned in front of something else) or, more generally, being in someone’s presence. It can also mean “before” in time or order. It’s often followed by a noun or pronoun: davanti a casa (in front of the house), davanti a me (in front of me).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo davanti alla stazione.
native_language_example: See you in front of the station.

additional_notes: "Degli" is the combination of "di" + "gli".
