It can be a partitive article meaning "some" (Ho visto degli uomini = I saw some men) or it can literally mean "of the" after certain verbs/expressions (parlare degli uomini = to talk about the men). In Italian, "uomini" is usually not capitalized unless it’s part of a title or name.
target_language_example: Ho visto degli uomini davanti alla stazione.
native_language_example: I saw some men in front of the station.

additional_notes: "Del" is the contraction of "di" + "il" and often appears in surnames and place names (especially when capitalized), meaning someone is "from" or "associated with" a place: e.g., "Marco del Bosco". In regular descriptions it can also mean something located in the woods/forest, like "un sentiero del bosco" (a forest path).
target_language_example: Abbiamo seguito un sentiero del bosco fino al lago.
native_language_example: We followed a forest path all the way to the lake.

additional_notes: “Del” is the contraction of “di” + “il” and means “of the.” You’ll see “del Mercato” in place names, shop names, or descriptions to indicate a connection to a market (e.g., “Piazza del Mercato” = Market Square). It agrees with masculine singular nouns (il mercato).
target_language_example: Abbiamo comprato frutta fresca del mercato.
native_language_example: We bought fresh fruit from the market.

additional_notes: Contraction of "di" + "il" = "del". Used to specify something with worldwide scope or fame, and very common in names/titles (e.g., "Coppa del Mondo" = World Cup; "la città più bella del mondo" = the most beautiful city in the world). Note: in the middle of a sentence it’s usually not capitalized ("del mondo"); it may be capitalized in official names and titles.
target_language_example: La Coppa del Mondo si gioca ogni quattro anni.
native_language_example: The World Cup is played every four years.

additional_notes: "Del" is the contraction of "di + il" and often means "of the" (sometimes "from the"). "Sole" is capitalized when referring to the Sun as a proper noun (the star), but you may also see lowercase "sole" meaning "sun/sunlight" in a general sense. Common in descriptions (e.g., light/heat of the sun) and in names/places (e.g., "Via del Sole").
target_language_example: La luce del Sole è molto forte oggi.
native_language_example: The Sun’s light is very strong today.

meaning: if necessary; if applicable; appropriate (to the situation).
additional_notes: Common in formal or semi-formal Italian, often in the set phrase "se del caso" (= "if necessary / if applicable"). You may also see it after nouns like "misure del caso" (= "appropriate measures") or "documenti del caso" (= "the necessary/appropriate documents").
target_language_example: Se del caso, ti richiamo domani.
native_language_example: If necessary, I’ll call you back tomorrow.

meaning: vulgar: “fucking / shitty / damn” (used to insult or emphasize something is bad or worthless).
additional_notes: Very vulgar (literally “of the dick”). Used after a noun to express contempt or frustration: "un lavoro del cazzo" = “a shitty job.” Common in spoken Italian; avoid in polite situations. Can also be used in expressions like "che cazzo" ("what the hell").
target_language_example: È un lavoro del cazzo, non lo sopporto più.
native_language_example: It’s a shitty job, I can’t stand it anymore.

additional_notes: Literally “of the heart” (di + il → del). Common after nouns to describe something as heartfelt or sincere (e.g., un ringraziamento del cuore). Also appears in phrases like "grazie di cuore" (thanks from the bottom of my heart).
target_language_example: Ti faccio un augurio del cuore.
native_language_example: I wish you this from the heart.

additional_notes: Used to specify a type or category (“something like…”). Often follows a noun or a pronoun: “cose del genere” = “things like that,” “qualcosa del genere” = “something like that.” It can also introduce examples, similar to “such as.”
target_language_example: Non mi piacciono le cose del genere.
native_language_example: I don’t like things like that.

additional_notes: Common discourse connector used to add a point, justify something, or soften/round off what you just said. Often translates as “besides” (adding an extra reason) or “after all/anyway” (reminding someone of a fact or concluding). Typically placed at the start or middle of a sentence.
target_language_example: Non posso venire; del resto domani lavoro presto.
native_language_example: I can’t come; besides, I work early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Often used to emphasize that something is 100% true/not true, or fully finished/absent. Common with negation (e.g., “non … del tutto” = “not completely”) and with verbs like essere/sembrare/capire (to be/seem/understand).
target_language_example: Non sono del tutto sicuro di aver capito.
native_language_example: I’m not completely sure I understood.

meaning: “of the (female) cat”; often part of a proper name (street name, place name, surname).
additional_notes: "della" is a common preposition+article combination (di + la = della) meaning “of the / from the.” With a capital letter ("Gatta"), it’s usually a proper noun (e.g., a street or place name, or a family name), so you’ll often see it in addresses like "via della Gatta."
target_language_example: Abito in via della Gatta.
native_language_example: I live on Via della Gatta.

meaning: “of the Reason” (often used in names, e.g., buildings/places).
additional_notes: This is the preposition+article combination “di + la” → “della” (“of the”). With “Ragione” capitalized, it’s usually part of a proper name (for example: “Palazzo della Ragione”). In everyday Italian, ragione (lowercase) means “reason” or “being right,” but in this fixed name-like use you typically don’t translate it word-for-word.
target_language_example: Ci vediamo davanti al Palazzo della Ragione.
native_language_example: Let’s meet in front of the Palazzo della Ragione.

additional_notes: Common in everyday speech, often interchangeable with "a volte" (a bit more common) and "talvolta" (more formal). It can appear at the beginning or end of a sentence: "Delle volte mi capita..." / "...delle volte."
target_language_example: Delle volte mi dimentico le chiavi.
native_language_example: Sometimes I forget my keys.

additional_notes: Used for a child’s temporary teeth that later fall out and are replaced by permanent teeth. Common in family/health contexts. Plural: "denti da latte". Often used with verbs like "cadere" (to fall out) or "perdere" (to lose): "Mi è caduto un dente da latte."
target_language_example: A mia figlia è caduto un dente da latte ieri.
native_language_example: My daughter lost a baby tooth yesterday.

additional_notes: Common in dental/health contexts. Singular; plural: "denti del giudizio". Often used with verbs like "togliere" (remove) or "spuntare" (come in): "Mi hanno tolto un dente del giudizio" / "Mi sta spuntando un dente del giudizio".
target_language_example: Mi fa male il dente del giudizio, devo andare dal dentista.
native_language_example: My wisdom tooth hurts; I need to go to the dentist.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify something is intended for or related to women, especially in shopping and clothing: "scarpe di donna" (women’s shoes), "abbigliamento di donna" (women’s clothing). It’s literally "of woman," but the natural English meaning is usually "women’s" or "for women."
target_language_example: Cerco un paio di scarpe di donna.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a pair of women’s shoes.

meaning: of May; in May (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used with dates, events, or descriptions to specify the month of May. Often appears as part of a fuller expression like “il 10 di maggio” (May 10th) or “un giorno di maggio” (a day in May). Note: months are usually lowercase in Italian (“maggio”), though you may see “Maggio” capitalized in titles or headings.
target_language_example: Ci vediamo il 10 di maggio.
native_language_example: See you on May 10th.

additional_notes: Used to specify that something comes from or is related to the sea (not lakes or rivers). It usually follows the noun: pesce di mare (sea fish), aria di mare (sea air), sale di mare (sea salt).
target_language_example: Preferisco il pesce di mare.
native_language_example: I prefer sea fish (fish from the sea).

additional_notes: Usually written lowercase as “di nuovo”. Common in everyday speech to say you will repeat an action: “Prova di nuovo” (try again), “Ci vediamo di nuovo” (see you again). It can also mean “anew/from scratch” depending on context.
target_language_example: Puoi ripetere di nuovo, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you repeat again, please?

additional_notes: Commonly used after a noun to specify that something relates to life, especially in set phrases like "stile di vita" (lifestyle), "qualità di vita" (quality of life), and "aspettativa di vita" (life expectancy). It can also appear in names/titles (e.g., "La dolce vita").
target_language_example: Sto cercando di migliorare la mia qualità di vita.
native_language_example: I’m trying to improve my quality of life.

additional_notes: Common with verbs like "essere" and "avere" to talk about someone’s basic nature or a basic level: "Sono di base timido" (I’m basically shy). It can also mean "basic/entry-level" in contexts like courses or skills: "un corso di base" (a basic course).
target_language_example: Di base, sono d’accordo con te.
native_language_example: Basically, I agree with you.

additional_notes: Common in the fixed expression "Che c’è di bello?" meaning "What’s new? / What’s good?" (often said as a casual greeting). It’s usually used with "c’è" or "hai" (e.g., "C’è di bello...", "Che hai di bello?"). Literally "of beautiful," but in everyday speech it means something pleasant or interesting.
target_language_example: C’è di bello che domani non lavoriamo!
native_language_example: The good news is that tomorrow we don’t work!

additional_notes: Informal expression used to intensify what you’re saying, similar to “like crazy,” “a ton,” or “really.” Common with weather, feelings, and situations: “piove di brutto” (it’s raining hard), “fa caldo di brutto” (it’s really hot). Depending on context it can also suggest something happens abruptly or hits hard.
target_language_example: Ha iniziato a piovere di brutto.
native_language_example: It started raining really hard / all of a sudden.

additional_notes: Common adverbial phrase used to express certainty or emphasis. Often goes with verbs like sapere/pensare (e.g., “so di certo…” = “I know for sure…”). You’ll also see the negative form “non di certo” meaning “certainly not” / “not exactly.” Word order is flexible but it often comes after the verb.
target_language_example: Non lo so di certo, ma penso che arrivi domani.
native_language_example: I don’t know for sure, but I think he’ll arrive tomorrow.

meaning: “colored” (having a particular color); also “of color” (about color).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe its color, similar to “colored” in English: un vestito di colore blu (“a blue-colored dress”). With no specific color given, it can mean “colored” vs. white/clear: carta di colore (“colored paper”), vetro di colore (“colored glass”). It can also appear in phrases like di colore rosso (“red”), or in a more abstract sense: parlare di colore (“to talk about color”).
target_language_example: Vorrei una maglietta di colore nero, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a black T-shirt, please.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that happens abruptly and unexpectedly. Often placed after the verb (e.g., "è successo di colpo") or at the end of the sentence for emphasis. Common with verbs like succedere (to happen), cambiare (to change), svegliarsi (to wake up), arrivare (to arrive).
target_language_example: È cambiato tutto di colpo.
native_language_example: Everything changed all of a sudden.

additional_notes: Used to link a cause to its result, often in more formal or written Italian (similar to “therefore”). It can appear at the start of a sentence or after a comma. Common alternatives: “quindi”, “perciò” (more everyday).
target_language_example: Ha perso l’autobus e, di conseguenza, è arrivato tardi.
native_language_example: He missed the bus and, as a result, he arrived late.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens repeatedly or without stopping. Similar to "continuamente". Often placed after the verb (e.g., "parla di continuo") but it can also go at the beginning for emphasis.
target_language_example: Parli di continuo: fammi finire, per favore.
native_language_example: You talk all the time: let me finish, please.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re doing something quickly or in a rush. With verbs like andare/venire/arrivare, it often implies literally running (e.g., "vengo di corsa" = “I’ll come running”). You can also use it for fast actions in general ("mangiare di corsa" = “to eat in a hurry”).
target_language_example: Scusa, devo andare di corsa.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go in a hurry.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize genuine, heartfelt feeling, especially in thanks, wishes, or apologies. Common with verbs/phrases like "grazie di cuore" (thank you from the bottom of my heart) and "ti ringrazio di cuore" (I thank you sincerely). It’s warm and polite, not slang.
target_language_example: Grazie di cuore per il tuo aiuto.
native_language_example: Thank you from the bottom of my heart for your help.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what is true in reality, sometimes contrasting with what is said, planned, or official (similar to English “in fact” or “actually”). It can also mean “in practice” or “effectively” (de facto), especially when talking about a situation that exists even if it isn’t formal or official. Often placed at the beginning or in the middle of a sentence.
target_language_example: Ufficialmente non è il capo, ma di fatto decide tutto lui.
native_language_example: Officially he isn’t the boss, but in fact he decides everything.

meaning: made of iron; iron (as a material).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to say what something is made of (e.g., una porta di ferro = an iron door). It can also be used figuratively to mean “very strong/tough” (e.g., una volontà di ferro = an iron will).
target_language_example: Ha una volontà di ferro.
native_language_example: He/She has an iron will.

additional_notes: Used to indicate position close to something/someone. Often appears as “di fianco a + noun/pronoun” (next to), and you may also see “a fianco” with the same meaning. Common in everyday directions and descriptions of where things are.
target_language_example: Il supermercato è di fianco alla stazione.
native_language_example: The supermarket is next to the station.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe a person or service you trust and regularly use. Common in phrases like "medico di fiducia" (your trusted doctor), "avvocato di fiducia" (trusted lawyer), "meccanico di fiducia" (trusted mechanic), and "negozio di fiducia" (your go-to shop).
target_language_example: Cerco un medico di fiducia in questa zona.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a trusted doctor in this area.

meaning: deep down; at the bottom; background/basic (as in "di fondo").
additional_notes: A common phrase meaning “at the bottom” in a literal sense (e.g., the bottom of a glass, sea, drawer). Figuratively, it can mean “deep down” (your real/inner feelings) or “basic/background” in set expressions like: "in fondo" (in the end/deep down), "di fondo" (background/underlying), "rumore di fondo" (background noise), "colore di fondo" (background color). Often follows a noun: "rumore di fondo", "il fondo del bicchiere" (note: "del" = di + il).
target_language_example: C’è un rumore di fondo che non mi fa concentrare.
native_language_example: There’s background noise that’s keeping me from concentrating.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say something is a quick, temporary solution made with what’s available (often not very comfortable or high-quality). Common with words like letto (bed), riparo (shelter), medicazione (bandage), parcheggio (parking), soluzione (solution).
target_language_example: Abbiamo dormito su un letto di fortuna.
native_language_example: We slept on a makeshift bed.

additional_notes: Often used to mean “necessarily/inevitably,” especially in negative sentences: “non … di forza” = “not necessarily.” It can also mean “by force/forcibly,” depending on context (less common in everyday beginner situations).
target_language_example: Non devi di forza venire oggi; possiamo vederci domani.
native_language_example: You don’t necessarily have to come today; we can see each other tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used mainly in the fixed phrase "di fronte a" + noun/pronoun to mean "in front of" or "facing" (location or position). It can also mean "opposite" (e.g., on the other side of the street). In more abstract contexts, "di fronte a" can mean "faced with" a situation (e.g., "di fronte a un problema").
target_language_example: La banca è di fronte alla stazione.
native_language_example: The bank is in front of the station.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify that something involves theft. Common in set phrases like "denuncia di furto" (theft report) and "merce di furto" (stolen goods). In English you often translate it more naturally as an adjective ("theft" / "stolen") rather than word-for-word "of theft."
target_language_example: Ho fatto una denuncia di furto alla polizia.
native_language_example: I filed a theft report with the police.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is much more (or less) than other things in comparison. Common with superlatives (e.g., il migliore, la più grande) and comparisons (più/meno). It’s fairly formal-neutral and often appears in writing and speech.
target_language_example: Questo è di gran lunga il miglior ristorante della zona.
native_language_example: This is by far the best restaurant in the area.

additional_notes: Used to make a request sound more courteous, often after imperatives or in questions (similar to “please”/“kindly”). Common in set phrases like “Per favore, mi dica di grazia…” It can sound a bit formal or old-fashioned compared with “per favore”.
target_language_example: Mi può dire, di grazia, dov’è la stazione?
native_language_example: Could you tell me, please, where the station is?

additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. Used after a noun to insult it or say it’s really bad (e.g., tempo/film/giornata/lavoro di merda). Can also be said alone as an expletive (“Merda!” = “Shit!”). Avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: Che giornata di merda oggi.
native_language_example: What a shitty day today.

meaning: in the way; involved; from the middle/in between (depending on context).
additional_notes: Common in set phrases. With "togliersi/levare" it means "to get out of the way" (Togliti di mezzo!). With "mettersi" it means "to get involved" (Non metterti di mezzo). It can also describe position: "in between" or "in the middle" (una casa di mezzo = a house in the middle, between others).
target_language_example: Non metterti di mezzo: me la vedo io.
native_language_example: Don’t get involved: I’ll handle it.

additional_notes: Used after a noun (or after verbs like essere/andare) to say something is currently popular or stylish. Often contrasts with "fuori moda" (out of fashion).
target_language_example: Quel vestito è molto di moda quest’anno.
native_language_example: That dress is very fashionable this year.

additional_notes: Used to describe doing something without others noticing or without permission. Often goes with verbs like fare (to do), andare (to go), vedere (to see), parlare (to talk). Similar to “di soppiatto.”
target_language_example: Lui ha letto il mio diario di nascosto.
native_language_example: He read my diary in secret.

additional_notes: Used to introduce someone’s/something’s name, often after a noun like persona/ragazzo/cane or after “si chiama”. Common in sentences like “un ragazzo di nome Luca” (= “a boy named Luca”).
target_language_example: Ho conosciuto una ragazza di nome Sara.
native_language_example: I met a girl named Sara.

additional_notes: Used to say when something happens (time of day). Very common with verbs like lavorare (to work), dormire (to sleep), guidare (to drive), uscire (to go out). Similar to other time phrases with di: di giorno (during the day).
target_language_example: Non mi piace guidare di notte.
native_language_example: I don’t like driving at night.

additional_notes: Used as a polite reply after someone says “grazie” (thank you), similar to “di niente” or “prego.” Often used in the fixed expression “(non) c’è di che / di nulla,” meaning “(don’t mention it).”
target_language_example: —Grazie per l’aiuto! —Di nulla!
native_language_example: —Thanks for the help! —You’re welcome!

additional_notes: Common way to say something happens one more time or is repeated. Often placed at the end of the sentence (e.g., “Fammi vedere di nuovo”), but it can also appear earlier for emphasis. Similar in meaning to “ancora” in many contexts.
target_language_example: Puoi ripetere di nuovo, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you repeat again, please?

additional_notes: Used mostly with verbs like "essere" or nouns like "persona"/"giudizio" to say someone is not impartial. Common in phrases such as "essere di parte" (to be biased) and "non essere di parte" (to be impartial).
target_language_example: Non essere di parte: ascolta anche l’altra versione.
native_language_example: Don’t be biased: listen to the other side too.

meaning: passing through; just visiting briefly (in transit).
additional_notes: Used to say you’re only somewhere temporarily, often while traveling, or that something/someone is passing by. Common with verbs like essere (“to be”) and with places: “Sono di passaggio a Roma” = “I’m just passing through Rome.” It can also describe people or things that are not permanent: “un lavoro di passaggio” (a temporary/stopgap job).
target_language_example: Sono di passaggio a Milano per lavoro, resto solo una notte.
native_language_example: I’m just passing through Milan for work; I’m only staying one night.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize physical presence (not by phone/email) or that someone does something themselves. Often follows verbs like vedere/incontrare/parlare (to see/meet/talk) and can contrast with "per telefono" (by phone) or "online".
target_language_example: Preferisco parlarne di persona.
native_language_example: I prefer to talk about it in person.

additional_notes: Used to say the price, amount, or measurement is calculated by weight (not per item). Common in shops/markets: "vendere a peso" or "pagare di peso". Often followed by a unit (al chilo / al grammo).
target_language_example: Queste ciliegie si pagano di peso, non a pezzi.
native_language_example: These cherries are paid for by weight, not by the piece.

meaning: a little; not much; by a small amount.
additional_notes: Often used after adjectives or comparisons to mean “slightly” or “by a little”: e.g., più alto di poco (“a little taller”). It can also mean “not much (money/time/value)” in phrases like per di poco (“for very little”).
target_language_example: Sono più stanco di poco oggi.
native_language_example: I’m a little more tired today.

additional_notes: Often used to refer to an earlier time or a previous situation/state (sometimes with an implied comparison to “now”). You’ll commonly see it after a noun or pronoun (e.g., “la casa di prima” = “the old/previous house”) or in phrases like “come prima” (“as before”) and “come di prima” (“like before,” slightly more emphatic).
target_language_example: Preferivo la vita di prima.
native_language_example: I preferred my old life / the life from before.

additional_notes: Used to say an action was deliberate (often contrasted with something done by mistake: “per sbaglio”). Common in everyday speech and can be placed after the verb or at the end of the sentence.
target_language_example: L’hai fatto di proposito?
native_language_example: Did you do it on purpose?

meaning: 'on this side of' (relative to a place/line).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is located on the same side as the speaker (or a chosen reference point), often contrasted with "di là da" (on the other side of). It’s followed by a noun (often with an article): "di qua dal fiume" = on this side of the river.
target_language_example: Il parcheggio è di qua dal fiume.
native_language_example: The parking lot is on this side of the river.

additional_notes: Common time expression meaning “in the current period” (often with a nuance like “given how things are lately”). It can refer to recent days/weeks or the present era. Often used to comment on trends or changes: “Di questi tempi, …”
target_language_example: Di questi tempi è difficile trovare un appartamento a buon prezzo.
native_language_example: These days it’s hard to find an apartment at a good price.

additional_notes: Common time expression meaning something happened not long ago. Often used with the past tense (e.g., passato prossimo) to talk about recent events, or more generally to mean “lately.”
target_language_example: Ho cambiato lavoro di recente.
native_language_example: I changed jobs recently.

additional_notes: Used to express what is normally true (a general habit or typical situation). Common in both spoken and written Italian. Similar in meaning to "di solito" or "in genere"; often placed near the beginning of the sentence.
target_language_example: Di regola, prendo il caffè senza zucchero.
native_language_example: As a rule, I take my coffee without sugar.

meaning: spare; backup; reserve (extra, kept in case it’s needed).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean “spare/backup” (e.g., a spare tire, a backup charger). It describes something kept available in case the main one is missing or fails. Common in everyday contexts and travel.
target_language_example: Hai una batteria di riserva per il telefono?
native_language_example: Do you have a spare battery for the phone?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the return part of a trip or movement back to a place (often with verbs like essere/andare/tornare, or after nouns like viaggio/strada). Common in travel contexts: “Sono di ritorno da…” = “I’m back from / I’m on my way back from…”.
target_language_example: Siamo di ritorno dall’aeroporto.
native_language_example: We’re on our way back from the airport.

additional_notes: Used to describe items that have had a previous owner (clothes, furniture, cars, etc.). Often appears after the noun: "una giacca di seconda mano". Common in shopping contexts; similar to "usato" (used).
target_language_example: Ho comprato una bici di seconda mano perché costava meno.
native_language_example: I bought a second-hand bike because it cost less.

meaning: below; following; next (in text or in sequence).
additional_notes: Common in written Italian (emails, documents, instructions) to introduce what comes next: "Di seguito trovi..." = "Below you’ll find...". Can also mean "afterwards/then" in a sequence of actions, similar to "poi" or "successivamente". Often paired with verbs like "trovare", "riportare", "elencare" (find, report, list).
target_language_example: Di seguito trovi l’elenco dei documenti richiesti.
native_language_example: Below you’ll find the list of required documents.

meaning: usual; the one you always go to / have had for a long time.
additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean your regular or longstanding choice (a place, person, thing, habit): "il bar di sempre" = your usual bar; "il medico di sempre" = your regular doctor. It often implies familiarity and routine. Not normally translated word-for-word as “of always” in English.
target_language_example: Andiamo al bar di sempre?
native_language_example: Shall we go to our usual bar?

meaning: in the evening; at night (in the evening).
additional_notes: Used to say when something happens during the evening hours. Common after verbs like andare (to go), uscire (to go out), lavorare (to work): “Esco di sera” = “I go out in the evening.” Often contrasts with di mattina (in the morning) and di pomeriggio (in the afternoon).
target_language_example: Di sera mi piace fare una passeggiata.
native_language_example: In the evening I like to take a walk.

additional_notes: Literally "of service." Common after a noun to describe something used for service/work or for the purpose of serving others. With people, it often means they are working/on duty (e.g., poliziotto di servizio). With objects/vehicles, it can mean "service" or "for official/work use" (e.g., auto di servizio = a service/official car).
target_language_example: C'è un medico di servizio stanotte?
native_language_example: Is there a doctor on duty tonight?

additional_notes: Common adverbial phrase used to express certainty. Often placed after the verb or at the start of the sentence for emphasis. Similar in meaning to “sicuramente” and “certamente.”
target_language_example: Di sicuro verrò alla festa domani.
native_language_example: I’ll definitely come to the party tomorrow.

additional_notes: Common adverbial phrase used to talk about habits or what happens most of the time. It often goes near the verb (e.g., before it in simple tenses), but it can also start a sentence for emphasis.
target_language_example: Di solito vado al lavoro in autobus.
native_language_example: I usually go to work by bus.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a higher position or something on an upper floor. Common in set phrases like "qui sopra" (up here/above), "là sopra" (up there/above), "al piano di sopra" or "di sopra" (upstairs), and "la stanza di sopra" (the upstairs room). Often contrasts with "di sotto" (below/downstairs).
target_language_example: Il bagno è di sopra, al piano di sopra.
native_language_example: The bathroom is upstairs, on the upper floor.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens suddenly or without warning. Common after verbs like arrivare/venire (to arrive/come) or to describe an action: “entrare di sorpresa” (to enter unexpectedly). You can also say “Di sorpresa,” at the start of a sentence to mean “Suddenly,”.
target_language_example: È arrivato di sorpresa ieri sera.
native_language_example: He arrived unexpectedly last night.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a lower position or the lower floor/level. Often appears with other words: "qui/laggiù/lì di sotto" (down here/there below), "da di sotto" (from below), "di sotto" as an adverb meaning "underneath" in contrasts like "sopra e di sotto" (above and below).
target_language_example: Il garage è di sotto, al piano terra.
native_language_example: The garage is downstairs, on the ground floor.

meaning: successful; popular; hit (of a product, event, person).
additional_notes: Literally “of success.” Used after a noun to describe something that has become successful or popular: un film di successo (a hit movie), un'azienda di successo (a successful company), un cantante di successo (a successful singer). Often implies recognition, sales, or public approval rather than just “good.”
target_language_example: È un ristorante di successo in centro.
native_language_example: It’s a successful/popular restaurant downtown.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens every now and then, not regularly. Often interchangeable with “ogni tanto” and “di tanto in tanto”. It can go at the beginning or end of a sentence.
target_language_example: Di tanto in tanto andiamo a cena fuori.
native_language_example: From time to time we go out to dinner.

meaning: around; all around (in the surrounding area).
additional_notes: Somewhat old-fashioned/literary; in everyday Italian you more often hear "intorno" or "attorno" (e.g., "guardare intorno" = to look around). Often used with verbs like "guardare" (to look) or "girarsi" (to turn) to mean looking/turning around.
target_language_example: Si guardò di torno, ma non vide nessuno.
native_language_example: He/She looked around, but didn’t see anyone.

additional_notes: Used as an adjective phrase meaning something is part of normal daily life (routine, common, not special). Often placed after the noun: "vita di tutti i giorni" (everyday life), "problemi di tutti i giorni" (everyday problems), "linguaggio di tutti i giorni" (everyday language).
target_language_example: Preferisco vestiti comodi per la vita di tutti i giorni.
native_language_example: I prefer comfortable clothes for everyday life.

additional_notes: Used after a noun (often with a superlative) to mean “in history / ever”: e.g., “il migliore di tutti i tempi” = “the best of all time.” Literally “of all the times.”
target_language_example: Questa è la mia canzone preferita di tutti i tempi.
native_language_example: This is my all-time favorite song.

meaning: “by sight” / “visually” (recognize or know someone/something just from seeing them).
additional_notes:
Most common in set phrases like:
- "conoscere qualcuno di vista" = to know/recognize someone by sight (you’ve seen them before, but you don’t personally know them)
- "perdere di vista" = to lose sight of (literally or figuratively: lose track of)
Also appears in "a prima vista" (at first sight), but the basic idea is always connected to seeing.
target_language_example: Lo conosco di vista, ma non ci ho mai parlato.
native_language_example: I recognize him by sight, but I’ve never spoken to him.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is imprisoned. Literally “behind the bars,” so it’s common in news, crime stories, and everyday speech. You can use it with verbs like "finire" (to end up) or "mandare" (to send).
target_language_example: Dopo la rapina, è finito dietro le sbarre.
native_language_example: After the robbery, he ended up behind bars.

meaning: to say goodbye; to bid farewell (often for good).
additional_notes: Literally “to say goodbye.” Used for farewells, especially emotional ones or when you don’t expect to see someone/something again. It can be used with people (Dire addio a qualcuno) or with things/habits (Dire addio alle sigarette = “say goodbye to cigarettes” / “quit smoking”). In everyday casual situations you more often hear "ciao" or "arrivederci."
target_language_example: È stato difficile dire addio ai miei nonni.
native_language_example: It was hard to say goodbye to my grandparents.

additional_notes: Used to express that you hope something will go well, or to wish someone luck. Often said on its own as an exclamation (e.g., “Dita incrociate!”). You can also use it in a sentence with verbs like “tenere” (to keep/hold): “Tengo le dita incrociate per te.”
target_language_example: Dita incrociate per l’esame di domani!
native_language_example: Fingers crossed for tomorrow’s exam!

additional_notes: Used to introduce an action/event that happens later than another one. It’s typically followed by a clause (subject + verb), often with the indicative in everyday Italian: "dopo che ho finito" = "after I finished". Contrast with "dopo" (often followed by a noun/infinitive, or used alone): "dopo la lezione" = "after the lesson"; "a dopo" = "see you later".
target_language_example: Dopo che ho finito il lavoro, torno a casa.
native_language_example: After I finish work, I go home.

additional_notes: Used to politely let someone go first (e.g., through a door, in a line). Often said on its own as a courteous gesture. You may also hear the shorter form “dopo di lei” (more formal) or “prima lei/lei prima” in similar situations.
target_language_example: Prego, dopo di te!
native_language_example: Please, after you!

additional_notes: Used to add a final thought or correction (“Actually, when you think about it…”), or to sum up a situation. Common in both speaking and writing. Often appears at the beginning or end of a sentence: “Dopo tutto, …” / “…, dopo tutto.”
target_language_example: Dopo tutto, non è così difficile imparare l’italiano.
native_language_example: After all, it’s not that hard to learn Italian.

meaning: a short walk (often just to stretch your legs).
additional_notes: Literally “two steps,” but it’s used idiomatically to mean a brief walk, often for pleasure or to get some air. Common in phrases like “fare due passi” (to take a short walk) and can also mean “nearby” in “a due passi (da...)” = “a short walk from...”.
target_language_example: Dopo cena facciamo due passi in centro.
native_language_example: After dinner, let’s take a short walk downtown.

meaning: “two pieces” / “two items” (i.e., a quantity of 2 of something).
additional_notes: Common when ordering or buying food and other countable items (especially pastries, slices, small portions, etc.). Often used with “ne” (“two of them”): “Ne prendo due pezzi.” The noun after it is frequently understood from context.
target_language_example: Ne prendo due pezzi, per favore.
native_language_example: I’ll take two (pieces/items), please.

meaning: a colon (:) in writing/punctuation; also “two points” in scoring.
additional_notes: Most commonly used for the punctuation mark “:” in Italian (e.g., in lists, before explanations, or in time like 10:30). In sports or grades it can also mean “two points.”
target_language_example: Metti i due punti prima della lista: pane, latte e uova.
native_language_example: Put a colon before the list: bread, milk, and eggs.

meaning: “so…?” / “and then?” (used to prompt what comes next, or to challenge: “so what?”)
additional_notes: Very common in spoken Italian. Use it to move the conversation forward (“So, what do we do now?”), to ask for the next step in a story (“And then?”), or to react to something with a mild challenge (“So what?”). Often said with a pause: “E allora…?” Tone depends heavily on intonation.
target_language_example: E allora, che facciamo adesso?
native_language_example: So, what do we do now?

additional_notes: Used at the end of a list to mean that there are more similar items you’re not naming. Common in both spoken and written Italian. Often shortened to "ecc." in writing (like "etc.").
target_language_example: Dobbiamo comprare pane, latte, pasta e così via.
native_language_example: We need to buy bread, milk, pasta, and so on.

additional_notes: Used after a quantity (often age or time) to mean “more than that amount,” like “thirty years and then some.” It’s common in speech and informal writing: "trent’anni e passa" = “thirty-something / over thirty,” "due ore e passa" = “two hours and more.”
target_language_example: Ho trent’anni e passa, ma mi sento ancora giovane.
native_language_example: I’m thirty-something (over thirty), but I still feel young.

additional_notes: Very common connector in spoken and written Italian. Use it to: (1) sequence actions in time (“and then…”), often when telling a story or giving instructions; (2) add another point or reason (“and besides / and what’s more…”). It can appear mid-sentence or at the start to continue a thought: “E poi…” = “And then/And besides…”.
target_language_example: Prima andiamo al supermercato, e poi torniamo a casa.
native_language_example: First we go to the supermarket, and then we go back home.

additional_notes: Common loanword in Italian. You’ll also see “email” (without the hyphen). Used with verbs like “mandare/inviare un’e-mail” (to send an email) and “ricevere un’e-mail” (to receive an email). Plural: “e-mail” or sometimes “email” (often invariable).
target_language_example: Ti mando un’e-mail con i dettagli.
native_language_example: I’ll send you an email with the details.

meaning: to spring into action; to take action (start operating).
additional_notes: Used when someone or something starts acting, intervening, or functioning, often suddenly or at a key moment. Common with people (police, firefighters, a team) or things/machines/systems. Can also be used figuratively (e.g., a plan or law starts to operate).
target_language_example: Appena ha sentito l’allarme, la squadra di soccorso è entrata in azione.
native_language_example: As soon as they heard the alarm, the rescue team sprang into action.

additional_notes: Common exclamation used when something happens later than expected, often showing impatience or relief. Literally “it was time,” and you’ll also hear it as “Era ora che…” (= “It was about time that…”).
target_language_example: Era ora! Ti stavo aspettando da mezz’ora.
native_language_example: About time! I’ve been waiting for you for half an hour.

meaning: to be (big) trouble; to be in deep trouble. (vulgar)
additional_notes: Vulgar expression built on the swear word "cazzi" (literally "dicks"). In real life you’ll чаще hear it as "sono cazzi" / "è un cazzo" in the sense of "we’re/you’re in trouble" or "this is serious"; also very common: "sono cazzi amari" (= "it’s going to be really bad"). Use only in very informal contexts with people you know well; it can sound aggressive.
target_language_example: Se lo scoprono, sono cazzi.
native_language_example: If they find out, we’re in deep trouble.

meaning: to be there for (someone); to support (someone).
additional_notes: Used to express emotional support, availability, or reliability for someone, especially in difficult moments. It’s often followed by a person ("per te", "per lui/lei", "per i miei amici"). Can also be used more generally for being available when needed.
target_language_example: Sono sempre lì per te, anche quando le cose vanno male.
native_language_example: I’m always there for you, even when things go wrong.

meaning: to be crazy; to be mad (insane or “crazy about” something).
additional_notes: Used literally for mental instability, but very often used informally to mean “to be crazy about” something or someone (very enthusiastic/in love): “essere pazzo di/per…”. You can change the adjective for gender/number: essere pazzo (m. sing.), essere pazza (f. sing.), essere pazzi/pazze (plural).
target_language_example: Sono pazzo di questa pizza!
native_language_example: I’m crazy about this pizza!

additional_notes: Common, neutral noun phrase used in everyday speech and in more formal contexts (science, ethics). Plural: esseri umani. Often used generically to talk about people as a species: "Gli esseri umani...".
target_language_example: Ogni essere umano merita rispetto.
native_language_example: Every human being deserves respect.

meaning: “It’s the same / it doesn’t matter / either way is fine.”
additional_notes: Used to say something is not important or that you don’t mind which option happens. Often functions like “no worries” or “that’s fine” when accepting a change or a small problem. Common in spoken Italian.
target_language_example: Va bene, fa lo stesso: possiamo andare domani.
native_language_example: Okay, it doesn’t matter: we can go tomorrow.

meaning: face-to-face; in person (directly, not online/by phone).
additional_notes: Used to describe meeting or talking directly with someone in the same place. Common with verbs like incontrarsi (to meet), parlare (to talk), and vedere (to see). Sometimes written with a hyphen: faccia-a-faccia.
target_language_example: Preferisco parlarne faccia a faccia.
native_language_example: I prefer to talk about it face-to-face.

additional_notes: Common, friendly way to give permission or encourage someone to proceed. Literally “do (it) freely,” often used on its own as a response (e.g., when someone asks if they can do something). You may also hear it as “fai pure!” with emphasis, or “fai pure, tranquillo/a” (“go ahead, don’t worry”).
target_language_example: Posso aprire la finestra? — Sì, fai pure.
native_language_example: Can I open the window? — Yes, go ahead.

meaning: “Do me a favor,” often used as “Give me a break / Cut it out.”
additional_notes: Literally “do me the pleasure.” In everyday speech it can be a normal request (“Fammi il piacere di chiudere la finestra”), but very often it’s said with irritation or disbelief to dismiss what someone said (similar to “Yeah, right” or “Come on”). Tone depends heavily on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Fammi il piacere, smettila di dire bugie.
native_language_example: Give me a break—stop telling lies.

meaning: to suck; to be really bad (very vulgar).
additional_notes: Very common slang and strongly vulgar. Used to say something is awful: "X fa cagare" ("X sucks"). Also used about people’s mood/health: "Sto facendo cagare" = "I’m doing terribly" (still vulgar). Literally it means "to make (someone) poop," but in everyday speech it’s usually the insult/complaint meaning.
target_language_example: Questo film fa cagare.
native_language_example: This movie sucks.

meaning: to make (someone) understand; to get (an idea/message) across.
additional_notes: Uses the verb fare (to make/do) + capire (to understand). It’s followed by the person who should understand (often with an indirect object pronoun like mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi) and the thing to understand, often introduced by che (“that”) or as a noun phrase. Common in explanations, clarifications, or when emphasizing that something wasn’t understood at first.
target_language_example: Te lo sto cercando di far capire, ma non mi ascolti.
native_language_example: I’m trying to make you understand it, but you’re not listening.

meaning: to introduce; to make known; to let (someone) know.
additional_notes: Literally “to make known.” Commonly used with a direct object (a person, a place, a product, an idea) to mean “to introduce” or “to familiarize someone with something.” Often appears as “far conoscere a [someone] [something/someone]” (to introduce someone to something/someone) or “far conoscere [something]” (to promote/make something known). In informal speech you may also hear “farsi conoscere” = “to get known / to make yourself known.”
target_language_example: Mi puoi far conoscere i tuoi amici?
native_language_example: Can you introduce me to your friends?

meaning: to point out; to draw attention to (something).
additional_notes: Used when you want to emphasize a detail or make someone notice something. Often followed by a clause with “che” (Far notare che…) or by a noun/pronoun (farlo notare = to point it out). Slightly formal/neutral; in more casual speech you can also say “far presente”.
target_language_example: Vorrei far notare che il prezzo include già le tasse.
native_language_example: I’d like to point out that the price already includes taxes.

meaning: to be part (of); to belong to.
additional_notes: Most commonly used with "di" + a group/organization/thing: "far parte di" = "to be part of". It’s a set phrase (you usually don’t translate it as "to make part"). You can also use it in the expression "fare parte di un gruppo / una squadra / un’associazione".
target_language_example: Vuoi far parte della nostra squadra?
native_language_example: Do you want to be part of our team?

meaning: to start (something); to send off / make (someone or something) leave.
additional_notes: Causative form of "partire" (to leave/to depart): "far" + infinitive means "to make/let someone or something do". Common with machines/programs (start them) and with people/vehicles/packages (send them off). In everyday speech you often see the direct-object pronoun: "farlo partire" (to start it / send him off).
target_language_example: Puoi far partire la lavatrice, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you start the washing machine, please?

meaning: to make (someone) think; to make one suspect/guess.
additional_notes: Uses **fare** + infinitive to mean “to make/let someone do something.” With **far pensare (a qualcuno)** it often means “to make someone think” or “to suggest/imply,” sometimes with a sense of raising suspicion: *Mi fa pensare che…* = “It makes me think that…” / “It suggests that…”. In speech you may also hear **fa pensare** instead of **far pensare** when conjugated.
target_language_example: Quello che hai detto mi fa pensare che tu abbia ragione.
native_language_example: What you said makes me think that you’re right.

meaning: to enforce; to make someone respect/observe (rules, orders, rights).
additional_notes: Uses the causative construction "fare + infinitive" meaning "to make/let someone do something." Often followed by what is being enforced (la legge, le regole, un contratto) and the person made to comply can be introduced with "a" (e.g., "far rispettare le regole agli studenti").
target_language_example: La polizia deve far rispettare la legge.
native_language_example: The police must enforce the law.

meaning: to blow up (make explode); also: to make something fall through/ruin it.
additional_notes: Literally means “to make (someone/something) jump,” but it’s very often used for causing an explosion (far saltare in aria un ponte = to blow a bridge up). It’s also used figuratively for making plans fail or canceling at the last moment: far saltare un appuntamento / una riunione (to make a date/meeting fall through).
target_language_example: Hanno fatto saltare il ponte durante la notte.
native_language_example: They blew up the bridge during the night.

additional_notes: Used when you want to inform someone about something, often with a direct or indirect object: “far sapere qualcosa a qualcuno” (to let someone know something). Very common in the imperative with pronouns: “Fammi sapere” = “Let me know.” Also: “Te lo faccio sapere” = “I’ll let you know.”
target_language_example: Fammi sapere a che ora arrivi.
native_language_example: Let me know what time you arrive.

meaning: to make sure that; to cause (something) to happen.
additional_notes: Used to express causing an effect or ensuring a result. It’s built from far(e) (“to make/do”) + sì (“yes/so”) + che (“that”) and is commonly followed by the subjunctive: "Ho fatto sì che venisse" (“I made sure that he came”). Often used in more formal or written Italian, similar to “ensure that”.
target_language_example: Dobbiamo far sì che tutto sia pronto per domani.
native_language_example: We have to make sure that everything is ready for tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used when someone causes another person to see something (showing an object, a photo, a place, etc.). It can take an indirect object pronoun: "fammi vedere" (show me / let me see), "faglielo vedere" (show it to him). It can also be used figuratively meaning "to prove" or "to make someone realize" (e.g., "ti farò vedere" = I’ll show you / I’ll prove it).
target_language_example: Mi fai vedere le foto della tua vacanza?
native_language_example: Can you show me the photos from your vacation?

meaning: to do without; to go without.
additional_notes: Used with "di" + infinitive: "fare a meno di (qualcosa)" = do without (something), or "fare a meno di (fare qualcosa)" = do without doing something / manage without. Often appears in the negative: "non posso fare a meno di..." = "I can’t help..." (I can’t stop myself from...).
target_language_example: Non posso fare a meno di pensarci.
native_language_example: I can’t help thinking about it.

meaning: to do business; to make deals (often, to make a profit).
additional_notes: Used for doing business in general or successfully making deals. Common in contexts like shopping, negotiating prices, sales, and commerce. In the singular you may also hear "fare un affare" = "to get a good deal/bargain".
target_language_example: In Italia è facile fare affari con le piccole imprese locali.
native_language_example: In Italy it’s easy to do business with small local companies.

meaning: to rely on; to count on.
additional_notes: Usually followed by "su" + person/thing: "fare affidamento su qualcuno/qualcosa". Common in everyday and slightly formal contexts when talking about depending on help, support, or reliability (similar to "contare su").
target_language_example: Posso fare affidamento su di te domani?
native_language_example: Can I count on you tomorrow?

meaning: to make friends; to become friends.
additional_notes: Common with "con" to say who you become friends with: "fare amicizia con qualcuno". You can also specify the place: "fare amicizia a scuola / al lavoro". Often used in the past tense to talk about meeting and befriending someone: "Ho fatto amicizia con...".
target_language_example: Ho fatto amicizia con i miei vicini.
native_language_example: I became friends with my neighbors.

meaning: to pay attention; to be careful.
additional_notes: Very common phrase used to warn someone or remind them to notice something. Often followed by "a" + noun/infinitive: "fare attenzione alla strada" (watch the road), "fare attenzione a non cadere" (be careful not to fall). Can also be used as an instruction: "Fai attenzione!" = "Be careful!"
target_language_example: Fai attenzione a non perdere le chiavi.
native_language_example: Be careful not to lose the keys.

meaning: to do well; to do something properly.
additional_notes: Commonly used to say someone performs an action well ("Fai bene!" = "Good job!") or to give advice/approval ("Fai bene a..." = "You’re right to... / It’s a good idea to..."). Also appears in the expression "far bene a" meaning "to be good for" (e.g., "La frutta fa bene alla salute" = "Fruit is good for your health").
target_language_example: Fai bene a studiare ogni giorno.
native_language_example: You’re right to study every day.

meaning: to advance in your career; to climb the career ladder.
additional_notes: Used to talk about progressing professionally (getting promotions, more responsibility, higher status). Often used with verbs like "volere" (to want) or "cercare di" (to try to). You can also say "fare carriera in (un settore/azienda)" = "to build a career/advance in (a field/company)".
target_language_example: Vuole fare carriera e diventare manager entro pochi anni.
native_language_example: He/She wants to advance in his/her career and become a manager within a few years.

meaning: to make a mess; to make a racket/commotion.
additional_notes: Common informal phrase. Often means causing noise, confusion, or trouble (physically or socially). It can be literal (making a mess in a room) or figurative (stirring things up, causing a scene). You’ll often hear it in the imperative: “Non fare casino!” (“Don’t make a fuss / don’t make a mess / don’t make so much noise!”).
target_language_example: Non fare casino in casa, per favore: i bambini stanno dormendo.
native_language_example: Please don’t make a racket/mess in the house: the kids are sleeping.

meaning: to pay attention (to); to notice; to care about.
additional_notes: Often used with **a** + noun/pronoun: *fare caso a qualcosa/qualcuno* (“to pay attention to something/someone”). Common in negatives: *Non fare caso!* = “Don’t worry about it / Don’t pay attention to it.” It’s also used as *fare caso che...* meaning “to happen to notice that...”.
target_language_example: Non fare caso a quello che dice: è solo arrabbiato.
native_language_example: Don’t pay attention to what he says: he’s just angry.

meaning: to sue (take legal action against someone).
additional_notes: Used in everyday speech to mean starting a lawsuit against a person or organization. Often followed by "a" + who you’re suing ("fare causa a qualcuno") or "contro" + who/what you’re suing ("fare causa contro qualcuno/qualcosa"). You may also hear "fare una causa" (to file/start a lawsuit).
target_language_example: Ha deciso di fare causa all’azienda per licenziamento ingiusto.
native_language_example: He/She decided to sue the company for unfair dismissal.

meaning: to gesture/sign (to someone); to make a signal.
additional_notes: Used for a small gesture (often with the hand, head, or eyes) to communicate quickly without words. Common patterns: "fare cenno a qualcuno" (to signal to someone) and "fare cenno di" + infinitive (to indicate doing something, e.g., leaving). It can also mean “to briefly mention,” but the most common everyday meaning is the physical gesture.
target_language_example: Mi ha fatto cenno di avvicinarmi.
native_language_example: He/she signaled to me to come closer.

meaning: to make an impression (often: to impress someone).
additional_notes: Used for having a strong effect on someone or something, often in a positive/romantic sense. Common patterns: "fare colpo su qualcuno" (to impress someone) and "fare colpo" on its own when the person is understood. Literal words are "to make" + "a hit/blow", but the natural meaning is "make an impression."
target_language_example: Lui ha fatto colpo su di lei con il suo italiano.
native_language_example: He impressed her with his Italian.

additional_notes: Used when you stay with someone so they aren’t alone, or when you join them somewhere. Common patterns: “fare compagnia a qualcuno” (to keep someone company) and “Ti faccio compagnia” (I’ll keep you company / I’ll come with you). It doesn’t necessarily imply entertainment—more the idea of being together.
target_language_example: Se vuoi, ti faccio compagnia mentre aspetti.
native_language_example: If you want, I’ll keep you company while you wait.

additional_notes: Used for praising someone (their appearance, work, cooking, etc.). Often followed by "a" + person: "fare i complimenti a qualcuno". You can also use "fare un complimento" (singular) for one specific compliment. Common in polite/social situations.
target_language_example: Voglio farti i complimenti per il tuo italiano!
native_language_example: I want to compliment you on your Italian!

additional_notes: Used for starting or keeping up light, polite talk, especially with someone you don’t know well (at a party, with neighbors, while waiting, etc.). Often implies small talk rather than a deep discussion. You can also say “fare due chiacchiere” for a more casual version.
target_language_example: Durante la cena ho cercato di fare conversazione con i colleghi.
native_language_example: During dinner I tried to make conversation with my coworkers.

meaning: to do everything (possible); to do anything; to do one’s best.
additional_notes: Used to express making every effort to achieve something. Often followed by a purpose clause (per + infinitive) or by di + infinitive: "farò di tutto per aiutarti" / "farò di tutto di finire in tempo" (less common). It can also mean you’re willing to do whatever it takes, depending on context.
target_language_example: Farò di tutto per arrivare in tempo.
native_language_example: I’ll do everything I can to arrive on time.

meaning: to have an effect; to work (e.g., a medicine).
additional_notes: Used for something that produces a result or impact. Common with medicines and treatments (e.g., a pill ‘works’), and also with emotional impact (something ‘affects’/‘makes an impression’). Often used with "su" + person: "Mi fa effetto" = "It affects me / It makes an impression on me" (sometimes meaning it feels strange or unsettling).
target_language_example: Questo farmaco fa effetto dopo mezz’ora.
native_language_example: This medicine works after half an hour.

additional_notes: Commonly used for celebrating an event (a birthday, a holiday, good news). It can also mean ‘to make a fuss over someone’ (especially welcoming them warmly), depending on context: e.g., the dog ‘fa festa’ when you come home. Often used with a reason introduced by “per” (for): “fare festa per…”
target_language_example: Stasera facciamo festa per il compleanno di Luca.
native_language_example: Tonight we’re celebrating Luca’s birthday.

meaning: to pretend; to act as if (something were true).
additional_notes: Often followed by **di + infinitive**: *fare finta di dormire* (“pretend to sleep”). You can also use it with **che + clause**: *fare finta che niente sia successo* (“pretend nothing happened”). Common in everyday speech; implies putting on an act or ignoring something on purpose.
target_language_example: Ha fatto finta di non sentirmi.
native_language_example: He pretended not to hear me.

meaning: to fire (a gun); to open fire.
additional_notes: Used especially in military/police contexts and in commands (often without the subject): «Fare fuoco!» = “Fire!”. Literally it’s “to make fire,” but in modern usage it usually refers to shooting rather than starting a campfire (for that you’d more often say «accendere un fuoco»).
target_language_example: I soldati hanno ricevuto l’ordine di fare fuoco.
native_language_example: The soldiers received the order to open fire.

meaning: to get rid of; to kill (informal, depending on context).
additional_notes: Very common spoken phrase with multiple meanings. Most often it means “to get rid of / remove / eliminate” someone or something (e.g., an object, a problem, a rival). In some contexts it can mean “to kill” (often in crime/thriller language). It can also mean “to finish off / use up” something (especially food: “to polish off”). The exact meaning depends heavily on context and tone.
target_language_example: Dobbiamo fare fuori queste vecchie scatole.
native_language_example: We need to get rid of these old boxes.

meaning: to do the math; to work out the numbers; (often) to deal with something.
additional_notes: Literally “to make the calculations.” Common both for literal calculations (expenses, bills, totals) and in the expression “fare i conti con …” meaning “to come to terms with / deal with / reckon with …” (a problem, a situation, reality).
target_language_example: Dobbiamo fare i conti con il budget prima di prenotare.
native_language_example: We need to work out the budget before booking.

meaning: (vulgar) to work your ass off; also: to kick someone’s ass (when used with a person).
additional_notes: Very vulgar/strong language (literally “to make the ass”). Often used reflexively: “(mi/ti/si) fare il culo” = to work extremely hard. With an object/person: “fare il culo a qualcuno” can mean to beat someone up or defeat them badly, and can sound threatening. Avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: Mi sono fatto il culo per finire il progetto in tempo.
native_language_example: I worked my ass off to finish the project on time.

meaning: to fill up (the tank); to refuel.
additional_notes: Most commonly used for vehicles when you fill the fuel tank completely at a gas station. You can also use it more generally for “stocking up/filling up,” but the core everyday meaning is refueling. Often used with "di" + what you’re filling up with: "fare il pieno di benzina".
target_language_example: Prima di partire, facciamo il pieno di benzina.
native_language_example: Before leaving, let’s fill up with gas.

meaning: to cheer for (a team/person); to root for.
additional_notes: Used for showing support for a sports team or a person (often in sports, but also contests). It’s usually followed by “per” (fare il tifo per…) or “per + pronoun” (per lui/lei/loro). You can also use it with a team name directly (Fare il tifo per l’Italia).
target_language_example: Domani giochiamo contro Milano: vieni allo stadio a fare il tifo per noi?
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re playing against Milan: will you come to the stadium to cheer for us?

meaning: to make sure; to arrange for.
additional_notes: Often used as "fare in modo che" + subjunctive to mean "make sure that..." or "see to it that...". Common in requests, plans, and instructions. You may also hear "fare in modo di" + infinitive (more informal/less strict in everyday speech) to mean "manage to / make it so as to".
target_language_example: Fai in modo che arrivi in tempo.
native_language_example: Make sure he/she arrives on time.

meaning: to break in; to storm in (suddenly/forcefully).
additional_notes: Used for a sudden, forceful entry into a place. Often used with police or criminals (e.g., raids), but it can also be used more generally for someone bursting into a room unexpectedly. Common patterns: “fare irruzione in + place” (break into), “fare irruzione a casa di + person” (break into someone’s home).
target_language_example: La polizia ha fatto irruzione nell’appartamento all’alba.
native_language_example: The police broke into the apartment at dawn.

meaning: to poop; to do a poo (often said by/with children).
additional_notes: Very common everyday phrase, especially when talking to or about small children; among adults it can sound childish (a more neutral option is “fare la popò,” and more direct/medical options include “fare i bisogni” or “defecare”). Literally “to do the poop.”
target_language_example: Il bambino deve fare la cacca.
native_language_example: The child needs to poop.

meaning: to make a difference; to matter.
additional_notes: Used when something has an important effect or changes the outcome. Often with "fa" (it makes) or "fanno" (they make): "Fa la differenza" = "It makes a difference." You can also use "che/quanto" to ask: "Fa differenza?" (Does it matter?) / "Quanto fa la differenza?" (How much does it matter?).
target_language_example: Anche un piccolo aiuto può fare la differenza.
native_language_example: Even a small help can make a difference.

meaning: to pee; to go pee (especially said about/with children).
additional_notes: Very common, mild and child-friendly way to say “to urinate.” Used both literally (“I need to pee”) and with children (“Do you need to go pee?”). More neutral/adult options include “fare pipì” or “urinare” (more formal/medical).
target_language_example: Scusa, devo fare la pipì.
native_language_example: Sorry, I need to pee.

meaning: to make room; to clear a path (for someone/something).
additional_notes: Used when you want people to move aside or create space, or when something/someone advances by opening a way through. Often appears as the reflexive form "farsi largo" (= to push/make one’s way through a crowd). Common in commands like "Fate largo!" (Make way!).
target_language_example: Scusi, devo passare: mi faccia largo, per favore.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I need to get through: please make room for me.

meaning: to pay the price; suffer the consequences (often: “farne le spese”).
additional_notes: Most common as the idiom **farne le spese** (“to end up paying for it”), where **ne** refers to what happened (a mistake, a decision, etc.). It’s used when someone is negatively affected by a situation, sometimes even if it wasn’t their fault. Don’t confuse it with **fare la spesa** (singular), which means “to do the grocery shopping.”
target_language_example: Alla fine, i dipendenti ne hanno fatto le spese.
native_language_example: In the end, the employees paid the price (suffered the consequences).

meaning: to teach a class; to give a lesson.
additional_notes: Used mainly with teachers/professors to mean they are teaching (giving a lesson) in a classroom or course. You’ll also hear it as "fare lezione a/di + subject" (to teach a subject) or in the plural "fare le lezioni". For attending lessons, Italians often say "seguire (una) lezione" (to attend/follow a class).
target_language_example: Il professore oggi fa lezione dalle nove alle undici.
native_language_example: The professor teaches class today from nine to eleven.

meaning: to give lessons; to tutor (or to take lessons, depending on context).
additional_notes: "Fare lezioni" literally means "to do lessons," but it’s commonly used for giving lessons (tutoring/teaching privately): "Faccio lezioni di inglese." It can also mean taking lessons when the context makes it clear (often with "di" + subject or a place/time phrase): "Faccio lezioni di piano". To be explicit, you can say "dare lezioni" (to give lessons) or "prendere lezioni" (to take lessons).
target_language_example: Faccio lezioni di matematica due volte a settimana.
native_language_example: I tutor math twice a week.

additional_notes: Commonly used as **fare pace con qualcuno** (“to make peace with someone”). You will also often hear **fare la pace** (same meaning, with the article). It can be used after an argument or to end a disagreement.
target_language_example: Dopo la lite, hanno deciso di fare pace.
native_language_example: After the argument, they decided to make peace.

additional_notes: Used to express that something is pleasing or welcome, often in polite conversation. Common patterns: "Mi fa piacere" = "I’m glad" / "That’s nice to hear"; "Mi fa piacere + infinitive" = "I’m happy to..." (e.g., "Mi fa piacere conoscerti" = "I’m happy to meet you"); "Mi farebbe piacere" is a more polite/conditional form ("I’d be pleased" / "I’d like"). Literally "to make pleasure," but in English you usually say "to be glad" rather than "it makes me pleasure."
target_language_example: Mi fa piacere sentirlo.
native_language_example: I’m glad to hear that.

meaning: to make room; to clear space.
additional_notes: Used when you want someone to move or shift things so there is space (e.g., on a bus, at a table, in a line). Often said as an imperative: "Faccia posto" (formal), "Fai posto" (informal), "Fate posto" (plural).
target_language_example: Scusi, può fare posto? Devo passare.
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you make room? I need to get through.

meaning: to put pressure (on someone); to pressure someone.
additional_notes: Used for trying to influence someone to do something (socially, emotionally, or at work). It can also be used more literally/physically (e.g., applying pressure to a wound), but in everyday conversation it most often means “to pressure” someone. Often followed by “su” + person/thing: “fare pressione su qualcuno”.
target_language_example: Non farmi pressione: decido io quando è il momento giusto.
native_language_example: Don’t pressure me: I’ll decide when the right time is.

meaning: to make something your own; to adopt/embrace (an idea).
additional_notes: Used mainly as "fare proprio + noun" meaning to take something on as your own: adopt an idea, accept a viewpoint, or internalize a concept (often after hearing it from someone else). Common in formal or neutral contexts (e.g., opinions, proposals, values). In the sense of physically taking possession, Italian more often uses "appropriarsi di".
target_language_example: Ho fatto propria la tua idea e l’ho proposta al team.
native_language_example: I made your idea my own and proposed it to the team.

meaning: to clean up; to do the cleaning.
additional_notes: Common everyday expression used for tidying or cleaning a space (home, room, office). Often used without an object when it’s clear from context: "Devo fare pulizia." You can add a place: "fare pulizia in casa / in camera". For a specific item, Italians often use "pulire" (e.g., "pulire il tavolo" = to clean the table).
target_language_example: Oggi devo fare pulizia in casa.
native_language_example: Today I have to clean up at home.

meaning: to report (something) / to make a report (often official).
additional_notes: Used for giving an official report, especially to a superior or to authorities (e.g., police, military, workplace). You may also hear "fare rapporto su (qualcosa)" = "to report on (something)". In everyday speech, Italians often use "riferire" or "fare una segnalazione/denuncia" depending on the context.
target_language_example: L’agente ha fatto rapporto al comandante sull’incidente.
native_language_example: The officer reported to the commander about the accident.

meaning: to refer to; to mention (as a reference).
additional_notes: Used with "a" + noun/pronoun to indicate what you are talking about: "fare riferimento a qualcosa/qualcuno". Common in formal, written, or professional contexts. In the past it becomes "ho/ha fatto riferimento".
target_language_example: Nel rapporto facciamo riferimento ai dati dell’anno scorso.
native_language_example: In the report we refer to last year’s data.

meaning: to be disgusting / to suck (be very bad).
additional_notes: Common spoken expression. Literally “to make disgust,” but it’s used to say something is gross (food, smells, messes) or that something is really bad (a movie, a job, your performance). Often used with “mi” to express your reaction: “Mi fa schifo” = “It disgusts me / I hate it.” Stronger and more blunt than “non mi piace” (I don’t like it), so be careful in polite situations.
target_language_example: Questo film fa schifo: non mi piace per niente.
native_language_example: This movie sucks: I don’t like it at all.

meaning: to be quiet; to keep quiet.
additional_notes: Common way to ask someone to stop making noise, often used as an instruction (especially with the imperative): “Fai silenzio!” (to one person) or “Fate silenzio!” (to more than one person / formal). You can also use it with “per favore” to sound more polite.
target_language_example: Per favore, fate silenzio: il film sta per cominciare.
native_language_example: Please, be quiet: the movie is about to start.

meaning: to make history; to be historic / groundbreaking.
additional_notes: Used for an event, achievement, or person that becomes important and memorable in history. In everyday Italian it can also mean “to make a big deal / cause a fuss” (especially in the negative: “Non fare storie!” = “Don’t make a fuss!”).
target_language_example: Quella vittoria ha fatto storia.
native_language_example: That victory made history.

meaning: to make a fuss; to complain unnecessarily.
additional_notes: Used when someone overreacts, complains, or creates unnecessary drama about something small. Often follows a negative command like “Non fare storie!” (Don’t make a fuss!).
target_language_example: Non fare storie: è solo un piccolo ritardo.
native_language_example: Don’t make a fuss: it’s just a small delay.

meaning: to make progress; to get somewhere (in life/career).
additional_notes: Used both literally and figuratively. Literally it can mean “to make your way / to go along a road” (often in contexts like travel or moving forward). Figuratively it means “to advance / succeed / make headway” (e.g., in work, studies, or a project). In the sense of “to succeed,” it’s not a direct, word-for-word translation into natural English.
target_language_example: Con impegno, nella vita si può fare strada.
native_language_example: With commitment, you can get somewhere in life.

meaning: to be brief; to make a long story short.
additional_notes: Common set phrase used to signal you’re summarizing or skipping details. Uses the pronoun “la” (referring to something like “the story/thing” you’re talking about). Often appears as “Per farla breve, ...” or “Insomma, per farla breve, ...”.
target_language_example: Per farla breve, abbiamo perso il treno e siamo tornati a casa.
native_language_example: To make a long story short, we missed the train and went back home.

meaning: to stop it; to cut it out; to be done with it.
additional_notes: Commonly used to tell someone to stop doing something annoying or to end an argument. Often in the imperative: "Falla finita!" / "Fatela finita!" (plural). Can also mean to finally finish something: "Ho deciso di farla finita con questa storia" (“I decided to be done with this matter”).
target_language_example: Basta, falla finita con queste scuse!
native_language_example: Enough—cut it out with these excuses!

meaning: to hurt yourself; to get injured.
additional_notes: Reflexive expression using fare + si: literally “to do (oneself) bad.” It’s used for accidental injuries (falling, cutting yourself, etc.). Common with the auxiliary essere in the past: "Mi sono fatto/a male" = “I hurt myself / I got hurt.” You can add where it hurts with "a" ("Mi sono fatto male alla gamba" = “I hurt my leg”).
target_language_example: Mi sono fatto male cadendo dalle scale.
native_language_example: I got hurt falling down the stairs.

additional_notes: Used in Italian just like in English to talk about quick, usually inexpensive meals (often from chain restaurants). Common with verbs like "mangiare" (to eat) or "andare" (to go): "mangiare fast food", "andare al fast food". You can also say "un fast food" (a fast-food place) or "un ristorante fast food".
target_language_example: Stasera non ho voglia di cucinare: prendiamo del fast food.
native_language_example: Tonight I don’t feel like cooking: let’s get some fast food.

additional_notes: A highly offensive insult. Literally means “get yourself fucked” (imperative). Used to angrily tell someone to go away or express strong contempt; avoid in polite or public situations.
target_language_example: Se non ti sta bene, fatti fottere.
native_language_example: If you don’t like it, fuck off.

additional_notes: Used for the wedding band exchanged during the wedding ceremony and then worn on the ring finger. In Italy it’s typically worn on the left hand. The plural is usually “fedi nuziali.”
target_language_example: Dopo la cerimonia ho messo la fede nuziale al dito.
native_language_example: After the ceremony I put the wedding ring on my finger.

additional_notes: A common New Year’s greeting said from late December through early January. Often used with the verb "Auguri" (best wishes): "Auguri e felice anno nuovo!" You’ll also see "Buon anno!" and "Buon anno nuovo!"; "Felice" sounds a bit more formal/warm than "buon" in this context.
target_language_example: Felice anno nuovo a te e alla tua famiglia!
native_language_example: Happy New Year to you and your family!

additional_notes: Used to talk about a celebration for someone’s birthday. Often appears with verbs like "fare" (to have/throw) and "organizzare" (to organize): "Fare una festa di compleanno" = to throw a birthday party. You can also specify whose it is: "la festa di compleanno di Marco".
target_language_example: Sabato facciamo una festa di compleanno per Giulia.
native_language_example: On Saturday we’re having a birthday party for Giulia.

meaning: “son of a bitch” / “motherf****r” (a very strong insult).
additional_notes: Very vulgar and offensive; used to insult someone directly or express intense anger. Avoid in polite conversation. Literally means “daughter of a prostitute,” but it’s commonly used like English “son of a bitch.”
target_language_example: Quel figlio di puttana mi ha rubato il portafoglio!
native_language_example: That son of a bitch stole my wallet!

additional_notes: Strong profanity used to insult someone or express intense anger. Avoid in polite conversation; it can easily start a fight. In Italian it’s often shouted as an expletive, sometimes even about a situation (“Che figlio di puttana!”), but it remains highly offensive.
target_language_example: Quel figlio di puttana mi ha tagliato la strada!
native_language_example: That son of a bitch cut me off!

meaning: only child (a child with no brothers or sisters).
additional_notes: Used to say someone has no siblings. You can use it for any gender: for a woman you still say "sono figlia unica". The plural is "figli unici" (male/mixed) or "figlie uniche" (female).
target_language_example: Sono figlio unico, quindi non ho fratelli né sorelle.
native_language_example: I’m an only child, so I don’t have any brothers or sisters.

additional_notes: Used to say something begins immediately and continues into the future. Often appears with verbs like "decidere" or "promettere" (e.g., "da fin d'ora" or "fin d'ora in poi" are common variations).
target_language_example: Da fin d'ora, cercherò di arrivare puntuale.
native_language_example: From now on, I’ll try to arrive on time.

meaning: “up to here”; “so far / up to now.”
additional_notes: Used to talk about a limit in place (“up to here”) or in time/progress (“so far, up to this point”). Often appears in phrases like “Fin qui tutto bene” (“So far, so good”) or “Siamo arrivati fin qui” (“We’ve made it this far”).
target_language_example: Fin qui tutto bene, ma adesso non so cosa fare.
native_language_example: So far, so good, but now I don’t know what to do.
