additional_notes: Common everyday term for Saturday–Sunday (or the end part of the week in general). Often used with prepositions: "nel fine settimana" (over the weekend), "questo fine settimana" (this weekend), "il fine settimana scorso" (last weekend). In Italian you can also hear the loanword "weekend".
target_language_example: Cosa fai questo fine settimana?
native_language_example: What are you doing this weekend?

additional_notes: Used to indicate an endpoint in time (fino a domani = until tomorrow), a maximum limit (fino a 10 euro = up to 10 euros), or a destination/range (fino a Roma = as far as Rome). Often followed by a date, time, number, or place.
target_language_example: Resto qui fino alle sei.
native_language_example: I’m staying here until six.

meaning: up to one’s neck; (figuratively) swamped/in deep (in something).
additional_notes: Literally means “up to the neck.” Often used figuratively to say you’re very busy or deeply involved in something, frequently with "+ di" (e.g., work) or "+ nei/nelle" (e.g., problems). Can also be literal about water/snow, etc.
target_language_example: Sono fino al collo nel lavoro questa settimana.
native_language_example: I’m swamped with work this week.

meaning: to the core; through and through.
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression meaning completely, deeply, or in an extreme way (often about being cold, wet, tired, or about someone’s character/beliefs). Literally “up to the marrow,” similar in idea to “to the bone,” but you usually translate it as “to the core/through and through.” Often used after adjectives: "bagnato fino al midollo" (soaking wet), "stanco fino al midollo" (exhausted), "onesto fino al midollo" (honest to the core).
target_language_example: Dopo la pioggia, ero bagnato fino al midollo.
native_language_example: After the rain, I was soaked to the bone.

meaning: until the end; all the way (to the end).
additional_notes: Used to say something continues or lasts up to the final point of an event, process, period of time, trip, etc. It can describe persistence or commitment (e.g., staying, fighting, watching) and is slightly emphatic. Often used with verbs like restare (to stay), aspettare (to wait), guardare (to watch), continuare (to continue).
target_language_example: Resto con te fino alla fine.
native_language_example: I’ll stay with you until the end.

meaning: (Usually written "fin da") “since (as far back as)…” / “ever since…”.
additional_notes: In modern Italian, this expression is almost always spelled and used as **fin da** (not *fino da*). It means “since” in the sense of “starting from a point in the past” and is commonly followed by a time expression (e.g., *fin da bambino* = “since I was a child”) or by *quando* + clause. It’s stronger/more emphatic than simple *da* (“since/from”).
target_language_example: Lo conosco fin da bambino.
native_language_example: I’ve known him since he was a child.

meaning: all the way; completely; through to the end.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize doing something fully or to the very end (physically or figuratively). Often with verbs like capire (to understand), andare (to go), seguire (to follow), and with expressions like in fondo in fondo (“deep down”).
target_language_example: Voglio capire fino in fondo cosa è successo.
native_language_example: I want to understand completely what happened.

additional_notes: Literally “flake of snow.” Common in weather talk and winter descriptions. Also used figuratively to mean a “snowflake” (a very sensitive person), but that meaning is more context-dependent and can sound mocking.
target_language_example: Guarda, sta cadendo un fiocco di neve!
native_language_example: Look, a snowflake is falling!

additional_notes: Used for the kitchen appliance that heats food with microwaves. Often shortened to just “microonde” in everyday speech. Note the plural form: “le microonde” (the microwave), and “un forno a microonde” for “a microwave oven.”
target_language_example: Scalda la pasta nel forno a microonde, per favore.
native_language_example: Heat up the pasta in the microwave, please.

additional_notes: Used to say something was heard/understood perfectly, or to emphasize that a message/instruction is very clear. Often appears after verbs like "sentire" (to hear) or "capire" (to understand): "Ti sento forte e chiaro". It can also describe how someone speaks: "Parla forte e chiaro" (Speak loudly and clearly).
target_language_example: Ti sento forte e chiaro.
native_language_example: I hear you loud and clear.

additional_notes: Used to refer collectively to a country’s military branches (army, navy, air force, etc.). Often appears with the definite article: "le Forze Armate" (capitalization is common in official contexts). Singular is uncommon in this meaning ("forza armata" is rare).
target_language_example: Mio fratello lavora nelle Forze Armate.
native_language_example: My brother works in the armed forces.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or emphasize that something should stay private. Common in everyday speech. You can also hear "tra noi" with the same meaning. Often followed by a comma: "Fra noi, ..."
target_language_example: Fra noi, non mi fido molto di lui.
native_language_example: Just between us, I don’t trust him very much.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen shortly (a small amount of time from now). It’s interchangeable with "tra poco" in everyday Italian. Often used with the future tense or the present to talk about the near future.
target_language_example: Arrivo fra poco, sto finendo una cosa.
native_language_example: I’ll be there in a little while; I’m finishing something.

meaning: a piece of seafood (literally, “fruit of the sea”).
additional_notes: More commonly used in the plural: **frutti di mare** = “seafood” (often meaning mixed seafood, especially shellfish) as a dish or category on menus (e.g., *spaghetti ai frutti di mare*). In restaurants you’ll also see *pesce e frutti di mare* (“fish and seafood”).
target_language_example: Vorrei gli spaghetti ai frutti di mare, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like the spaghetti with mixed seafood, please.

additional_notes: A shortened, more literary/old-fashioned form of "fuori di". It can mean physical location ("outside") or exclusion/exception ("except for" / "apart from"). Common in fixed expressions like "fuor di dubbio" (without a doubt), "fuor di qui!" (out of here!), and "fuor di stagione" (out of season).
target_language_example: Fuor di dubbio, è una buona idea.
native_language_example: Without a doubt, it’s a good idea.

meaning: outside of; out of (also: except for).
additional_notes: An older/less common spelling of "fuori di". Used to indicate being outside a place ("fuora di casa" = outside the house) or, in some contexts, to mean "except for". In modern everyday Italian you’ll more often see "fuori di" or "tranne" (except).
target_language_example: Aspettami fuora di casa.
native_language_example: Wait for me outside the house.

meaning: out of the house; away from home.
additional_notes: Used to say you’re not at home (e.g., you’re out running errands) or to describe things you do away from home (e.g., eating out, working outside the home). Often follows the verb: “essere fuori casa” = “to be out/away from home.”
target_language_example: Stasera non sono a casa: sono fuori casa con degli amici.
native_language_example: Tonight I’m not at home: I’m out with some friends.

additional_notes: Used to describe a situation, person, emotion, or event that is no longer manageable or regulated. Often follows a form of “essere” (e.g., “è fuori controllo”, “sono fuori controllo”). Can be literal (a vehicle) or figurative (anger, spending, a party).
target_language_example: La situazione è fuori controllo.
native_language_example: The situation is out of control.

meaning: out of the way; (also) out of here / leave me alone.
additional_notes: Literally “out of (my) feet,” used to tell someone to move away or stop bothering you. Often sounds annoyed or rude, especially as an order (e.g., “Stai fuori dai piedi!”). Can also be used more neutrally to mean something is not in the way (e.g., an object).
target_language_example: Stai fuori dai piedi, sto lavorando!
native_language_example: Get out of the way / Leave me alone, I’m working!

additional_notes: Used to indicate being outside a physical place or beyond a boundary. It’s commonly followed by a noun or pronoun: "fuori di casa" (outside the house), "fuori di qui" (out of here). In everyday Italian, "fuori" alone is often used with "da" or without "di" (e.g., "fuori casa", "fuori dal negozio").
target_language_example: Aspettami fuori di casa.
native_language_example: Wait for me outside the house.

meaning: crazy; out of your mind (often: really excited/enthusiastic).
additional_notes: Informal expression. It can mean someone is acting irrationally (“You’re crazy!”), but very often it means you’re extremely excited or obsessed with something (“I’m crazy about it”). Common patterns: “Sei fuori di testa!” and “Sono fuori di testa per + [noun/person]” (I’m crazy about…).
target_language_example: Sono fuori di testa per questa canzone!
native_language_example: I’m crazy about this song!

additional_notes: Used to say that a style, item, or habit is no longer fashionable. Often used after the noun: "un vestito fuori moda" (an out-of-fashion dress). Opposite: "di moda" / "alla moda" (fashionable).
target_language_example: Quel cappotto è un po' fuori moda, ma è ancora molto comodo.
native_language_example: That coat is a bit out of fashion, but it’s still very comfortable.

meaning: out of place; inappropriate; not in the right spot.
additional_notes: Used for both things and people/situations. For objects it can mean something is in the wrong position (not where it belongs). For behavior/clothes/comments it often means “inappropriate” or “doesn’t fit the situation.” Often used with the verb essere: “è fuori posto.”
target_language_example: Mi sento fuori posto a questa festa.
native_language_example: I feel out of place at this party.

meaning: out of service; not working (temporarily unavailable).
additional_notes: Used for machines, services, lines, elevators, toilets, ticket machines, etc. It means something isn’t operating or available at the moment. You’ll often see it on signs: “Ascensore fuori servizio” (elevator out of service).
target_language_example: Mi scusi, il bancomat è fuori servizio.
native_language_example: Excuse me, the ATM is out of service.

meaning: off the road; off track / lost (wrong way).
additional_notes: Used both literally (a vehicle leaving the road, or off-road driving) and figuratively (a person going the wrong way or being mistaken). With verbs like essere/andare: “Sono fuori strada” = “I’m lost / I’m mistaken.”
target_language_example: Scusi, credo di essere fuori strada: questa è la strada per il Duomo?
native_language_example: Excuse me, I think I’m lost: is this the road to the cathedral?

meaning: to give up; to throw in the towel.
additional_notes: Common idiom from boxing: when a corner “throws the sponge/towel” to stop the fight. Used for quitting or admitting defeat in many everyday situations. It’s not rude, but it is informal/idiomatic. Often used as “Non gettare la spugna!” (Don’t give up!) or “Ho gettato la spugna.” (I gave up).
target_language_example: Dopo tanti tentativi, stavo per gettare la spugna, ma poi ci sono riuscito.
native_language_example: After many attempts, I was about to throw in the towel, but then I managed to do it.

additional_notes: Used for games played on a table (often with a board and pieces/cards). Plural: "giochi da tavolo". You’ll often see it in shops or when suggesting an activity: "Ti piacciono i giochi da tavolo?"
target_language_example: Stasera giochiamo a un gioco da tavolo con gli amici.
native_language_example: Tonight we’re playing a board game with friends.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a joke or clever effect based on words with similar sounds or multiple meanings. Often appears with verbs like fare (to make) or essere (to be): “È un gioco di parole.” / “Ho fatto un gioco di parole.”
target_language_example: È un gioco di parole: “piano piano” può voler dire anche “slowly.”
native_language_example: It’s a pun/wordplay: “piano piano” can also mean “slowly.”

meaning: a magic trick; a sleight-of-hand trick.
additional_notes: Used for stage/close-up magic tricks performed by a magician (often involving dexterity and misdirection). You’ll also see it in the plural: “giochi di prestigio”. Not related to “prestige” in the sense of social status.
target_language_example: Il mago ha fatto un gioco di prestigio con le carte.
native_language_example: The magician did a magic trick with the cards.

meaning: “day and night”; all the time, continuously.
additional_notes: Literally “day and night.” Used to emphasize that something happens constantly or without stopping (often about working, studying, thinking, or caring for someone).
target_language_example: Da quando è nato il bambino, lavoriamo giorno e notte.
native_language_example: Since the baby was born, we’ve been working day and night.

meaning: to go/turn around; also: to beat around the bush.
additional_notes: Used literally for moving around a place or object: "girare intorno a" = "to go around" (e.g., a building). Figuratively, it means avoiding the main point instead of saying something directly (similar to "beat around the bush").
target_language_example: Smettila di girare intorno e dimmi la verità.
native_language_example: Stop beating around the bush and tell me the truth.

meaning: to turn your head; (often: “mi gira la testa”) to feel dizzy / have your head spinning.
additional_notes: Literal sense: physically turning your head (e.g., to look behind you). Very common is the impersonal pattern with an indirect pronoun: “Mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi gira la testa” = “I/you/he/she/we/you all feel dizzy” (literally “my/your/etc. head is spinning”). You may also hear “girare la testa a qualcuno” meaning to make someone infatuated or to make someone’s head turn.
target_language_example: Mi gira la testa, devo sedermi.
native_language_example: I feel dizzy; I need to sit down.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a significant occasion (often a wedding day, an exam, a graduation, or another long-awaited event). It’s the shortened form of "grande giorno"; "gran" is used before a masculine singular noun (giorno). Often appears with "il" ("il gran giorno").
target_language_example: Finalmente è arrivato il gran giorno: domani ci sposiamo!
native_language_example: The big day has finally arrived: tomorrow we’re getting married!

additional_notes: Used to talk about a majority or a big portion of something. Often followed by “di” + noun: “gran parte della giornata” (a large part of the day). It can mean “most of” when the context implies a majority: “gran parte degli italiani” (most Italians). “Gran” is a shortened form of “grande” before a noun.
target_language_example: Ho passato gran parte della giornata a studiare.
native_language_example: I spent a large part of the day studying.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens because of someone/something. Often positive (“thanks to you”), but it can also be neutral or even negative (“due to the traffic”). It is followed by a noun/pronoun: grazie a te, grazie al tuo aiuto, grazie alla pioggia.
target_language_example: Grazie al tuo aiuto, ho finito il lavoro in tempo.
native_language_example: Thanks to your help, I finished the work on time.

additional_notes: Used to express relief or gratitude that something happened (or didn’t happen). Often said on its own as an exclamation ("Grazie a Dio!") or followed by a clause ("Grazie a Dio, ..."). Also commonly written "grazie a Dio" or "Grazie a Dio" at the start of a sentence.
target_language_example: Grazie a Dio, siamo arrivati in tempo.
native_language_example: Thank God, we arrived on time.

additional_notes: Very common, polite way to express strong thanks. Often used on its own, or followed by “per…” (“Grazie mille per l’aiuto!” = “Thanks a lot for the help!”). You may also hear “mille grazie,” which means the same.
target_language_example: Grazie mille per il tuo aiuto!
native_language_example: Thanks a lot for your help!

additional_notes: Used in medical contexts to indicate someone’s blood classification (e.g., A, B, AB, O, with Rh factor: positivo/negativo). Common in phrases like “Qual è il tuo gruppo sanguigno?” (What’s your blood type?) and on medical forms.
target_language_example: Qual è il tuo gruppo sanguigno?
native_language_example: What’s your blood type?

meaning: to buy time; to gain time.
additional_notes: Used when you want to delay or postpone something so you have more time to decide, prepare, or solve a problem. Common in everyday speech and work/school contexts. Similar idea to English “buy time.”
target_language_example: Dobbiamo guadagnare tempo finché arrivano i rinforzi.
native_language_example: We have to buy time until reinforcements arrive.

meaning: to look (someone) in the face; to face (something).
additional_notes: Often used literally with a person: “Guardami in faccia” = “Look me in the face.” It can also be figurative, meaning to face reality or a problem: “Guardare in faccia la realtà” = “Face reality.” A common fixed expression is “non guardare in faccia a nessuno” (“to show no mercy / not to care who you hurt”).
target_language_example: È difficile guardare in faccia la realtà, ma dobbiamo farlo.
native_language_example: It’s hard to face reality, but we have to do it.

additional_notes: Refers to a person whose job is to protect someone (often a celebrity, politician, or important person). It’s usually singular in Italian; plural: "guardie del corpo". The more general word for a security guard is "guardia" or "guardia giurata" (armed/security guard), but "guardia del corpo" specifically means a personal bodyguard.
target_language_example: Il cantante è arrivato con la sua guardia del corpo.
native_language_example: The singer arrived with his bodyguard.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a large-scale war involving many countries. Often used with an ordinal number: "la Prima guerra mondiale" (World War I) and "la Seconda guerra mondiale" (World War II). "Guerra" is feminine, so it takes feminine articles (la/una).
target_language_example: Mio nonno è nato durante la Seconda guerra mondiale.
native_language_example: My grandfather was born during World War II.

additional_notes: A formal/neutral term used in news, history, politics, and discussions about international relations and weapons. It’s typically used with articles ("una/ la guerra nucleare").
target_language_example: Speriamo che non ci sia mai una guerra nucleare.
native_language_example: Let’s hope there is never a nuclear war.

meaning: tour guide; travel guidebook (depending on context).
additional_notes: Most commonly means a person who guides visitors (a tour guide). It can also mean a guidebook, especially in shops/bookstores (e.g., "una guida turistica di Roma"). For a person you can also say "una guida"; for a book you may also hear "guida di viaggio".
target_language_example: Abbiamo prenotato una guida turistica per visitare il centro storico.
native_language_example: We booked a tour guide to visit the historic city center.

additional_notes: Literally “you have understood” (2nd person singular). Common in conversation to check that someone understands, like “You understand?” or “You get it?”. It can be neutral, but depending on tone it may sound impatient or like “You hear me?/Get it?”
target_language_example: Allora giri a destra e poi a sinistra, hai capito?
native_language_example: So you turn right and then left—got it?

meaning: “you bet!/definitely!” (often used to strongly agree or emphasize).
additional_notes: Colloquial expression used to intensify what comes next, often with **se**: *Hai voglia se…* = “You bet… / Definitely…”. Depending on tone, it can also be ironic, closer to “yeah, right / as if”. Related pattern: **hai voglia a + infinitive** = “try as you might / no matter how much you…”.
target_language_example: Hai voglia se mi piace questo posto!
native_language_example: You bet I like this place!

additional_notes: Common polite phrase to ask to speak or get clarification (in class, at a meeting, in a store, etc.). Often followed by a question introduced by “su” (about): “Ho una domanda su…” You can soften it with “Scusi/Scusa” (Excuse me) or “Posso fare una domanda?” (Can I ask a question?).
target_language_example: Scusi, ho una domanda: a che ora apre il museo?
native_language_example: Excuse me, I have a question: what time does the museum open?

meaning: a hot dog (sausage in a bun).
additional_notes: Common English loanword in Italian, especially in fast-food contexts. It usually stays the same in the plural (due hot dog), though you may also see hot dogs. You can also describe it as a "panino con würstel".
target_language_example: Vorrei un hot dog con senape, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a hot dog with mustard, please.

additional_notes: Literally “Greek i.” Used when spelling out letters (e.g., names, codes). A common alternative name is “ipsilon.”
target_language_example: Come si scrive? Con la i greca.
native_language_example: How do you spell it? With a Y.

additional_notes: In standard Italian this idea is usually expressed as **alla lunga** (“in the long run”). The form **i lunga** is not common and may be a typo or nonstandard writing. **Alla lunga** is used to say what happens after some time or what becomes true eventually.
target_language_example: Alla lunga, è meglio dire la verità.
native_language_example: In the long run, it’s better to tell the truth.

additional_notes: Used to describe orientation/position along the length of something (not across it). Common with verbs like tagliare (to cut), piegare (to fold), mettere (to place). Often paired with "in largo" (widthwise). Note: learners sometimes mistype it as "i lungo"; the correct form is "in lungo".
target_language_example: Taglia la carta in lungo, per favore.
native_language_example: Cut the paper lengthwise, please.

additional_notes: Italian possessives usually take the definite article and agree with the thing possessed (gender/number), not with the owner. So i suoi is used with masculine plural nouns (e.g., i suoi amici = his friends). On its own, i suoi can mean “his family/relatives/people,” depending on context (e.g., tornare dai suoi = to go back to his family).
target_language_example: Ha chiamato i suoi per dire che stava bene.
native_language_example: He called his family to say he was fine.

meaning: as soon as possible; as early as possible.
additional_notes: Used to express urgency or a request to do something at the earliest opportunity. In everyday Italian, you’ll very often hear/see the equivalent forms “il prima possibile”, “prima possibile” (without “il”), and “il più presto possibile”. It commonly follows verbs like “fare” (to do), “venire” (to come), “tornare” (to return), “chiamare” (to call).
target_language_example: Puoi chiamarmi il prima possibile?
native_language_example: Can you call me as soon as possible?

additional_notes: Used like a more formal, precise alternative to "che" to introduce a relative clause. It agrees in gender and number with the noun it refers to: il quale (m.sg.), la quale (f.sg.), i quali (m.pl.), le quali (f.pl.). Often used after prepositions: "nel quale" = "in which", "con la quale" = "with which/whom".
target_language_example: Ho parlato con Marco, il quale mi ha dato un buon consiglio.
native_language_example: I spoke with Marco, who gave me good advice.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a person’s fingerprint (biometrics), used for identification (police, passports, phones). It can also refer more generally to a “digital footprint/fingerprint” in tech contexts, but the everyday meaning is the physical fingerprint. Plural: "impronte digitali".
target_language_example: Per sbloccare il telefono, usa l’impronta digitale.
native_language_example: To unlock the phone, use the fingerprint.

additional_notes: Used for rental housing, cars, etc. With "essere" it means something is rented/for rent ("La casa è in affitto"). With "dare" it means to rent out ("Dare in affitto"), and with "prendere" it means to rent ("Prendere in affitto"). Often contrasted with "in vendita" (for sale).
target_language_example: Cerco un appartamento in affitto vicino al centro.
native_language_example: I’m looking for an apartment for rent near the city center.

meaning: lying in wait; hiding and ready to attack (or act).
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is hidden and waiting for the right moment. Common with verbs like "stare" (to be) and "mettersi" (to get). It can be literal (an animal/a person) or figurative (a danger/problem): "un pericolo in agguato" = a lurking danger.
target_language_example: C’era un gatto in agguato dietro l’angolo.
native_language_example: There was a cat lying in wait behind the corner.

meaning: up (above), high up; at/on the top.
additional_notes: Used to indicate a higher position or direction (often paired with verbs like andare/guardare/mettere: "go/look/put up"). It can also mean "at the top" of something (e.g., a page or a list). Often contrasted with "in basso" (down, at the bottom).
target_language_example: Guarda in alto: c’è un uccello sul tetto.
native_language_example: Look up: there’s a bird on the roof.

meaning: "in other words" / "to put it another way."
additional_notes: Used to rephrase or clarify what you just said, often to make it simpler or more precise. Common in both spoken and written Italian; it can also introduce a summary or explanation.
target_language_example: Non posso venire stasera; in altre parole, devo restare a casa.
native_language_example: I can’t come tonight; in other words, I have to stay home.

additional_notes: Used for people, trains/planes, deliveries, messages, etc. Very common on signs and announcements (e.g., at stations) and in shipping/tracking updates. Often followed by a place or time: “in arrivo a Roma” (arriving in Rome), “in arrivo tra 5 minuti” (arriving in 5 minutes).
target_language_example: Il treno per Milano è in arrivo.
native_language_example: The train to Milan is arriving.

additional_notes: Used with "essere" ("sono/siamo in ascolto") to say someone is listening. Often used in announcements and media contexts (radio/TV/podcasts): "Restate in ascolto" = "Stay tuned." You can also specify what you’re listening to with "di": "in ascolto di musica".
target_language_example: Restate in ascolto: tra poco iniziamo.
native_language_example: Stay tuned: we’ll start shortly.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something in the most general sense, without comparing to anything else (e.g., “overall”) or to emphasize “absolutely.” Common in phrases like “il migliore in assoluto” (the best ever/absolutely the best) and “in assoluto, sì/no” (absolutely yes/no).
target_language_example: Per me, questo è il miglior gelato in assoluto.
native_language_example: For me, this is the best ice cream ever.

additional_notes: Used to say you are waiting for someone/something: “in attesa di” + noun/infinitive (in attesa del treno = waiting for the train; in attesa di partire = waiting to leave). You can also use it like “pending” in emails or notices (in attesa di una risposta = pending a reply).
target_language_example: Sono in attesa del treno.
native_language_example: I’m waiting for the train.

meaning: based on; according to (often used as “in base a”).
additional_notes: Used to indicate the criterion or information something is decided or done by. Very common in formal and everyday Italian, especially as **in base a + noun/pronoun**: *in base ai dati* (based on the data), *in base a quello che hai detto* (based on what you said).
target_language_example: In base alle previsioni, domani pioverà.
native_language_example: According to the forecast, it will rain tomorrow.

meaning: down; at the bottom; lower down.
additional_notes: Used to indicate a lower position (often compared to something else) or a place at the bottom of a page/screen/map. Common with verbs like essere/stare/mettere/andare: “Sta in basso” (it’s down low), “Mettilo in basso” (put it at the bottom). Often paired with “in alto” (up, at the top).
target_language_example: L’uscita è in basso a destra.
native_language_example: The exit is at the bottom right.

additional_notes: Used for forms, documents, and fields you haven’t completed yet: “lasciare in bianco” = to leave blank. Also used with “assegno” (check): “un assegno in bianco” = a blank/signed check (a ‘blank check’).
target_language_example: Ho lasciato in bianco l’ultima domanda del modulo.
native_language_example: I left the last question on the form blank.

meaning: “Good luck!” (said to wish someone luck, especially before a test, performance, interview, etc.).
additional_notes: A very common idiomatic good-luck wish. The traditional reply is “Crepi!” or “Crepi il lupo!” (roughly “May the wolf die!”). You’ll also hear a more modern/polite reply: “Viva il lupo!” (“Long live the wolf!”). Often used with verbs like “fare”: “In bocca al lupo per l’esame!”.
target_language_example: In bocca al lupo per l’esame di domani!
native_language_example: Good luck for tomorrow’s exam!

additional_notes: Common in speech and writing to introduce a summary (like “in short”) or to say something will happen soon (like “shortly”). Often followed by a comma when used to summarize: “In breve, …”.
target_language_example: In breve, dobbiamo partire adesso.
native_language_example: In short, we have to leave now.

additional_notes: Used to say what you receive or do as compensation for something else. Often followed by "di" + noun/pronoun ("in cambio di...") or used with verbs like "dare" (to give) and "ricevere" (to receive).
target_language_example: Ti aiuto con i compiti in cambio di un caffè.
native_language_example: I’ll help you with your homework in exchange for a coffee.

additional_notes: Used to say what you get (or give) as a trade-off or compensation. It’s followed by a noun or an infinitive (e.g., "in cambio di aiutarmi" = "in exchange for helping me"). Often used in deals, favors, or negotiations.
target_language_example: Ti aiuto con i compiti in cambio di un caffè.
native_language_example: I’ll help you with your homework in exchange for a coffee.

meaning: assigned to; under the responsibility/authority of (often in legal/administrative language).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something (a duty, right, decision, cost, responsibility, authority) belongs to a person/office/entity. Common in formal documents: "è in capo a..." = "it is the responsibility of..." / "it falls under...". Not used much in everyday casual speech.
target_language_example: La responsabilità della pratica è in capo all’ufficio amministrativo.
native_language_example: Responsibility for the case is with the administrative office.

meaning: “in case” (if it happens; as a precaution).
additional_notes: Often followed by **di** + infinitive (in case of doing something): *in caso di arrivare tardi…*. For “in case of + noun” you usually say **in caso di**: *in caso di pioggia…* (“in case of rain…”). Common in warnings, instructions, and planning.
target_language_example: Porta un ombrello in caso di pioggia.
native_language_example: Bring an umbrella in case of rain.

meaning: in a circle; in a circular shape/formation.
additional_notes: Used to describe people or objects arranged in a circle, or moving in a circular way. Common with verbs like stare/essere (to be), mettersi (to get into a formation), sedersi (to sit), andare/camminare (to go/walk).
target_language_example: Ci sediamo in cerchio e parliamo un po'.
native_language_example: We sit in a circle and chat a bit.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "sentirsi" (or "essere") to say you feel guilty or responsible for something. Often followed by "per" + noun/infinitive ("in colpa per...") or "con" + person ("in colpa con...").
target_language_example: Mi sento in colpa per averti mentito.
native_language_example: I feel guilty for lying to you.

additional_notes: Used to say that two or more people/things share the same thing (an interest, opinion, characteristic, etc.). Often used with "avere" (to have): "avere qualcosa in comune" = "to have something in common."
target_language_example: Io e mia sorella abbiamo molti interessi in comune.
native_language_example: My sister and I have many interests in common.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens without stopping or keeps happening again and again. Common in everyday speech; often pairs with verbs like parlare (to talk), suonare (to ring), piovere (to rain), chiedere (to ask). Similar to "continuamente" and "sempre" but can sound a bit more emphatic/annoyed depending on tone.
target_language_example: Il telefono squilla in continuazione.
native_language_example: The phone keeps ringing nonstop.

additional_notes: Used to say something is happening now or is underway. Common with nouns like lavori (work/roadworks), lezione (lesson/class), riunione (meeting), trattative (negotiations), and cambiamenti (changes). Often appears in signs or announcements: “Lavori in corso” = “Work in progress / Roadworks.”
target_language_example: Ci sono lavori in corso, quindi la strada è chiusa.
native_language_example: There are roadworks in progress, so the road is closed.

meaning: in detail; in a detailed way.
additional_notes: Used to say you want more specific information or a thorough explanation. Often with verbs like spiegare (to explain), descrivere (to describe), raccontare (to tell), vedere/guardare (to look at), parlare (to talk). Common in both spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Puoi spiegarmelo in dettaglio?
native_language_example: Can you explain it to me in detail?

additional_notes: Used for live TV/radio/streaming or any event happening right now (not recorded). Often appears with verbs like essere/andare/trasmettere: “Siamo in diretta”, “Va in diretta alle 8”, “Trasmettono in diretta”.
target_language_example: La partita è in diretta su Rai 1.
native_language_example: The match is live on Rai 1.

additional_notes: Used with “essere” to say people have different opinions: “essere in disaccordo (con qualcuno/su qualcosa)”. Slightly formal; in everyday speech you’ll also hear “non essere d’accordo”.
target_language_example: Sono in disaccordo con te su questo punto.
native_language_example: I disagree with you on this point.

meaning: under discussion; being debated; in question (not certain).
additional_notes: Used to say something is currently being talked about/negotiated (e.g., a proposal, a plan), or that something is doubtful/at risk. Common patterns: “mettere in discussione” = to call into question/challenge; “essere in discussione” = to be under discussion/in doubt.
target_language_example: Il progetto è ancora in discussione, quindi la data potrebbe cambiare.
native_language_example: The project is still under discussion, so the date could change.

meaning: aside; off to the side; apart (away from others).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is positioned away from the main group or action, often implying privacy or discretion (e.g., to talk in private). Can describe a place or a person: "mettersi/stare in disparte" = to step/stay aside.
target_language_example: Possiamo parlare un attimo in disparte?
native_language_example: Can we talk for a moment in private (aside)?

additional_notes: Used to say you’re uncertain about something or that something is not clear. Common with verbs like essere (to be) and avere (to have): “Sono in dubbio” (I’m unsure), “Ho un dubbio” (I have a doubt). Also appears in the set phrase “Nel dubbio, …” meaning “When in doubt, …”.
target_language_example: Sono in dubbio su quale treno prendere.
native_language_example: I’m not sure which train to take.

additional_notes: Used to confirm, correct, or add emphasis to what was just said. Often translates as “actually” in conversation (sometimes with a mild correction), and as “in fact/indeed” in more formal contexts. Placement is flexible: commonly at the beginning (“In effetti, ...”) or after the verb (“È in effetti ...”).
target_language_example: In effetti, hai ragione: non è così difficile.
native_language_example: Actually, you’re right: it’s not that difficult.

meaning: in the face; (straight) in front of someone; (figuratively) right in someone’s face.
additional_notes: Used to indicate location on the face (often with verbs like dare “to give,” sputare “to spit,” guardare “to look,” dire “to say”). It can also mean directly to someone’s face (dire qualcosa in faccia = to say something to someone’s face). Common in expressions like: in faccia a ("in the face of" / "right in front of"), sbattere in faccia ("to slam in someone’s face"), ridere in faccia ("to laugh in someone’s face"), tirare in faccia ("to throw at someone’s face").
target_language_example: Non dirglielo in faccia: potrebbe offendersi.
native_language_example: Don’t say it to his face: he might get offended.

meaning: when it comes to; regarding (a specific topic).
additional_notes: Used to introduce the area/topic you’re talking about, similar to “as for…” or “in terms of…”. It’s common in more neutral or slightly formal contexts (writing, explanations). Typically followed by a noun, pronoun, or infinitive phrase: “in fatto di soldi” (when it comes to money), “in fatto di cucinare” (when it comes to cooking).
target_language_example: In fatto di cucina, mia nonna è la migliore.
native_language_example: When it comes to cooking, my grandma is the best.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that is burning. Often follows the verb essere (to be): "La casa è in fiamme". Also used figuratively to mean something is very intense or in turmoil (e.g., "La città è in fiamme" = the city is in chaos).
target_language_example: La macchina è in fiamme!
native_language_example: The car is on fire!

additional_notes: Used to describe plants/trees/flowers when they are blooming (often in spring). It can also be used figuratively to mean someone or something is “in full bloom” or thriving (e.g., a business, a career, health).
target_language_example: In primavera il giardino è in fiore.
native_language_example: In spring the garden is in bloom.

meaning: at the end; deep down; basically/after all.
additional_notes: Common with place/direction meaning “at the end (of a room/street/line)”: "in fondo alla strada" = “at the end of the street.” It can also mean “deep down” (your true feelings/opinion): "in fondo lo so" = “deep down I know it.” With a summary/justification tone it can mean “after all / basically,” often followed by a reason: "In fondo, hai ragione" = “After all, you’re right.”
target_language_example: Il bagno è in fondo al corridoio.
native_language_example: The bathroom is at the end of the hallway.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is physically fit or feeling well/energetic. Common with the verb "essere": "Sono in forma" (I’m in shape). It can also describe things that are in good condition or properly working: "Il computer è in forma" (the computer is working well), though this is less common than for people.
target_language_example: Dopo le vacanze devo rimettermi in forma.
native_language_example: After the vacation I need to get back in shape.

additional_notes: Emphatic version of “in forma” (“in shape”), using the superlative suffix -issima. Common in casual speech to say you’re doing very well physically or energetically. You can also say “essere in formissima” (to be in great shape).
target_language_example: Dopo le vacanze mi sento in formissima!
native_language_example: After the holidays I feel in great shape!

additional_notes: Used to say you need to do something quickly or without delay. Often appears with verbs like andare/venire/fare (e.g., andare in fretta = to go quickly). Similar in meaning to "di fretta" and "in fretta e furia" (more emphatic).
target_language_example: Devo andare in fretta, sono in ritardo.
native_language_example: I have to go quickly, I’m late.

additional_notes: Commonly used with "essere" ("essere in gamba") to say someone is good at what they do or quick and reliable. It’s often a friendly compliment: "Sei in gamba!" It can also describe being physically up and about (not stuck in bed), especially after being sick: "Oggi sono di nuovo in gamba."
target_language_example: Sei proprio in gamba: hai risolto il problema in cinque minuti.
native_language_example: You’re really capable: you solved the problem in five minutes.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something as a general rule, not in specific cases. Common at the start of a sentence or after the topic: "In generale, ..." / "Le persone, in generale, ...".
target_language_example: In generale, preferisco il caffè al tè.
native_language_example: In general, I prefer coffee to tea.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what is true most of the time, on average, or as a general rule. It’s common at the start of a sentence or after the verb: “In genere vado…” / “Vado in genere…”. Similar to “di solito” (usually), but slightly more neutral/formal.
target_language_example: In genere, il lunedì lavoro da casa.
native_language_example: In general, on Mondays I work from home.

additional_notes: Used to describe being in a kneeling position (often for prayer, asking, or doing something on the floor). It can also be used figuratively to mean “brought to its knees” (overwhelmed or crippled), e.g., by problems or an emergency.
target_language_example: Si è messo in ginocchio per fare una proposta.
native_language_example: He got down on one knee to make a proposal.

meaning: at stake; in play; being played.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is involved, could be won or lost, or is at risk (“at stake”). It can also mean something is currently happening/active (“in play”) or literally “being played” (a game or match). Often used with verbs like essere/mettere/tenere: “essere in gioco” (to be at stake/in play), “mettere in gioco” (to put at stake; to put into play, also figuratively ‘to put yourself on the line’).
target_language_example: In questa partita ci sono tre punti in gioco.
native_language_example: In this match there are three points at stake.

meaning: around; out and about (also: around/on the loose).
additional_notes: Very common phrase. Often used with verbs like andare/essere/stare: "andare in giro" = to go around, to wander; "essere/stare in giro" = to be out and about. It can also mean "around" in the sense of "available/present": "Non c’è nessuno in giro" = There’s nobody around. With some nouns it can imply something is circulating or loose: "un virus in giro" = a virus going around; "un cane in giro" = a dog on the loose. Not the same as "in giro per" (= around/through + a place, e.g., around the city).
target_language_example: Oggi pomeriggio sono in giro per il centro.
native_language_example: This afternoon I’m out and about in the city center.

additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or direction toward a lower place ("go down"), and very commonly to mean "from (a certain age/level) down" (e.g., "18 and under"). Often follows a verb of movement: "andare/scendere in giù". For "downstairs," Italian usually uses "giù" or "di sotto" rather than "in giù".
target_language_example: L’ingresso è per i 18 anni in giù.
native_language_example: Admission is for ages 18 and under.

additional_notes: Usually followed by a verb in the infinitive with “di” (e.g., “in grado di + infinitive”). Common in polite or formal contexts to talk about ability or possibility. Often appears with “essere” (e.g., “Sono in grado di…” = “I am able to…”).
target_language_example: Non sono in grado di venire oggi.
native_language_example: I’m not able to come today.

meaning: on a large scale; in a big way.
additional_notes: Used to say something is done with big ambitions, lots of resources, or with a big/extra-large version. Common in phrases like “pensare in grande” (to think big) and “fare le cose in grande” (to do things in a big way).
target_language_example: Per il nuovo progetto dobbiamo pensare in grande.
native_language_example: For the new project we need to think big.

meaning: on guard; watch out; be careful.
additional_notes: Used to warn someone to be alert or cautious. Common in spoken Italian as a short warning, sometimes with the article: "stai in guardia" (be on your guard). Also used after verbs like "mettere" (to put) or "tenere" (to keep): "mettere in guardia" / "tenere in guardia" = to warn, to put someone on their guard.
target_language_example: Stai in guardia: c’è molto traffico qui.
native_language_example: Be careful: there’s a lot of traffic here.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is not confined or controlled (e.g., a prisoner released, an animal not in a cage) or that you can do/speak “freely” (more casually: "a ruota libera"). Often follows verbs like "essere", "lasciare", "mettere" (e.g., "lasciare in libertà").
target_language_example: Dopo la prigione, è finalmente tornato in libertà.
native_language_example: After prison, he finally regained his freedom.

additional_notes: Common in two main contexts: (1) internet/technology: "essere/andare/mettere in linea" = to be/go/put online (e.g., a website, a system, a service). (2) physical queues: "essere/stare in linea" = to be standing in line (more common in some regions; "in fila" is very common too). Meaning is understood from context.
target_language_example: Il sito è finalmente in linea.
native_language_example: The website is finally online.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something you can see or hear far from you (often with verbs like vedere/sentire). It can describe a place or a vague, distant area: "in lontananza" = somewhere far off.
target_language_example: In lontananza si vede il mare.
native_language_example: In the distance you can see the sea.

meaning: in (someone’s) hand; in one’s possession / under control.
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like avere/tenere/prendere/dare/lasciare: "in mano" can mean physically in your hand ("Ho il telefono in mano") or more generally in someone’s possession or control ("È in buone mani" = it’s in good hands; "L’azienda è in mano a..." = the company is in the hands of...). Often you’ll hear "in mano a + person" for "in the hands of". Not usually a full standalone phrase; it’s a prepositional expression that needs context.
target_language_example: Ho il passaporto in mano, ma i biglietti sono in mano a Marco.
native_language_example: I have my passport in my hand, but the tickets are with Marco (in Marco’s possession).

additional_notes: Used in formal or semi-formal contexts to introduce the topic area you’re talking about (often followed by di + noun: in materia di lavoro = regarding work/labor matters). Common in bureaucracy, laws, rules, and official communication. Less common in casual speech, where you might hear su/quanto a/a proposito di instead.
target_language_example: In materia di sicurezza, dobbiamo seguire queste regole.
native_language_example: Regarding safety, we must follow these rules.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an average value or what usually happens. In Italian, "media" here means "average" (not "media" = TV/newspapers). Often used with numbers or general statements: "In media spendo 30 euro" = "On average I spend 30 euros."
target_language_example: In media ci metto mezz’ora per arrivare al lavoro.
native_language_example: On average it takes me half an hour to get to work.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like avere/tenere (to have/keep) or venire (to come): “avere in mente” = to have in mind (an idea/plan), “tenere in mente” = to keep in mind/remember, “venire in mente” = to come to mind (often with an indirect object: “Mi è venuto in mente…” = “It occurred to me…”). Commonly refers to ideas, plans, or remembering something.
target_language_example: Tieni in mente che domani il negozio è chiuso.
native_language_example: Keep in mind that the shop is closed tomorrow.

meaning: in the middle of; among; between.
additional_notes: Used to indicate position inside/among something (physical or figurative). Often followed by an article + noun (in mezzo al traffico, in mezzo alla gente). With plural nouns it can mean “among” (in mezzo agli amici). It can also mean “between” two things/people (in mezzo a due case = between two houses).
target_language_example: Mi sono ritrovato in mezzo alla folla.
native_language_example: I found myself in the middle of the crowd.

meaning: "so that" / "in such a way that" (in order that).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a purpose or desired result. It’s often followed by the subjunctive (congiuntivo): "Ti spiego in modo che tu capisca". If the subject doesn’t change, Italian often prefers "in modo da" + infinitive: "Ti scrivo in modo da chiarire tutto" (= so as to clarify everything).
target_language_example: Parla più lentamente, in modo che tutti possano capire.
native_language_example: Speak more slowly, so that everyone can understand.

meaning: "so as to" / "in order to" (to express purpose).
additional_notes: Used to introduce the purpose or goal of an action, often followed by an infinitive (in modo da + infinitive). It can also be followed by "che" + subjunctive (in modo che...) when the subject changes or to sound more formal. Common in both spoken and written Italian.
target_language_example: Parla lentamente in modo da farti capire meglio.
native_language_example: Speak slowly so as to make yourself understood better.

meaning: in the name of; on behalf of.
additional_notes: Used to say something is done with someone’s authority or for their sake. Common in formal contexts (letters, announcements, legal language) and also in set phrases like “in nome della legge” (“in the name of the law”). Often followed by a noun or pronoun: “in nome di Maria,” “in nome suo.”
target_language_example: Parlo in nome di tutta la squadra.
native_language_example: I’m speaking on behalf of the whole team.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is true regardless of what happens or regardless of details just mentioned. Often used to change topic or conclude: similar to English “anyway,” “in any event.”
target_language_example: In ogni caso, ci vediamo domani.
native_language_example: Anyway, we’ll see each other tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to move on, conclude, or downplay what was just said (similar to “anyway” in English). It can also mean “in every way,” but that sense is less common in everyday conversation. Often appears at the start of a sentence: “In ogni modo, …”.
target_language_example: In ogni modo, ci vediamo domani.
native_language_example: Anyway, see you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used for TV, radio, streaming, or any program that is currently broadcasting (or scheduled to broadcast). Often with "andare/essere in onda" (to go/be on air) and "mandare in onda" (to air, to broadcast). You can also use it more generally for something currently being shown/streamed.
target_language_example: Il telegiornale è in onda alle otto.
native_language_example: The news is on air at eight.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens at the scheduled time (e.g., a train) or that a place/office is open at that time. Common with verbs like essere/arrivare/partire ("to be/arrive/leave on time") and with "venire" ("to come during opening hours").
target_language_example: Il treno è arrivato in orario.
native_language_example: The train arrived on time.

meaning: originally; at first; in the beginning.
additional_notes: Used to talk about how something was at the start (before changes happened). Often paired with a contrast like "ma poi..." (but then...). Similar to "origin" in English, so it’s easy to remember.
target_language_example: In origine volevo studiare medicina, ma poi ho cambiato idea.
native_language_example: Originally I wanted to study medicine, but then I changed my mind.

additional_notes: Used to say something is true or done only to some extent (not completely). Often followed by a clause introduced with "perché" (because) or used to soften a statement: "Hai ragione, in parte" (You’re right, partly).
target_language_example: Hai ragione, in parte, perché non abbiamo tutti i dati.
native_language_example: You’re right, partly, because we don’t have all the data.

additional_notes: Used to single out one item from a general statement, or to add emphasis. Common in both spoken and written Italian; often followed by a noun or by "in particolare" at the end of the sentence. Similar to "soprattutto" (especially), but "in particolare" highlights one specific thing among others.
target_language_example: Mi piacciono i dolci, in particolare il tiramisù.
native_language_example: I like desserts, in particular tiramisù.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a time before now, often in general statements or when contrasting past vs. present. Common with the imperfect or past tenses (e.g., "in passato facevo...", "in passato ho..."), and can be placed at the beginning or end of a sentence for emphasis.
target_language_example: In passato vivevo a Milano, ma adesso vivo a Roma.
native_language_example: In the past I lived in Milan, but now I live in Rome.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is physically present (not by phone/email) or is acting directly themselves. Often appears as "di persona" as well, which has the same meaning.
target_language_example: Preferisco parlarne in persona.
native_language_example: I’d rather talk about it in person.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like "essere" or "ridurre" to say something is physically broken ("Il telefono è in pezzi"), emotionally/physically worn out ("Sono a/in pezzi"), or that something has been torn apart/dismantled. Often means "shattered" in a figurative sense too ("Sono in pezzi dopo la notizia").
target_language_example: Dopo il viaggio sono in pezzi.
native_language_example: After the trip I’m exhausted.

additional_notes: Used to describe being upright (not sitting/lying down) or to ask/tell someone to stand up. Common in everyday situations: on public transport (essere/stare in piedi), in a queue (stare in piedi), or when something remains upright/functioning (restare/rimanere in piedi can also mean “to stay standing/keep going”).
target_language_example: Sul bus sono rimasto in piedi per tutto il viaggio.
native_language_example: On the bus I stayed standing for the whole trip.

meaning: in the middle of; at the height of.
additional_notes: Used before a noun to say something is happening right in the middle/peak of a time or activity (often with seasons, events, work, or holidays): "in piena estate" (in the middle of summer), "in pieno centro" (right in the city center). It agrees with the noun: in pieno (masc. sing.), in piena (fem. sing.), in pieni (masc. pl.), in piene (fem. pl.). Often strengthened as "in pieno giorno" (in broad daylight).
target_language_example: Siamo in piena estate e fa molto caldo.
native_language_example: We’re in the middle of summer and it’s very hot.

additional_notes: Used to add something on top of what was already mentioned: quantity (un euro in più = one more euro), items (una cosa in più = an extra thing), or information (E in più… = And what’s more…). Often follows the noun or amount it modifies.
target_language_example: Vorrei un caffè e, in più, una bottiglia d’acqua.
native_language_example: I’d like a coffee and, in addition, a bottle of water.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a practical explanation, simplify what was just said, or sum up the real-world result (similar to “basically” or “so, in other words”). In formal writing it often means “in practice,” while in everyday speech it can mean “basically.”
target_language_example: In teoria è semplice, ma in pratica è più difficile.
native_language_example: In theory it’s simple, but in practice it’s harder.

additional_notes: Used to contrast with "a distanza" or "online" (remote/online). Common for classes, meetings, exams, work, and events: "lezione/riunione/esame/lavoro in presenza". Often implies physically being at the place (e.g., in the classroom/office).
target_language_example: Domani abbiamo una riunione in presenza in ufficio.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we have an in-person meeting at the office.

meaning: in the front row; at the very front.
additional_notes: Used for seating or position (theater, class, concert) and also figuratively to mean being prominently involved or visible ("at the forefront"). Often used with verbs like sedersi/essere/stare: "Siamo in prima fila" (We’re in the front row).
target_language_example: Al concerto eravamo in prima fila, proprio davanti al palco.
native_language_example: At the concert we were in the front row, right in front of the stage.

additional_notes: Common in formal Italian (often in writing) to introduce the most important point or priority. It’s a Latin-derived expression meaning literally “in the first (place)”. In everyday speech, Italians often use alternatives like “prima di tutto” or “per prima cosa”.
target_language_example: In primis, dobbiamo parlare del budget.
native_language_example: First of all, we need to talk about the budget.

additional_notes: Used to say something should be said/done away from other people, or to request a one-on-one conversation. Often follows verbs like parlare (to talk), discutere (to discuss), dire (to say), or sentire (to speak with). You can also use it as a short request: “In privato, per favore.”
target_language_example: Possiamo parlare in privato?
native_language_example: Can we talk in private?

additional_notes: Used mainly with times to say something happens exactly at that moment: "alle 8 in punto" = "at 8 o’clock sharp." Often appears after the time expression (alle 3 in punto).
target_language_example: Il treno parte alle 9 in punto.
native_language_example: The train leaves at 9 o’clock sharp.

meaning: "as" / "in the capacity of" (someone’s role or function).
additional_notes: Used in formal or professional contexts to specify the role in which someone is acting or speaking. Often followed by a noun (job/role): "in qualità di medico". Similar in meaning to "come", but more formal and explicit.
target_language_example: Parlo in qualità di rappresentante dell’azienda.
native_language_example: I’m speaking in my capacity as the company’s representative.

meaning: as; insofar as; since (in the capacity of).
additional_notes: Used to explain a reason or specify someone/something’s role or status. Common in more formal Italian. Often appears as “in quanto + noun” (“as a/an …”) or “in quanto + clause” (“since/because …”).
target_language_example: In quanto studente, hai diritto a uno sconto.
native_language_example: As a student, you’re entitled to a discount.

meaning: these days; lately; around this time.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the recent period or the current time in general (not necessarily literally “today”). Often implies a temporary situation. You can also hear it as a time marker at the start or end of a sentence.
target_language_example: In questi giorni ho molto lavoro.
native_language_example: These days I have a lot of work.

additional_notes: Used to correct, уточify, or contrast what was just said/assumed (“actually…”). Common in conversation and writing. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence or after the subject: “In realtà, … / …, in realtà, …”.
target_language_example: Pensavo fosse chiuso, ma in realtà è aperto.
native_language_example: I thought it was closed, but actually it’s open.

meaning: in order; compliant (up to date with rules/payments/documents).
additional_notes: Used to say something (or someone) meets requirements: papers/documents are valid, payments are up to date, or you are following the rules. Common with verbs like essere/stare/tenere: "essere in regola" (to be in order), "tenere i documenti in regola" (to keep documents in order). Often followed by "con" + what you’re compliant with: "in regola con le tasse" (up to date with taxes), "in regola con i pagamenti" (up to date with payments).
target_language_example: Devi essere in regola con i documenti per noleggiare l’auto.
native_language_example: You must have your documents in order to rent the car.

meaning: in line; lined up; in a row.
additional_notes: Used for people or objects arranged one behind another (a line/queue) or in a straight row. Common in instructions: "Mettetevi in riga" (Line up) or "Stare in riga" (to stay in line / keep your place). Often refers to a physical line of people, but can also mean items aligned neatly.
target_language_example: I bambini sono in riga davanti alla porta.
native_language_example: The children are lined up in front of the door.

additional_notes: Used with essere/stare/arrivare to say someone or something is late. Common in everyday situations (appointments, transport, deadlines). Often followed by di + time amount (e.g., di cinque minuti = by five minutes).
target_language_example: Scusa, sono in ritardo di cinque minuti.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m five minutes late.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is safe after a risky situation (accident, storm, emergency). Common with verbs like essere (“to be”), mettersi (“to get”), portare (“to bring”), and mettere (“to put”): “Siamo in salvo” (We’re safe), “Mettersi in salvo” (to get to safety), “Portare in salvo qualcuno” (to bring someone to safety).
target_language_example: Dopo l'incendio, siamo tutti in salvo.
native_language_example: After the fire, we’re all safe.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say something is sold/kept packaged, especially food. Most commonly means “canned” (e.g., tonno in scatola, pomodori in scatola). More generally it can mean “boxed/cartoned” depending on the item and context (e.g., latte in scatola = milk in a carton).
target_language_example: Preferisco i pomodori in scatola per fare il sugo.
native_language_example: I prefer canned tomatoes to make the sauce.

additional_notes: Used to say something is done privately, without other people knowing. Often with verbs like fare (to do), dire (to say), incontrarsi (to meet), parlare (to talk). You can also say "tenere qualcosa segreto" (to keep something secret).
target_language_example: Si sono incontrati in segreto.
native_language_example: They met in secret.

additional_notes: Common in both speech and writing. Often refers to something that happens later in time (like “later/on”): “Ne parliamo in seguito” (“We’ll talk about it later”). It can also mean “as a consequence” in more formal contexts: “In seguito all’incidente…” (“Following/As a result of the accident…”).
target_language_example: Ne parliamo in seguito.
native_language_example: We’ll talk about it later.

meaning: in reserve; saved up for later.
additional_notes: Used mostly with verbs like "tenere/mettere da parte" or especially "tenere in serbo" to mean keeping something (money, energy, information, food, etc.) for future use. Not related to "serbo" meaning "Serbian" here.
target_language_example: Tengo in serbo un po’ di soldi per le emergenze.
native_language_example: I’m keeping a bit of money in reserve for emergencies.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone is currently working and available as part of their job (police, staff, drivers, waiters, etc.). You can also use it for a device/utility that is functioning or operating (e.g., an elevator). Often contrasted with "fuori servizio" (off duty/out of service).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, il medico è in servizio solo la mattina.
native_language_example: Sorry, the doctor is on duty only in the morning.

meaning: safely; in a safe way; in safety.
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is safe or that an action is done safely. Common with verbs like "essere/stare" (to be), "mettere" (to put), "tenere" (to keep), "viaggiare" (to travel). Also used in fixed phrases like "mettere in sicurezza" = to secure/make safe (e.g., a building, an area).
target_language_example: Siamo arrivati a casa in sicurezza.
native_language_example: We got home safely.

meaning: in sync; on the same wavelength; in tune (with someone/something).
additional_notes: Used to say people agree, understand each other well, or have good rapport: "Siamo in sintonia". It can also refer to being aligned with an idea, a situation, or a goal: "in sintonia con le tue esigenze" (= in line with your needs). Common with verbs like "essere", "sentirsi", "mettersi" + "con".
target_language_example: Siamo subito stati in sintonia, quindi lavorare insieme è stato facile.
native_language_example: We were immediately in sync, so working together was easy.

additional_notes: Used mostly in medical, literary, or formal contexts to describe something that happens during sleep (e.g., dying, talking, moving). Often appears after the verb: “morire in sonno” (to die in one’s sleep), “parlare in sonno” (to talk in one’s sleep).
target_language_example: Ha parlato in sonno tutta la notte.
native_language_example: He talked in his sleep all night.

additional_notes: Used for things that haven’t been decided, finished, or completed yet (a decision, a payment, a request). Common with verbs like rimanere/lasciare/mettere “to remain/leave/put” and in contexts like "pagamento in sospeso" (pending payment) or "questione in sospeso" (unresolved issue).
target_language_example: Il pagamento è ancora in sospeso.
native_language_example: The payment is still pending.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something considered alone, by its own nature, or without comparing it to other things. Often appears in phrases like “di per sé” (“by itself / on its own”) or “in sé e per sé” (“in and of itself”).
target_language_example: Il problema, in sé, non è grave, ma può diventarlo se lo ignori.
native_language_example: The problem, in itself, isn’t serious, but it can become serious if you ignore it.

meaning: in (your) pocket; on you (carried with you).
additional_notes: Literally “in pocket.” Used for things you physically have in your pocket (money, keys, phone). By extension it can mean you have something on you/with you (e.g., documents). Often appears in expressions like “avere X in tasca” (to have X in your pocket/on you) and “tenere X in tasca” (to keep X in your pocket).
target_language_example: Hai dei contanti in tasca?
native_language_example: Do you have any cash in your pocket?

meaning: on time; in time (before it’s too late).
additional_notes: Used to talk about punctuality or meeting a deadline. Often appears with verbs like arrivare/essere (to be punctual) or fare (to do something before a deadline): "arrivare in tempo" = arrive on time; "essere in tempo" = be on time / still have time; "fare in tempo (a + infinitive)" = manage to do something in time. In everyday speech you may also hear "in tempo per" (in time for).
target_language_example: Sono arrivato in tempo per il treno.
native_language_example: I arrived in time for the train.

additional_notes: Used to specify the aspect or point of view you’re talking about (prices, time, results, etc.). Common in formal and neutral speech. Often followed by a noun or noun phrase: "in termini di tempo", "in termini di costi". Similar alternatives: "per quanto riguarda" (as for/regarding), "dal punto di vista di" (from the point of view of).
target_language_example: In termini di costi, questa soluzione è la più conveniente.
native_language_example: In terms of costs, this solution is the most convenient.

meaning: at the top; in (someone’s) head / on (someone’s) mind.
additional_notes: Common with different meanings depending on context. Physical position: "in testa" = at the front/top of a line, list, ranking, or race (often with "essere" or "stare": "Siamo in testa" = We’re in the lead). Mental focus: with verbs like "avere" or "mettere" it means in someone’s head/mind ("Ho in testa un’idea" = I have an idea in my head; "Mi hai messo in testa..." = You put it in my head...).
target_language_example: Dopo l’ultima tappa, siamo in testa alla classifica.
native_language_example: After the last stage, we’re at the top of the standings.

meaning: in the round; in a circle (round shape).
additional_notes: Used to describe something shaped like a circle or arranged in a circular way. Common in cooking (e.g., cutting food into round slices) and in art/architecture (a tondo = a round painting/relief).
target_language_example: Taglia il pane in tondo, per favore.
native_language_example: Cut the bread into round slices, please.

meaning: in every way; by all means; no matter what.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize doing something using any method possible, or strongly insisting on something. Often pairs with verbs like "cercare" (to try), "fare" (to do), "aiutare" (to help), or "evitare" (to avoid): "cercherò in tutti i modi" = "I’ll try in every way / by all means."
target_language_example: Cercherò in tutti i modi di arrivare in tempo.
native_language_example: I’ll try in every way to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used to give a total number or amount (often after listing parts). Can appear with numbers: "in tutto sono..." (in total there are...). Also used more generally to mean "altogether/overall".
target_language_example: Abbiamo speso 35 euro in tutto.
native_language_example: We spent 35 euros in total.

additional_notes: Formal or literary way to introduce the last point in a list or argument. Common in writing and speeches; in everyday conversation Italians more often say "infine", "alla fine", or "per finire". Can also mean "ultimately" when wrapping up a reasoning.
target_language_example: In ultimo, vorrei ringraziare tutti per la collaborazione.
native_language_example: Finally, I’d like to thank everyone for their collaboration.

meaning: for sale; on sale (available to buy).
additional_notes: Used on signs, ads, and listings to say something is being sold: *Casa in vendita* (house for sale), *biglietti in vendita* (tickets on sale). It focuses on availability rather than a discount; for “on sale” (discounted) you often see *in saldo/saldi* or *scontato*.
target_language_example: Questa casa è in vendita da due mesi.
native_language_example: This house has been for sale for two months.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a truthful clarification or correction, similar to “actually” or “to tell the truth.” It can sound a bit formal/literary compared with common everyday options like “in realtà” or “a dire il vero.”
target_language_example: In verità, non ho tempo oggi.
native_language_example: Actually, I don’t have time today.

meaning: in the process of; about to (be/do).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (e.g., "in via di partire") or with a noun (e.g., "in via di definizione") to say something is underway or nearing completion. Common in formal/written Italian (news, notices); in everyday speech you may also hear "stare per" or "essere sul punto di" for "about to".
target_language_example: Il progetto è in via di completamento.
native_language_example: The project is in the process of being completed.

meaning: traveling; on a trip; in transit.
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is currently traveling or en route. Often with essere/andare (e.g., “sono in viaggio”, “vado in viaggio”) and in phrases like “in viaggio di lavoro” (on a business trip). It can refer to people or to items being shipped/delivered (“Il pacco è in viaggio”).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non posso rispondere: sono in viaggio.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t reply: I’m traveling.

meaning: in view; in sight; with a view to (in preparation for).
additional_notes: Common in two main uses: (1) physical/visual: "in vista" = visible, within sight (often with "essere/venire"). (2) figurative: "in vista di" = in anticipation of / with a view to a future event (e.g., a trip, an exam). Often followed by "di" when it means “in preparation for.”
target_language_example: Sto studiando in vista dell’esame.
native_language_example: I’m studying in preparation for the exam.

meaning: alive; living (while someone is still alive).
additional_notes: Often used to contrast with “dead” or “no longer living,” especially when talking about someone’s lifetime or what happened while a person was alive. Common in phrases like “quando era in vita” (when he/she was alive) and “l’unico parente in vita” (the only living relative).
target_language_example: Mio nonno, quando era in vita, raccontava sempre storie di guerra.
native_language_example: My grandfather, when he was alive, always told war stories.

additional_notes: Used in formal or neutral contexts (news, police reports, insurance) to refer to an accident happening on a road (car, scooter, bicycle, etc.). In everyday speech, people may also say "un incidente" or "un incidente in macchina" depending on context.
target_language_example: C’è stato un incidente stradale sulla tangenziale questa mattina.
native_language_example: There was a road accident on the ring road this morning.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something is with another person/thing. It often works like the preposition “with” in English and is followed by a noun or pronoun: “insieme a Maria” (with Maria). You can also use it with stressed pronouns: “insieme a me/te/lui/lei/noi/voi/loro.”
target_language_example: Vengo insieme a te al cinema.
native_language_example: I’m coming with you to the movies.

additional_notes: Commonly used for location ("around" a place/object) and for approximate quantities or times ("around/about" 10, "around" 3 o’clock). Often followed by a noun, pronoun, or number: "intorno a casa" (around home), "intorno a me" (around me), "intorno a dieci euro" (about ten euros).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo intorno alle tre.
native_language_example: See you around three o’clock.

meaning: “Mrs./Ms. Duca” (a woman with the surname Duca); literally “the duke” (but as a title this is usually not correct).
additional_notes: In Italian, you can put an article before a surname to refer to someone (common in speech and in some regions): *la Duca* = “Ms. Duca,” *il Duca* = “Mr. Duca.” If you mean the noble title “duke/duchess,” the usual forms are *il duca* (duke, male) and *la duchessa* (duchess, female)—*la duca* is generally not used as the standard title.
target_language_example: La Duca lavora in banca.
native_language_example: Ms. Duca works at the bank.

additional_notes: Common feminine noun used for baking/cooking (e.g., flour for bread, pizza, cakes). Often you’ll see it lowercase as “la farina.” In recipes you may also see types like “farina 00” (very finely milled flour) or “farina integrale” (whole wheat flour).
target_language_example: Mi serve la farina per fare la pizza.
native_language_example: I need flour to make pizza.

meaning: "the Fat (one)"; a nickname for Bologna, referring to its rich food tradition.
additional_notes: Capitalized when used as a nickname (especially in the phrase "Bologna la Grassa"). It’s one of Bologna’s traditional epithets ("la Dotta, la Grassa, la Rossa" = the Learned, the Fat, the Red). Literally it’s the feminine form of "grasso" (fat/rich), but in this context it’s affectionate and refers to the city’s cuisine.
target_language_example: Bologna è detta anche la Grassa per la sua cucina.
native_language_example: Bologna is also called “the Fat one” because of its cuisine.

additional_notes: Uses the feminine form of the adjective "greco/greca" (Greek). With the article "la", it can work as a noun meaning “the Greek woman.” You might also see it as a label for nationality (e.g., in a story or on a seating chart). Capitalization may vary; as a general adjective it’s usually lowercase ("la greca"), but it may be capitalized in titles, nicknames, or names (e.g., a restaurant).
target_language_example: Maria è la Greca del gruppo: viene da Atene.
native_language_example: Maria is the Greek woman in the group: she’s from Athens.

meaning: the (female) teacher; also a respectful title for a female teacher or instructor.
additional_notes: Capitalizing it (Maestra) often makes it a title, similar to “Teacher” as a form of address. In many school contexts it can refer specifically to an elementary school teacher. You can use it to address her directly (e.g., “Maestra, …”) or to talk about her (“la maestra di italiano”).
target_language_example: Maestra, posso andare in bagno?
native_language_example: Teacher, can I go to the bathroom?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the morning in general (routine or a typical morning). Often you’ll see it without capitalization: “la mattina.” With parts of the day, Italian commonly uses the definite article: “la mattina / il pomeriggio / la sera / la notte.” For a specific morning, you may use “questa mattina” (this morning) or “stamattina” (more common in speech).
target_language_example: La mattina bevo un caffè prima di andare al lavoro.
native_language_example: In the morning I drink a coffee before going to work.

additional_notes: Common noun phrase: definite article + noun (la + pietra). Used literally for a stone/rock (a material, an object, a landmark). Not usually capitalized unless it’s part of a place name, surname, or title (e.g., “Pietra” as a proper noun).
target_language_example: Ho trovato una pietra interessante sulla spiaggia.
native_language_example: I found an interesting stone on the beach.

additional_notes: "Porta" is a feminine noun, so it takes the article "la". Most often it means a door of a building/room (e.g., "la porta di casa" = the front door), but it can also mean a city gate or gateway (especially in place names, like "Porta Romana"). Not to be confused with "porta" as a verb form meaning "(he/she/it) brings/carries."
target_language_example: Chiudi la porta, per favore.
native_language_example: Close the door, please.

additional_notes: Used as a title for a queen (real or fictional) or as a respectful/formal way to refer to one. Capitalized (Regina) when it’s a title/name; lowercase (regina) when speaking generally (e.g., “una regina”). In modern Italy there is no monarchy, but you’ll still see it in history, movies, books, and games (e.g., chess: la regina = the queen).
target_language_example: La Regina arriva al palazzo alle dieci.
native_language_example: The Queen arrives at the palace at ten.

meaning: 'the rose' (a rose flower); also a female name 'Rosa'.
additional_notes: Usually written lowercase for the flower (la rosa). Capitalized (la Rosa / Rosa) when it’s a person’s name, a surname, or part of a proper name (e.g., a place or organization). In Italian, rose (the color) is usually "rosa" (invariable) as in "un vestito rosa".
target_language_example: Mi piace la rosa rossa nel giardino.
native_language_example: I like the red rose in the garden.

additional_notes: Feminine noun with the definite article: *la ruota* (plural: *le ruote*). Used for any kind of wheel (bike, car, suitcase, etc.). You may also see it in set phrases like *ruota di scorta* (“spare tire/wheel”) or *la ruota della fortuna* (“Wheel of Fortune”).
target_language_example: Devo cambiare la ruota della macchina.
native_language_example: I have to change the car’s wheel (tire).

meaning: the room; the hall; (often) the living room.
