native_language_example: I lost patience with him because he kept interrupting me.

meaning: to lose your head; to go crazy; to lose control.
additional_notes: Used both literally (panic, not thinking clearly) and figuratively (lose control because of strong feelings, especially love/infatuation). Common in everyday speech. Often used with "per" + person/thing: "Ho perso la testa per lui/lei" = "I’m crazy about him/her."
target_language_example: Quando l’ho vista, ho perso la testa.
native_language_example: When I saw her, I lost my head / I went crazy.

meaning: to lose one’s life; to die (especially in an accident/tragic event).
additional_notes: Common in news and formal contexts to refer to someone dying, often in accidents, disasters, wars, or crimes. It’s more indirect and formal than simply saying "morire" (to die). Can be used in different tenses: "ha perso la vita" (lost his/her life), "hanno perso la vita" (lost their lives).
target_language_example: Due persone hanno perso la vita nell’incidente.
native_language_example: Two people lost their lives in the accident.

meaning: to lose your temper; to fly off the handle.
additional_notes: Common idiom used when someone suddenly gets angry and stops controlling themselves. Often used with "con" (with) or after a situation: "Ho perso le staffe con lui" (I lost my temper with him). In the past tense you’ll often hear: "ha perso le staffe" / "ho perso le staffe".
target_language_example: Quando mi ha accusato ingiustamente, ho perso le staffe.
native_language_example: When he accused me unfairly, I lost my temper.

meaning: to waste time; to lose time.
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase. Use it for doing something unproductive (wasting time) or for delays that make you late (losing time). Often used with “a/in + [activity]” (e.g., perdere tempo a discutere) or with “con” (perdere tempo con i social). In the negative, it can mean “not to waste time” / “to get straight to it” (Non perdiamo tempo!).
target_language_example: Non voglio perdere tempo: cominciamo subito.
native_language_example: I don’t want to waste time: let’s start right away.

additional_notes: Usually refers to the common pet fish (often kept in a bowl or aquarium). Plural: pesci rossi. Literally “red fish,” but in everyday Italian it’s the standard word for “goldfish.”
target_language_example: Mia sorella ha un pesce rosso in un acquario.
native_language_example: My sister has a goldfish in an aquarium.

additional_notes: Very vulgar and aggressive; used to insult someone you strongly dislike or are angry at. Avoid in polite conversation and in most public situations. You may hear it in arguments or in movies/TV.
target_language_example: Non parlare con me, pezzo di merda!
native_language_example: Don’t talk to me, you piece of shit!

meaning: a big shot; an important/influential person.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone powerful or high-ranking (in business, politics, a company, etc.). It can be neutral but often has a slightly ironic tone (like “bigwig”). Literally means “big piece,” but the idiomatic meaning is what’s intended.
target_language_example: Al meeting c’era un pezzo grosso dell’azienda.
native_language_example: There was a big shot from the company at the meeting.

additional_notes: A common tool name; literally “pig’s foot,” referring to the shape of the metal end used to pry things open or pull out nails. Used in everyday contexts (DIY, construction, moving).
target_language_example: Mi presti il piede di porco per togliere quel chiodo?
native_language_example: Can you lend me the crowbar to pull out that nail?

additional_notes: Used to describe someone who thinks very highly of themselves (often in a negative, critical way). It agrees with the person described: "pieno di sé" (male), "piena di sé" (female), "pieni/e di sé" (plural). Often used with "essere": "È pieno/a di sé".
target_language_example: Da quando ha avuto quella promozione, è sempre più pieno di sé.
native_language_example: Since he got that promotion, he’s more and more full of himself.

meaning: table tennis; (by extension) a back-and-forth exchange.
additional_notes: Used for the sport played on a table with paddles (often also called “tennis da tavolo”). Figuratively, it can describe repeated back-and-forth messages, calls, or decisions (“fare ping pong” / “un ping pong di email”).
target_language_example: Abbiamo giocato a ping pong dopo cena.
native_language_example: We played table tennis after dinner.

meaning: to rain heavily; to pour down (rain).
additional_notes: Common idiom for very heavy rain (like “it’s pouring” / “raining cats and dogs”). Used with the verb "piove" (it rains) or in other tenses: "Ha piovuto a catinelle". Literally "to rain in buckets/basins".
target_language_example: Oggi piove a catinelle, meglio prendere l’ombrello.
native_language_example: It’s pouring today, better take an umbrella.

meaning: more or less; approximately; roughly; kind of.
additional_notes: Common in everyday speech to give an approximate number or estimate (often with time, price, distance), or to say you’re doing “so-so.” Can also soften an answer to mean “sort of / not exactly.” Often used with quantities: “più o meno alle 8” (around 8), “più o meno 10 euro” (about 10 euros).
target_language_example: Arrivo più o meno alle otto, ma non ne sono sicuro.
native_language_example: I’ll arrive around eight, but I’m not sure.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens repeatedly. Often used with the passato prossimo to mean something happened multiple times in the past: "L’ho visto più volte" (I’ve seen him/it several times). Can also be used with the present/future: "Te l’ho detto più volte" (I’ve told you more than once).
target_language_example: Ci sono stato più volte.
native_language_example: I’ve been there several times.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens slowly over time, step by step. Often placed near the verb (e.g., "Imparo poco a poco") or at the end of the sentence for emphasis. Similar in meaning to "a poco a poco" and "pian piano" (more colloquial).
target_language_example: Sto imparando l’italiano poco a poco.
native_language_example: I’m learning Italian little by little.

additional_notes: Often written as one word: **poiché**. It introduces a reason (similar to *perché* in the sense of “because”). Common in more formal or written Italian. Usually followed by the indicative: *Poiché piove, restiamo a casa.*
target_language_example: Poi che non hai tempo, possiamo sentirci domani.
native_language_example: Since you don’t have time, we can talk tomorrow.

meaning: “Fuck!” / “Goddamn it!” (a very strong swear used in anger or frustration).
additional_notes: Very vulgar Italian profanity, used as an exclamation when something goes wrong (like “for fuck’s sake!”). Not appropriate in polite settings, with strangers, at work, or around children. You may also hear shortened/softer alternatives like “porca miseria!” or “porca vacca!”.
target_language_example: Porca puttana! Ho perso il portafoglio.
native_language_example: Fuck! I lost my wallet.

meaning: a very strong swear/exclamation (like “for f***’s sake!” / “holy sh*t!”).
additional_notes: Very vulgar and offensive. Used to express anger, frustration, or surprise. Avoid in polite company; it’s much stronger than mild exclamations like “accidenti!” or “cavolo!”. Literally it refers to a “sow,” but the real meaning is just an insult/swear.
target_language_example: Porca troia! Ho perso le chiavi.
native_language_example: For f***’s sake! I lost my keys.

meaning: to put an end to; to end (something).
additional_notes: Usually followed by "a" + noun/infinitive: "porre fine a qualcosa" / "porre fine a fare qualcosa". It’s fairly formal and common in writing or official speech; in everyday conversation you might also hear "finire" or "mettere fine a".
target_language_example: Dobbiamo porre fine a questa discussione.
native_language_example: We have to put an end to this discussion.

additional_notes: Literally “open door.” Common in everyday situations (e.g., “leave the door open”). Can also be used figuratively in expressions like “a porta aperta” (“openly / in public” or “with the door open,” e.g., job interviews or meetings held with the door open).
target_language_example: Puoi lasciare la porta aperta, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you leave the door open, please?

meaning: to take/bring home; (figurative) to achieve/secure (a result).
additional_notes: Literally means “to carry to home.” Used for physically taking something back to your home (often after shopping, work, or a trip). In sports, work, or everyday talk it can also mean “to bring home a win/result” (i.e., to secure it): *portare a casa una vittoria / un risultato / un buon voto*. You can also hear it as *portarsi a casa* (“to take home for oneself”).
target_language_example: Speriamo di portare a casa una vittoria stasera.
native_language_example: Let’s hope we can bring home a win tonight.

meaning: to complete; to carry through (finish something).
additional_notes: Used with a project, task, plan, or goal meaning “finish successfully.” Often followed by a direct object (e.g., un lavoro, un progetto, un compito). Past participle: "portato a termine" (completed). Slightly formal/common in work or study contexts.
target_language_example: Alla fine siamo riusciti a portare a termine il progetto in tempo.
native_language_example: In the end we managed to complete the project on time.

meaning: to carry on; to move forward; to continue (a project/work).
additional_notes: Common with things like projects, plans, negotiations, or tasks: "portare avanti un progetto" = to carry a project forward / to keep it going. In Italian it can also mean to physically bring something forward (move it ahead), but the figurative sense (continue/proceed) is very frequent.
target_language_example: Non è facile, ma dobbiamo portare avanti questo progetto.
native_language_example: It’s not easy, but we have to carry on with this project.

meaning: to take away; to remove; to take (someone) away.
additional_notes: Common in everyday situations: taking food from a restaurant, removing an object, or taking someone away from a place. Often used with a direct object (Porto via il piatto = I take the plate away). In restaurants you may also hear "da asporto" for "to go/takeaway"; "portare via" is the verb phrase.
target_language_example: Possiamo portare via questo?
native_language_example: Can we take this away?

additional_notes: Used both for the position/role you have (a job) and for the physical workstation/desk. Common in formal contexts (contracts, HR, job ads): e.g., creare/offrire un posto di lavoro (“create/offer a job”), cercare un posto di lavoro (“look for a job”).
target_language_example: Sto cercando un posto di lavoro a Milano.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a job in Milan.

meaning: to target; to single out (often to pick on).
additional_notes: Used when someone or something is deliberately chosen as a target. It can be neutral (targeting a goal, a market, an object) or negative when talking about people being singled out, teased, or bullied. Often followed by a direct object: "prendere qualcuno di mira" (pick on someone) or "prendere qualcosa di mira" (target something).
target_language_example: A scuola prendevano spesso Marco di mira.
native_language_example: At school they often picked on Marco.

meaning: to take shape; to start to become clear or real.
additional_notes: Used for ideas, plans, projects, or situations as they develop and become more defined. Can also be used literally for something physically forming (less common). Often followed by a subject like "il progetto" or "l’idea".
target_language_example: Dopo alcune riunioni, il progetto ha iniziato a prendere forma.
native_language_example: After a few meetings, the project started to take shape.

additional_notes: Used when something starts burning (often suddenly). It can be literal (a building, a pan, clothes) and also figurative for a situation that “flares up” (e.g., an argument). In the past tense you’ll often hear: "ha preso fuoco" = "it caught fire."
target_language_example: La padella ha preso fuoco mentre cucinavo.
native_language_example: The pan caught fire while I was cooking.

additional_notes: Used when you are the person renting/borrowing the property or item (tenant/customer). Common for apartments, rooms, cars, bikes, etc. Often followed by what you’re renting: “prendere in affitto un appartamento/una macchina”. Contrast with “dare in affitto” = to rent out (as the owner/landlord).
target_language_example: Vorrei prendere in affitto un appartamento per due mesi.
native_language_example: I’d like to rent an apartment for two months.

meaning: to consider; to take into account.
additional_notes: Used in formal and everyday Italian when you mean you will think about an idea, option, or request seriously. Often followed by a noun (un’idea, una proposta, una possibilità) or by a clause introduced with “di” (e.g., prendere in considerazione di + infinitive).
target_language_example: Possiamo prendere in considerazione questa proposta?
native_language_example: Can we take this proposal into account / consider this proposal?

meaning: to tease; to make fun of (someone); to trick/joke with someone.
additional_notes: Common with a direct object: "prendere qualcuno in giro". It can be lighthearted (teasing) or mean (mocking), depending on tone and context. Also used when someone is being fooled or not taken seriously: "Mi stai prendendo in giro?" = "Are you kidding me? / Are you messing with me?".
target_language_example: Mi stai prendendo in giro? Non è vero!
native_language_example: Are you kidding me? That’s not true!

meaning: to take note; to write down.
additional_notes: Used to mean noting something important, often by writing it down. Common in polite requests or instructions (e.g., in class, at work, or on the phone). You’ll often hear it as an imperative: "Prenda nota" (formal) or "Prendi nota" (informal). You can also use it with "di" + noun/verb: "prendere nota di (qualcosa)" = "to take note of (something)".
target_language_example: Prendi nota dell’indirizzo, per favore.
native_language_example: Write down the address, please.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone participates in an event, activity, meeting, class, or competition. It’s followed by "a" + noun ("prendere parte a una riunione") or "a" + infinitive ("prendere parte a discutere"). Common synonym: "partecipare (a)".
target_language_example: Vuoi prendere parte alla riunione di domani?
native_language_example: Do you want to take part in tomorrow’s meeting?

meaning: to make fun of someone; to tease someone (often rudely).
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. Used when someone is mocking you, treating you like an idiot, or “pulling your leg” (sometimes jokingly, but often insulting). You’ll also hear it as "Mi stai prendendo per il culo?" (“Are you kidding me/Are you messing with me?”).
target_language_example: Non prendermi per il culo: so benissimo che non è vero.
native_language_example: Don’t mess with me: I know very well it’s not true.

meaning: to take a seat; to sit down.
additional_notes: Used in polite contexts (restaurants, waiting rooms, events) to invite someone to sit. Often appears as an invitation or instruction: "Prego, prenda/prendete posto" (formal). In informal speech you may also hear "Prendi posto". Literally "to take place," but in Italian it means taking a seat.
target_language_example: Prego, prendete posto: il film sta per cominciare.
native_language_example: Please, take a seat: the movie is about to start.

additional_notes: Used when someone delays making a decision or giving an answer, often to think, prepare, or avoid committing. Common in everyday speech and also in work situations. It can imply a strategic delay (not necessarily negative), similar to English “buy time.”
target_language_example: Devo prendere tempo prima di rispondere alla tua proposta.
native_language_example: I need to buy time before replying to your proposal.

meaning: to come to life; to take shape (to start to exist or develop).
additional_notes: Used for living things (e.g., a creature comes to life) and very commonly for projects, ideas, stories, plans, or artworks that start becoming real or start developing. Often appears as "prendere vita" or "prendere vita piano piano" (gradually). In the past: "ha preso vita" = "it came to life / took shape."
target_language_example: Con l’aiuto di tutti, il progetto ha preso vita in poche settimane.
native_language_example: With everyone’s help, the project took shape in a few weeks.

additional_notes: Common reflexive phrase used with "di" + noun/infinitive: "prendersi cura di qualcuno/qualcosa" (to look after someone/something). Conjugates like a reflexive verb (mi prendo cura, ti prendi cura, si prende cura, ecc.). Often used in caring contexts (health, responsibilities, maintenance).
target_language_example: Mi prendo cura di mia nonna ogni weekend.
native_language_example: I take care of my grandmother every weekend.

meaning: to make fun of; to tease (someone).
additional_notes: Used with "di" ("prendersi gioco di qualcuno") to say you’re mocking or teasing someone, often in an unkind way. It can also mean “to trick” or “to toy with” someone. Common in everyday speech and slightly informal.
target_language_example: Non prenderti gioco di me!
native_language_example: Don’t make fun of me!

meaning: President of the Republic (head of state).
additional_notes: Official title used in Italy for the head of state (Il Presidente della Repubblica). Often written with capital letters in formal contexts. Not the same as the Prime Minister (il Presidente del Consiglio). You may also hear it shortened to "il Presidente" when context is clear.
target_language_example: Il Presidente della Repubblica vive al Quirinale.
native_language_example: The President of the Republic lives at the Quirinal Palace.

additional_notes: Common medical/health term used in clinics, pharmacies, and everyday health talk. Often appears with verbs like misurare/controllare (“to measure/check”) and with alta/bassa (“high/low”). You may also hear the synonym pressione arteriosa.
target_language_example: Devo controllare la pressione sanguigna.
native_language_example: I need to check my blood pressure.

meaning: to pay attention; to be careful.
additional_notes: Common in instructions, warnings, and polite requests. Often followed by "a" + noun/verb: "Prestare attenzione alla strada" (to the road), "Prestare attenzione a non cadere" (to not fall). Similar meaning: "fare attenzione" (more everyday).
target_language_example: Presta attenzione quando attraversi la strada.
native_language_example: Pay attention when you cross the street.

presto e bene non vanno insieme

target_language_multi_word_term: presto e bene non vanno insieme
meaning: “Quickly and well don’t go together.” (You can’t do something both fast and well.)
additional_notes: A common saying used to warn someone not to rush, because speed often reduces quality. Often said when someone wants something done immediately, to suggest taking the time to do it properly. You may also hear similar versions like “Presto e bene non si fanno insieme.”
target_language_example: Non posso finire oggi: presto e bene non vanno insieme.
native_language_example: I can’t finish today: you can’t do it both quickly and well.

meaning: first of all; before anything else.
additional_notes: Used to introduce the first point in a list, priority, or initial step. Common in both spoken and written Italian. It can also mean “above all” in the sense of what matters most, depending on context.
target_language_example: Prima di tutto, devo chiamare mia madre.
native_language_example: First of all, I have to call my mother.

additional_notes: Used to say that something will happen at some point in the future (even if you don’t know exactly when). Very common in everyday speech. Literally means “sooner or later” (prima = sooner/first, poi = later/then).
target_language_example: Prima o poi devo chiamare il medico.
native_language_example: Sooner or later I have to call the doctor.

additional_notes: Used to say you experienced something directly yourself or you met/saw something in person. Common with verbs like vedere (to see), conoscere (to know/meet), sentire (to hear), and with the expression "di prima persona" = "first-hand". Also related to grammar: "prima persona" can mean "first person" (io/noi), but that’s a separate use.
target_language_example: Ho visto la situazione di prima persona.
native_language_example: I saw the situation first-hand.

additional_notes: Used for the leader of the government in countries that have a prime minister. In Italy, the official term is often "Presidente del Consiglio (dei Ministri)", but "primo ministro" is commonly understood and used in news and everyday conversation.
target_language_example: Il primo ministro ha annunciato nuove misure economiche.
native_language_example: The prime minister announced new economic measures.

meaning: the first floor (in Italy, the level above the ground floor); also “close-up” (in film/photo).
additional_notes: In buildings, Italian numbering usually starts with the ground floor (piano terra), so primo piano is one level up (often called the “second floor” in the US). In media contexts, un primo piano means a close-up shot or close-up photo (e.g., of a face).
target_language_example: L’ufficio è al primo piano, accanto all’ascensore.
native_language_example: The office is on the first floor, next to the elevator.

additional_notes: Used to describe a person who has lost consciousness (not awake or responsive), often in emergencies or after an accident. It agrees with the person described: "privo di sensi" (masc.), "priva di sensi" (fem.). Common in news reports and when calling for help (e.g., "C’è una persona priva di sensi").
target_language_example: Ho trovato un uomo privo di sensi per terra: ho chiamato subito il 112.
native_language_example: I found a man unconscious on the ground: I called 112 right away.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that has no meaning or logic (an idea, a sentence, a gesture, an action). It’s fairly formal/neutral and common in writing and conversation. Often appears with “è” (it is) or after a noun: “un discorso privo di senso”. Similar to “senza senso.”
target_language_example: Questa spiegazione è priva di senso.
native_language_example: This explanation is meaningless.

additional_notes: Used for hospital emergency departments and urgent medical care. Often appears on signs in hospitals; you can say "al pronto soccorso" (to the ER) or "andare al pronto soccorso" (to go to the ER). The literal meaning is "ready help."
target_language_example: Devo andare al pronto soccorso: mi sono fatto male.
native_language_example: I have to go to the ER: I got hurt.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a person’s weakness (a character flaw or a temptation) or a weak spot in a plan, argument, or system. Often followed by "di" + noun/pronoun ("il mio punto debole"), or used with "essere" ("è il mio punto debole").
target_language_example: I dolci sono il mio punto debole.
native_language_example: Desserts are my weakness.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s/ something’s main advantage or what they do best. Common with the verb "essere": "Il punto di forza di... è..." You can also use the plural "punti di forza" for multiple strengths.
target_language_example: Il punto di forza di questo ristorante è la pasta fatta in casa.
native_language_example: The strong point of this restaurant is the homemade pasta.

additional_notes: Used to express someone’s perspective or opinion. Very common in conversation and writing. Often appears with possessives (il mio/il tuo/il suo punto di vista = my/your/his-her point of view) and in phrases like "dal mio punto di vista" (from my point of view) or "da questo punto di vista" (from this point of view, in this respect).
target_language_example: Dal mio punto di vista, è una buona idea.
native_language_example: From my point of view, it’s a good idea.

additional_notes: A common winter term. Literally “snow puppet/doll,” but in everyday English it’s “snowman.” Use with an article: "un pupazzo di neve" (a snowman), "il pupazzo di neve" (the snowman).
target_language_example: I bambini stanno facendo un pupazzo di neve in giardino.
native_language_example: The children are making a snowman in the garden.

meaning: just to / in order to (often: even if it means…).
additional_notes: Used to express doing something solely to achieve a goal, sometimes implying willingness to accept a cost or sacrifice. Common pattern: "pur di" + infinitive (e.g., "pur di finire", "pur di risparmiare"). Often translated as "just to" or "in order to," and in contexts of sacrifice as "even if it means" / "at any cost".
target_language_example: Ha mentito pur di ottenere il lavoro.
native_language_example: He lied just to get the job.

additional_notes: A common side dish in Italy. You’ll also see it written as "puré" or "purea". Often served with meat, sausages, or stews; you can order it as a contorno (side dish).
target_language_example: Per contorno, prendo il purè di patate.
native_language_example: For a side dish, I’ll have mashed potatoes.

additional_notes: Common way to say something happens from time to time. It’s similar in meaning to "a volte" and "talvolta". Often used at the start or end of a sentence: "Qualche volta..." / "...qualche volta."
target_language_example: Qualche volta vado al cinema con i miei amici.
native_language_example: Sometimes I go to the cinema with my friends.

additional_notes: Used to refer to another person (not the one already mentioned). Common in questions and negatives: “C’è qualcun altro?” (Is there anyone else?), “Non c’è qualcun altro.” (There isn’t anyone else.). It agrees in meaning, not form: it stays the same regardless of who it refers to.
target_language_example: C’è qualcun altro che può aiutarmi?
native_language_example: Is there someone else who can help me?

additional_notes: Used to mean “anything at all,” often when you don’t care which specific thing. Common in offers and questions (e.g., “Do you want anything?”) and in negative sentences to mean “anything” (often with non …): “Non ho visto qualsiasi cosa” is unusual; more natural is “Non ho visto niente / Non ho visto nulla.” With verbs like “dire/fare,” it can mean “say/do anything” in a broad sense.
target_language_example: Vuoi qualsiasi cosa da bere?
native_language_example: Do you want anything to drink?

additional_notes: Used to mean “any thing at all,” often emphasizing that the specific item doesn’t matter. It can appear as an object (“Vuoi qualunque cosa?”) or after a relative clause like “(tutto) quello che…” in phrases such as “qualunque cosa tu voglia” (“whatever you want”).
target_language_example: Puoi scegliere qualunque cosa dal menu.
native_language_example: You can choose anything from the menu.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a topic or switch focus to a particular person/thing. It’s followed by a noun, pronoun, or an infinitive (e.g., “quanto a me…”, “quanto a pagare…”). Similar to “per quanto riguarda…”, but usually shorter and slightly more conversational.
target_language_example: Quanto a me, preferisco restare a casa stasera.
native_language_example: As for me, I’d rather stay home tonight.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the main office or central base of an organization (company, military, police, a project team, etc.). Often appears with the preposition "a" or "nel": "Sono al quartier generale" (I’m at HQ), "Ci vediamo nel quartier generale" (We’ll meet at HQ). In Italian it’s commonly written as two words: "quartier generale".
target_language_example: Domani ci vediamo al quartier generale per fare il punto sulla situazione.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’ll meet at headquarters to review the situation.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens very rarely. It’s made of quasi (“almost”) + mai (“never”), and it typically goes near the verb. Similar in meaning to “raramente” (“rarely”), but “quasi mai” stresses the idea of “almost never.”
target_language_example: Quasi mai mangio carne.
native_language_example: I almost never eat meat.

additional_notes: Used to point out a specific person/thing that is close to the speaker or just mentioned. “Qua” adds emphasis like “here/this one right here.” Common in spoken Italian; in more neutral/formal Italian you can just say “questo” (or “questa” for feminine).
target_language_example: Preferisco questo qua, non quello lì.
native_language_example: I prefer this one here, not that one over there.

additional_notes: Used to point out or emphasize a specific thing/person that is close to the speaker. Common in spoken Italian; "qui" adds emphasis and physical proximity. Often used with gestures: "Questo qui, per favore." You can also hear similar forms like "quello lì" (that one there).
target_language_example: Prendo questo qui, grazie.
native_language_example: I’ll take this one here, thanks.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the main purpose or justification of something (a project, rule, company, habit, etc.). Often appears with verbs like "essere" or "avere": "Qual è la tua ragione di essere?" / "La nostra ragione di essere è..." It’s fairly formal and common in writing and speeches.
target_language_example: La ragione di essere di questa associazione è aiutare le famiglie in difficoltà.
native_language_example: The purpose of this association is to help families in need.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a gift given at Christmas. You can also say "un regalo per Natale" (“a gift for Christmas”). The plural is "regali di Natale".
target_language_example: Ho comprato un regalo di Natale per mia sorella.
native_language_example: I bought a Christmas present for my sister.

meaning: to account for; to report/explain (also: to realize, in the form "rendersi conto")
additional_notes: Used with different patterns: (1) "rendere conto di [cosa]" = to account for / explain something: "rendere conto delle spese" (account for the expenses). (2) "rendere conto a [persona]" = to report to / answer to someone: "rendere conto al capo" (report to the boss). Very common variant: "rendersi conto (di)" = to realize / become aware: "Mi sono reso/a conto dell’errore".
target_language_example: Devi rendere conto delle tue azioni.
native_language_example: You have to account for your actions.

meaning: to stay still; to remain motionless.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone not to move (e.g., for safety, a photo, a medical check, or while you do something). Often said as an instruction: “Resta fermo!” It can also be used figuratively to mean not making progress: “sono rimasto fermo con l’italiano” (I got stuck / didn’t progress).
target_language_example: Resta fermo un attimo, devo controllare la ferita.
native_language_example: Stay still a moment, I need to check the wound.

meaning: to feel hurt or disappointed (to take it badly).
additional_notes: Informal idiom used when someone is upset because something they expected didn’t happen, or because a comment/action hurt them. Often used with "ci" referring to the situation: "Ci sono rimasto/a male" = "I was really disappointed/hurt." Conjugate "rimanere" and match the past participle to the speaker: rimasto (male speaker), rimasta (female speaker).
target_language_example: Ci sono rimasta male quando non mi hai invitata.
native_language_example: I was really hurt/disappointed when you didn’t invite me.

meaning: to feel hurt/offended; to be upset (often by something someone said or did).
additional_notes: Used when someone reacts negatively emotionally—feeling hurt, disappointed, or offended. Commonly in the past tense (e.g., "ci sono rimasto/a male" = “I was really upset/hurt”), with the pronoun "ci". Agree the past participle with the subject: rimasto (male speaker), rimasta (female speaker). Often followed by "per" + reason ("per quello che hai detto").
target_language_example: Ci sono rimasta male per quello che mi hai detto.
native_language_example: I was really hurt/upset by what you said to me.

meaning: “Rest in peace.” (used to express condolences after someone has died).
additional_notes: A respectful, formal expression often written in messages, condolences, or on gravestones. It uses the polite form (Lei): literally “may he/she rest in peace.” Common variants: “RIP” and “Riposa in pace” (more direct/less formal).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace molto per la tua perdita: riposi in pace.
native_language_example: I’m very sorry for your loss: may they rest in peace.

additional_notes: Common term in news, school, and environmental discussions. Often used with verbs like "combattere" (to fight), "ridurre" (to reduce), and "causare" (to cause). Related terms: "cambiamento climatico" (climate change).
target_language_example: Dobbiamo ridurre le emissioni per combattere il riscaldamento globale.
native_language_example: We need to reduce emissions to fight global warming.

additional_notes: Used on menus and in grocery stores to refer to whole-grain rice (less refined than white rice). Often contrasted with "riso bianco". "Integrale" literally means "whole/whole-grain" in food contexts.
target_language_example: Vorrei un’insalata con riso integrale, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a salad with brown rice, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about materials or assets found in nature that people can use (e.g., water, wood, oil, minerals). Often appears in environmental, geography, economics, and sustainability contexts. Plural: “risorse naturali.”
target_language_example: L’acqua è una risorsa naturale fondamentale.
native_language_example: Water is a fundamental natural resource.

additional_notes: Common preposition used to compare things or to introduce a reference point (a topic, a baseline, or another person/thing). Often followed by a noun or pronoun: rispetto a me/te/lui/lei, rispetto all'anno scorso. In everyday speech it frequently means 'compared to'.
target_language_example: Rispetto a ieri, oggi fa più caldo.
native_language_example: Compared to yesterday, today it’s warmer.

meaning: to really annoy someone; to pester (very vulgar).
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar (literally “to break the balls”). Used to complain that someone/something is bothering you a lot. Common patterns: “Non mi rompere i coglioni!” (Stop bothering me!), “Mi rompi i coglioni.” (You’re pissing me off / you’re really annoying me), “Che rompimento di coglioni!” (What a pain in the ass!). Avoid in polite/company situations.
target_language_example: Non mi rompere i coglioni, sto lavorando.
native_language_example: Stop bothering me, I’m working.

meaning: (vulgar) to annoy someone; to be a pain in the ass.
additional_notes: Very vulgar/impolite expression. Used to say someone is bothering you or being annoying. Often appears with an indirect object pronoun: "Non rompermi il cazzo" = "Don’t bother/bug me" (literally very crude). Also used generally: "Smettila di rompere il cazzo" = "Stop being so annoying." Avoid in polite settings.
target_language_example: Oh, smettila di rompere il cazzo!
native_language_example: Oh, stop being so annoying!

meaning: (very vulgar) to kick someone’s ass; to beat someone up badly.
additional_notes: Strongly offensive/vulgar expression, usually used as a threat or to say someone will defeat someone decisively. Commonly used with an indirect object: "rompere il culo a qualcuno" (e.g., "Ti rompo il culo"). Avoid in polite conversation; it can easily escalate a situation.
target_language_example: Se lo fai un’altra volta, ti rompo il culo.
native_language_example: If you do it one more time, I’ll kick your ass.

meaning: to be a pain / to annoy (someone) a lot; to “bust someone’s balls”.
additional_notes: Very vulgar and informal. Used when someone is seriously annoying you or bothering you: "Mi stai rompendo le palle" (You’re really annoying me). You can also use it about a situation: "Che palle!" / "Mi rompe le palle" (It really annoys me). Avoid in polite settings; a milder option is "dare fastidio" (to bother) or "scocciare" (to bug).
target_language_example: Smettila di rompere le palle e lasciami lavorare.
native_language_example: Stop being a pain and let me work.

additional_notes: From the verb "sapere" (to know), 3rd person singular "sa" + "tutto" (everything). Used to say someone knows everything, sometimes neutrally but often with an ironic/annoyed tone (similar to "he thinks he knows everything"). You can change the subject for other people: "so tutto" (I know everything), "sai tutto" (you know everything).
target_language_example: Non ascoltarlo: sa tutto lui.
native_language_example: Don’t listen to him: he knows everything (he thinks he knows it all).

additional_notes: Common in camping/travel contexts. Often used with the verb "portare" (to bring) or "avere" (to have): "Ho portato il sacco a pelo." Plural: "sacchi a pelo".
target_language_example: Per la notte in tenda serve un sacco a pelo caldo.
native_language_example: For the night in the tent you need a warm sleeping bag.

additional_notes: Used in hospitals to refer to the room where surgery is performed. Often appears with prepositions like in sala operatoria (“in the operating room”) or essere/andare in sala operatoria (“to be/go into surgery”).
target_language_example: Il paziente è già in sala operatoria.
native_language_example: The patient is already in the operating room.

additional_notes: A common food item on menus and in grocery stores. You’ll often see it with prepositions like "al/col" (with) or "di" (of), e.g., "panino al salmone affumicato" (smoked salmon sandwich) or "pasta con salmone affumicato" (pasta with smoked salmon).
target_language_example: Vorrei un panino al salmone affumicato, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a smoked salmon sandwich, please.

meaning: to come out; to pop up; to turn up (unexpectedly).
additional_notes: Used when something/someone appears suddenly or unexpectedly, or when information/details emerge (often in conversation: "È saltato fuori che..."). Literally "to jump out," but in everyday Italian it often means "to show up" or "to come to light."
target_language_example: È saltato fuori un problema all’ultimo momento.
native_language_example: A problem popped up at the last moment.

meaning: to blow up; to explode (literally: to jump into the air).
additional_notes: Used for explosions (a bomb, gas leak, car, building) and also figuratively to mean a plan/meeting/deal gets suddenly ruined or cancelled ("the plan blew up"). In everyday speech you often hear it in the past: "è saltato/a in aria" (it blew up / went up in the air).
target_language_example: Il piano è saltato in aria all’ultimo momento.
native_language_example: The plan blew up at the last moment.

additional_notes: Used in everyday and formal contexts (healthcare, news, school, work) to talk about psychological well-being. Often appears with verbs like “prendersi cura della salute mentale” (to take care of your mental health) or “problemi di salute mentale” (mental health problems).
target_language_example: È importante prendersi cura della salute mentale.
native_language_example: It’s important to take care of your mental health.

additional_notes: Often used in the expression "avere il sangue freddo" (to keep your cool / stay calm), especially in stressful or dangerous situations. It can also describe someone’s personality (a person who stays calm and doesn’t panic).
target_language_example: Durante l’emergenza, ha mantenuto il sangue freddo.
native_language_example: During the emergency, he/she kept his/her cool.

additional_notes: Used to say someone arrived or came through an experience without injury or problems. Common with verbs like "arrivare" and "tornare" (to arrive/return): "arrivare/tornare sano e salvo". Literally "healthy and safe", but in English the natural phrase is "safe and sound".
target_language_example: Sono tornati a casa sani e salvi dopo il viaggio.
native_language_example: They returned home safe and sound after the trip.

additional_notes: A respectful title used to refer to the Pope in Catholic contexts. Usually written with capital letters when used as a title (Santo Padre), and often appears with the definite article: "il Santo Padre". Not typically used for ordinary fathers; it specifically refers to the Pope.
target_language_example: Domani il Santo Padre parlerà in piazza San Pietro.
native_language_example: Tomorrow the Holy Father will speak in St. Peter’s Square.

meaning: “Oh my God!” / “Good heavens!” (an exclamation of surprise, shock, or frustration).
additional_notes: Used as an interjection, often on its own or at the start of a sentence. It’s common and generally mild (less strong than some swear words). Literally means “holy sky/heaven,” and can also appear as “Santo cielo!”
target_language_example: Santo cielo! Ho dimenticato le chiavi in macchina.
native_language_example: Oh my God! I forgot the keys in the car.

additional_notes: Used for a box/container with nothing inside. Common in everyday contexts (packages, storage, recycling). You can also say “una scatola vuota” (an empty box) or make it plural: “scatole vuote”.
target_language_example: Ho trovato solo una scatola vuota.
native_language_example: I found only an empty box.

scivolare su una buccia di banana

target_language_multi_word_term: scivolare su una buccia di banana
meaning: to slip on a banana peel.
additional_notes: Often used literally (a classic slapstick accident), but it can also be used figuratively to mean making an embarrassing mistake or “slipping up” because of something small or unexpected. Verb: scivolare = to slip; buccia di banana = banana peel.
target_language_example: Durante il discorso ha scivolato su una buccia di banana e ha detto il nome sbagliato.
native_language_example: During the speech he slipped on a banana peel and said the wrong name.

additional_notes: Used in tech/computer contexts to mean a combination of keys that performs an action quickly (e.g., Ctrl+C). Often appears in plural: "scorciatoie da tastiera". You can also say "scorciatoia" alone when the context is clear. Related: "tastiera" = keyboard.
target_language_example: Qual è la scorciatoia da tastiera per copiare e incollare?
native_language_example: What is the keyboard shortcut to copy and paste?

additional_notes: Used for the first years of compulsory schooling in Italy (typically ages 6–11). It’s a common, neutral term; you may also hear "scuola primaria" as the official/formal name.
target_language_example: Mia figlia frequenta la scuola elementare vicino a casa.
native_language_example: My daughter attends the elementary school near our house.

additional_notes: In Italy, this usually refers to the 3 years after elementary school (roughly ages 11–14), officially called "scuola secondaria di primo grado". It can be used with the article ("la scuola media") and often in the plural ("le scuole medie").
target_language_example: Mio fratello va ancora alle scuole medie.
native_language_example: My brother still goes to middle school.

additional_notes: In Italy this refers to the school level after "scuola media" (middle school) and before university; it’s commonly called "scuola superiore" or "scuola secondaria di secondo grado". The word "media" here relates to the school level (middle school), not to "media" in English.
target_language_example: Mia sorella frequenta la scuola media superiore a Milano.
native_language_example: My sister goes to high school in Milan.

additional_notes: Refers to the first stage of compulsory schooling for children, roughly ages 6–11 in Italy. Often used in school-related contexts (enrollment, grades, teachers). Also said as "scuola elementare" (more traditional/older term).
target_language_example: Mia figlia frequenta la scuola primaria vicino a casa.
native_language_example: My daughter attends the primary (elementary) school near our house.

additional_notes: In Italy this refers to the years after middle school (scuola media), typically ages 14–19. It’s often said as "le scuole superiori" (plural) to mean "high school" in general. Not to be confused with "università" (university) or "scuola elementare" (primary school).
target_language_example: Mia sorella frequenta una scuola superiore a Milano.
native_language_example: My sister attends a high school in Milan.

additional_notes: Used to state a condition or consequence: 'Do X, otherwise Y will happen.' Very common in spoken Italian; it’s often written as one word, **sennò**, with the same meaning. Can also be used after a request/warning to add urgency or a consequence.
target_language_example: Sbrigati, se no perdiamo il treno.
native_language_example: Hurry up, otherwise we’ll miss the train.

additional_notes: Used mainly in two ways: (1) conditional: “if not” (often like “otherwise”): Se non studi, non passi l’esame. (2) exception/limitation: “except for / other than”: Non ho niente se non un po’ di pane (“I have nothing except a bit of bread”). In the exception sense, it often follows negatives like non/nessuno/niente.
target_language_example: Non ho visto nessuno se non Marco.
native_language_example: I didn’t see anyone except Marco.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular subject to mean “herself,” often after verbs like vedere, guardare, considerare, sentire, trovare (e.g., “She sees herself…”). For a male subject it’s “se stesso”; for plural it’s “se stessi / se stesse.” Often appears with prepositions too: “da se stessa” (by herself), “tra se stessa” (to herself).
target_language_example: Si è guardata allo specchio e ha sorriso tra se stessa.
native_language_example: She looked at herself in the mirror and smiled to herself.

additional_notes: Used after verbs to refer back to the subject (“to oneself”). It agrees with the subject’s gender/number: se stesso (he/it), se stessa (she/it), se stessi (they masc./mixed), se stesse (they fem.). Often appears with verbs like guardare, parlare, prendere, convincere.
target_language_example: Ha parlato di se stesso per tutto il tempo.
native_language_example: He talked about himself the whole time.

meaning: in my opinion; according to me.
additional_notes: Common way to give your opinion. Often used at the start of a sentence, or after the verb: “Secondo me, …” / “…, secondo me.” You can change the person: secondo te (in your opinion), secondo lui/lei (in his/her opinion), secondo noi (in our opinion), secondo loro (in their opinion).
target_language_example: Secondo me, questo ristorante è il migliore del quartiere.
native_language_example: In my opinion, this restaurant is the best in the neighborhood.

additional_notes: Most commonly used for floors in a building: in Italy the floor at street level is usually the "piano terra" (ground floor), so "secondo piano" is two levels above street level. Figuratively, "in secondo piano" means "in the background" or "not the main focus".
target_language_example: L’ufficio è al secondo piano, ma in questa discussione i dettagli passano in secondo piano.
native_language_example: The office is on the second floor, but in this discussion the details take a back seat.

additional_notes: Common everyday term for a mobility aid. Often used with the verb "essere" (to be) or "avere" (to have): "Sono in sedia a rotelle" = "I’m in a wheelchair." You may also hear the shorter form "carrozzina" in some contexts.
target_language_example: Mia nonna è in sedia a rotelle.
native_language_example: My grandma is in a wheelchair.

meaning: “provided that” / “as long as” (on the condition that).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition that must be met for something to be true or to happen. Often followed by the subjunctive (e.g., “sempre che tu venga”), and it’s common in more formal or written Italian. Similar to “a condizione che” and “purché.”
target_language_example: Vengo alla festa, sempre che io finisca di lavorare in tempo.
native_language_example: I’ll come to the party, provided that I finish work in time.

additional_notes: Used in philosophical or reflective conversation to talk about life’s ultimate purpose or meaning. Commonly appears with verbs like cercare (“to look for”) or capire (“to understand”). Similar to English “the meaning of life.”
target_language_example: Mi chiedo spesso qual è il senso della vita.
native_language_example: I often wonder what the meaning of life is.

additional_notes: Used when you learn about a person/thing/place from other people’s talk, news, or general chatter (not necessarily by listening directly). Often followed by "di" + noun ("sentire parlare di Roma") or "di" + person ("sentire parlare di lui/lei"). Common in the past: "Ho sentito parlare di..." = "I’ve heard about...".
target_language_example: Ho sentito parlare di questo ristorante: dicono che sia ottimo.
native_language_example: I’ve heard about this restaurant; they say it’s great.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause meaning that something does NOT happen. It’s typically followed by the subjunctive (congiuntivo), often with different subjects: “Sono uscito senza che mi vedesse” (“I left without him seeing me”). If the subject stays the same, Italian often uses “senza” + infinitive instead: “Sono uscito senza salutare” (“I left without saying goodbye”).
target_language_example: Sono uscito senza che nessuno mi vedesse.
native_language_example: I left without anyone seeing me.

additional_notes: Used to strongly agree or to say you’re certain about something. It can be used as a short reply (like “Definitely.”) or inside a sentence. Slightly more formal than "sicuramente", but common in everyday speech too.
target_language_example: Senza dubbio, è la scelta migliore.
native_language_example: Without a doubt, it’s the best choice.

additional_notes: Literally “without breath.” Used for being physically winded (after running, climbing stairs, etc.) and also figuratively for being stunned or amazed. Often used with verbs like essere/restare/rimanere: “Sono senza fiato” (I’m out of breath), “Sono rimasto senza fiato” (I was left speechless/breathless).
target_language_example: Dopo aver corso per prendere l’autobus, sono arrivato senza fiato.
native_language_example: After running to catch the bus, I arrived out of breath.

additional_notes: Literally 'without name'. Used to describe something that doesn’t have a name (e.g., a street, a file) or someone/something anonymous/unnamed. It can also be used as an adjective phrase after a noun (e.g., "una strada senza nome").
target_language_example: Ho trovato un file senza nome sul desktop.
native_language_example: I found an unnamed file on the desktop.

additional_notes: Used to express strong surprise, shock, admiration, or disappointment. It can be literal (you’re truly unable to speak) or figurative (you’re amazed or outraged). Often said as a stand-alone reaction: “Senza parole!”
target_language_example: Quando ho visto il panorama, sono rimasto senza parole.
native_language_example: When I saw the view, I was left speechless.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that lacks meaning, logic, or purpose (an idea, sentence, explanation, rule, etc.). Common in phrases like “È senza senso” (“It’s nonsense”) or “Una cosa senza senso” (“a meaningless thing”).
target_language_example: Quello che dici è senza senso.
native_language_example: What you’re saying doesn’t make sense.

additional_notes: Used to describe an action that continues continuously, without breaks. Common with verbs like lavorare (to work), parlare (to talk), correre (to run), and expressions like piove senza sosta (“it’s raining nonstop”).
target_language_example: Ha lavorato senza sosta tutto il giorno.
native_language_example: He worked nonstop all day.

meaning: to get out of hand; to slip out of one’s control.
additional_notes: Used when a situation becomes hard to manage or control. It can also be literal (something physically slips from your hand), but it’s very common figuratively for problems, arguments, parties, etc. Conjugate the verb: mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli sfugge di mano (present).
target_language_example: La situazione ci è sfuggita di mano e abbiamo chiamato la polizia.
native_language_example: The situation got out of hand and we called the police.

additional_notes: Commonly used to comment that something is visible or obvious: “Si vede!” = “You can tell!” / “It shows.” With “non” it often means something isn’t visible: “Non si vede” = “You can’t see it.” In some contexts, especially when parting, it can mean “See you” (short for “Ci si vede”).
target_language_example: È troppo scuro: non si vede niente.
native_language_example: It’s too dark: you can’t see anything.

meaning: “may (he/it) be praised” / “praise be (to…)” (an expression of praise or thanks).
additional_notes: Fixed, slightly formal/old-fashioned expression, often used with religious references (e.g., "Sia lodato Gesù Cristo" = "Praised be Jesus Christ"). Grammatically it uses the present subjunctive of "essere" (sia = "may it be"). In everyday Italian you’ll more often hear simpler options like "grazie a Dio" (thank God) or "meno male" (thank goodness), depending on context.
target_language_example: Sia lodato il Signore, siamo arrivati in tempo.
native_language_example: Praise be to the Lord, we arrived on time.

meaning: "be that as it may" / "whatever happens" (accepting it).
additional_notes: Fixed expression used to show resignation or acceptance: you’ll proceed or decide anyway, regardless of the outcome or details. Often followed by a main clause (e.g., “Sia quel che sia, andiamo.”). Uses the subjunctive of “essere” (sia) and “what” (quel che).
target_language_example: Sia quel che sia, domani parto lo stesso.
native_language_example: Be that as it may, I’m leaving tomorrow anyway.

additional_notes: A polite, formal way to address a group, often at the start of announcements, speeches, or public events. It’s the plural of “signora/signore” used as a form of address; you may also hear “Signore e signori, benvenuti…” (“Ladies and gentlemen, welcome…”).
target_language_example: Signore e signori, lo spettacolo sta per cominciare.
native_language_example: Ladies and gentlemen, the show is about to begin.

additional_notes: Common everyday term. Usually masculine: il sito web (plural: i siti web). Often shortened to "sito" when the context is clear. You can also hear "il sito" or simply "il web" in related phrases.
target_language_example: Puoi visitare il nostro sito web per maggiori informazioni.
native_language_example: You can visit our website for more information.

meaning: to daydream; to have your head in the clouds.
additional_notes: Literally “to dream with eyes open.” Used for imagining things while awake (often pleasantly), or for not paying attention because you’re lost in thoughts. Common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Durante la lezione, mi capita di sognare ad occhi aperti.
native_language_example: During the lesson, I sometimes daydream.

meaning: “I’m in love with you” (said by a woman).
additional_notes: Used to express romantic love. In Italian, the adjective changes with the speaker: a man would say “sono innamorato di te”. You can also say “sono innamorata di te” to a person you address as “tu”; for a formal “you” (Lei), you’d say “sono innamorata di Lei”.
target_language_example: Sono innamorata di te da mesi.
native_language_example: I’ve been in love with you for months.

meaning: “I’m in love with you” (said by a man).
additional_notes: Used to express romantic love. A woman would say “sono innamorata di te.” Often shortened to “ti amo” (I love you), but “sono innamorato/a di te” emphasizes being in love with someone. You can also replace “di te” with a name: “Sono innamorato di Marco.”
target_language_example: Sono innamorato di te da mesi.
native_language_example: I’ve been in love with you for months.

meaning: under your arm; tucked under your arm.
additional_notes: Used to say you’re holding or carrying something tucked against your side under your arm (e.g., a book, folder, bag). It’s a fixed phrase with the definite article (il) in the singular; in the plural you can also say "sotto le braccia" (under your arms).
target_language_example: Aveva un libro sotto il braccio mentre entrava in classe.
native_language_example: He had a book tucked under his arm as he walked into class.

additional_notes: Used to say something is below the surface of the earth (literally: "under ground"). Often with verbs like essere/stare (to be), andare (to go), or vivere (to live). It can be both literal (a metro line, a tunnel) and figurative in some contexts (e.g., being buried).
target_language_example: La metropolitana corre sotto terra.
native_language_example: The subway runs underground.

additional_notes: Used to talk about causing deep emotional pain (often in love, but also in sad situations). It’s commonly used with an indirect object pronoun: “Mi hai spezzato il cuore” (You broke my heart). You may also hear the reflexive/indirect form “spezzarsi il cuore” meaning “to feel heartbroken” or “to break one’s heart (to see/hear something)”.
target_language_example: Mi hai spezzato il cuore quando te ne sei andato.
native_language_example: You broke my heart when you left.

meaning: spine; backbone (also: the main support/central part of something).
additional_notes: Literal meaning is “dorsal spine.” Most commonly refers to the human spine in everyday conversation or at the doctor. Figuratively, it can mean the “backbone” or core support of an organization, plan, or system (e.g., the backbone of the network/company).
target_language_example: La spina dorsale è molto importante per la postura.
native_language_example: The spine is very important for posture.

additional_notes: Used to report information based on a source or evidence, often meaning “according to what X says/according to X.” It’s built from the gerund of *stare* (“stando”) + *a*. Common patterns: *stando a quanto dice...* (“according to what ... says”), *stando alle previsioni* (“according to the forecasts”), *stando ai documenti* (“according to the documents”). Slightly formal; common in news/writing.
target_language_example: Stando a quanto dice il giornale, domani pioverà.
native_language_example: According to what the newspaper says, it will rain tomorrow.

meaning: to be/stay at (a place); to keep doing (something).
additional_notes: Used with a place: “sto a casa” = “I’m at home.” It can also be followed by an infinitive to show an action that continues or that someone is busy doing: “sto a studiare” = “I’m studying / I’m busy studying.” In everyday Italian, “stare + gerund” (sto studiando) is often more common for “I am doing…,” but “stare a + infinitive” is still used, especially to stress “staying there doing it” or “keeping at it.”
target_language_example: Sto a casa a studiare.
native_language_example: I’m at home studying.

meaning: to wait and see; to see how things turn out.
additional_notes: Used when you’re not sure what will happen and you prefer to wait before deciding or reacting. Often appears as "stiamo a vedere" (let’s wait and see) or "sto a vedere" (I’ll wait and see).
target_language_example: Non so se verrà davvero: stiamo a vedere.
native_language_example: I don’t know if he’ll really come: let’s wait and see.

meaning: to keep up with; to stay on top of; to look after.
additional_notes: Usually used with "a" + a person/thing: "stare dietro a qualcuno/qualcosa". It can mean (1) physically following behind or chasing after someone, (2) managing/keeping up with tasks, work, or study, or (3) looking after someone (often kids). In the sense of "keep up with/manage", it’s often used in negatives: "Non riesco a starci dietro" = "I can’t keep up with it."
target_language_example: Con tutto questo lavoro, non riesco a stare dietro alle email.
native_language_example: With all this work, I can’t keep up with the emails.

additional_notes: Used to describe being upright (not sitting/lying down). It can be literal (a person standing) and also used for things that “stay up” or “hold up” (e.g., a structure that remains standing). Often contrasted with "sedersi" (to sit down) and "sdraiarsi" (to lie down).
target_language_example: Non posso più stare in piedi: mi fanno male le gambe.
native_language_example: I can’t stand anymore: my legs hurt.

meaning: to be together; to date / be in a relationship (as a couple).
additional_notes: Literally "to stay together," but very commonly used to mean two people are a couple (dating or in a relationship). Also used more generally for spending time together (friends/family). In the couple sense, it’s often phrased as "stanno insieme" (they’re together) or "state insieme?" (are you together?).
target_language_example: Da quanto tempo state insieme?
native_language_example: How long have you been together (dating)?

meaning: to be about to (do something); to be on the point of.
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to talk about an action that is going to happen very soon: "stare per" + infinitive (e.g., "sto per uscire"). The verb "stare" changes with the subject (sto, stai, sta, stiamo, state, stanno). Often interchangeable with "essere sul punto di" (more formal).
target_language_example: Sto per uscire: ci vediamo dopo.
native_language_example: I’m about to go out: see you later.

meaning: to be quiet; to shut up.
additional_notes: Means “to keep quiet/to stay silent,” often used as an instruction or command (especially in the imperative: “Stai zitto!”). Can sound harsh/impolite depending on tone and context; a softer alternative is “Stai in silenzio” or “Per favore, stai zitto.” It changes for gender/number: “stai zitta” (to a woman), “state zitti/e” (to a group).
target_language_example: Stai zitto, per favore: sto ascoltando.
native_language_example: Be quiet, please: I’m listening.

meaning: “you were saying …” (imperfect; used to refer back to what someone was saying).
additional_notes: From *stare* (imperfect: *stavi*) + gerund (*dicendo*). Common in questions to ask someone to continue after an interruption or to clarify: *Che cosa stavi dicendo?* = “What were you saying?”
target_language_example: Scusa, non ho sentito: che cosa stavi dicendo?
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t hear: what were you saying?

additional_notes: Used to refer to the local police station (the building/office). Often appears with the article: "la stazione di polizia". You may also hear "questura" (main police headquarters) or "commissariato" (police precinct), but "stazione di polizia" is a clear, beginner-friendly term.
target_language_example: Devo andare alla stazione di polizia per fare una denuncia.
native_language_example: I have to go to the police station to file a report.

additional_notes: A formal/standard way to refer to a train station; commonly seen on signs and in travel contexts. Often shortened in speech to “stazione” when it’s clear you mean the train station.
target_language_example: Dov’è la stazione ferroviaria più vicina?
native_language_example: Where is the nearest train station?

additional_notes: Commonly used when making a wish: often said as you spot one in the night sky (e.g., "Esprimi un desiderio!"). Literally means "falling star" even though it refers to a meteor. Plural: "stelle cadenti".
target_language_example: Ho visto una stella cadente e ho espresso un desiderio.
native_language_example: I saw a shooting star and made a wish.

additional_notes: Common in everyday talk about habits, health, work-life balance, and personal choices. Often used with adjectives (e.g., stile di vita sano = healthy lifestyle, stile di vita sedentario = sedentary lifestyle) or with verbs like avere/condurre (to have/lead) and cambiare (to change).
target_language_example: Da quando ho iniziato a fare sport, ho cambiato stile di vita.
native_language_example: Since I started exercising, I changed my lifestyle.

additional_notes: Used to say you feel good physically or emotionally, often as an answer to “Come stai?” (How are you?). It can also mean you’re comfortable or satisfied (“I’m good like this”). From the verb “stare” (to be/to stay) + “bene” (well), so it’s fairly literal.
target_language_example: —Come stai? —Sto bene, grazie.
native_language_example: —How are you? —I’m fine, thank you.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase used for any instrument used to make music (e.g., piano, chitarra, batteria). Often used with articles and with verbs like suonare (to play). Plural: strumenti musicali.
target_language_example: Sai suonare qualche strumento musicale?
native_language_example: Can you play any musical instrument?

additional_notes: Used to describe movement in opposite directions repeatedly (walking/pacing, going between floors, going up and down stairs), or a fluctuating situation (e.g., prices, mood). In speech it can also suggest doing something repeatedly/aimlessly: “andare su e giù” = to go back and forth / to pace around.
target_language_example: Ha camminato su e giù per la stanza tutta la sera.
native_language_example: He walked back and forth around the room all evening.

meaning: on the field; in practice (in real-world conditions).
additional_notes: Literally “on the field” (su + il = sul). Used both for sports (“on the pitch/field”) and more generally to mean doing something in real conditions rather than in theory (similar to “in the field” or “on the ground”).
target_language_example: La teoria è utile, ma è sul campo che si impara davvero.
native_language_example: Theory is useful, but it’s in practice that you really learn.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to a specific fact or situation already mentioned. Very common with verbs like "insistere" (to insist), "tornare" (to come back to a topic), or with phrases like "discutere sul fatto che...". Often followed by "che" + a clause: "sul fatto che...". Also used as "di fatto" (different meaning: "in fact"), so don’t confuse them.
target_language_example: Vorrei tornare sul fatto che non mi hai avvisato.
native_language_example: I’d like to come back to the fact that you didn’t let me know.

additional_notes: Common in everyday speech and in practical situations (work, emergencies, deliveries) to mean someone/something is physically at the location. Often used with verbs like essere/arrivare (to be/arrive) and fare (to do) when something is handled immediately: "risolvere sul posto" = "fix it on the spot".
target_language_example: Il tecnico può intervenire sul posto entro un’ora.
native_language_example: The technician can come on site within an hour.

meaning: 'about to' (on the verge of doing something).
additional_notes: Used to say something is going to happen very soon. It’s followed by an infinitive verb: "sul punto di partire" (about to leave). It can also be used with "essere": "Sono sul punto di...". Related: "stare per" is another common way to say "about to".
target_language_example: Ero sul punto di uscire quando mi hai chiamato.
native_language_example: I was about to go out when you called me.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you mean something genuinely, or to ask if something is true. Common in everyday speech. Often used alone as a reaction (“Sul serio?” = “Seriously?”). Similar in meaning to “davvero” and “veramente,” but “sul serio” can sound a bit more emphatic.
target_language_example: Sul serio? Non sapevo che abitassi qui.
native_language_example: Seriously? I didn’t know you lived here.

additional_notes: Used to say something is true in principle or according to plans/rules, but may not match reality in practice. Common in contrasts like “sulla carta … ma …” (“on paper… but…”). Literally “on the paper.”
target_language_example: Sulla carta il progetto è perfetto, ma nella pratica è difficile da realizzare.
native_language_example: On paper the project is perfect, but in practice it’s hard to carry out.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone who feels attacked/criticized and reacts by protecting themselves, denying, or being guarded. Often follows verbs like essere/mettersi/andare (e.g., “essere sulla difensiva”). Literally “on the defensive.”
target_language_example: Quando gli hanno fatto quella domanda, si è messo subito sulla difensiva.
native_language_example: When they asked him that question, he immediately got defensive.

meaning: “on the skin of”; often “at the expense of / to the detriment of”.
additional_notes: Literally refers to someone’s skin, but it’s very common in figurative expressions meaning that someone suffers the consequences while someone else benefits. Often used with verbs like "arricchirsi" (to get rich), "guadagnare" (to profit), or "fare carriera" (to get ahead): "arricchirsi sulla pelle di qualcuno" = to profit off someone’s suffering.
target_language_example: Si è arricchito sulla pelle dei lavoratori.
native_language_example: He got rich at the workers’ expense.

meaning: “in the same boat” (in the same situation, usually a difficult one).
additional_notes: Used to say that you and someone else share the same problem or circumstances, so you can understand each other. It’s a common, neutral idiom. Often used with verbs like “essere” (to be): “Siamo tutti sulla stessa barca.”
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: siamo tutti sulla stessa barca.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: we’re all in the same boat.

additional_notes: Literally 'on the shoulders' (su + le). Used both physically (carrying/wearing something on your shoulders) and figuratively to express responsibility or burden: avere qualcosa sulle spalle = to have something on your shoulders (to carry a responsibility). Often appears with possessives: sulle mie/tue/sue spalle.
target_language_example: Ho tante responsabilità sulle spalle.
native_language_example: I have a lot of responsibilities on my shoulders.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to a female subject, often for emphasis (like English “herself”). It’s commonly used after prepositions: "di sé stessa" (of herself), "per sé stessa" (for herself). The accent in "sé" helps distinguish it from "se" (if). Masculine: "sé stesso"; plural: "sé stessi/sé stesse".
target_language_example: Ha parlato di sé stessa con molta sincerità.
native_language_example: She spoke about herself very honestly.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize the reflexive pronoun “sé” (“oneself/himself/itself”), often after prepositions (di sé, a sé, con sé). The accent in “sé” is used when it’s a stressed pronoun (especially after a preposition). You may also see it written as “se stesso” in some contexts; both refer to the same idea of “self.”
target_language_example: Ha parlato di sé stesso senza vergogna.
native_language_example: He talked about himself without shame.

additional_notes: Most often written as two words and used in more formal or written Italian. As a conjunction, it links a cause to a consequence: “..., sì che ...” = “..., so that/therefore ...”. It can also be used to reinforce what you’re saying (“indeed/really”), though beginners more often hear emphasis with "sì" alone. Don’t confuse it with "sicché" (often one word), which has the same basic meaning (“so/therefore”).
target_language_example: Pioveva forte, sì che siamo rimasti a casa.
native_language_example: It was raining hard, so we stayed at home.

additional_notes: Common noun in Italian too (often written "T-shirt" or "t-shirt"). Feminine: "una t-shirt". Plural usually "t-shirt" (invariable in everyday use), though you may also see "T-shirt" used for both singular and plural.
target_language_example: Vorrei una t-shirt nera, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a black T-shirt, please.

additional_notes: Used when talking about getting a haircut or describing a hairstyle. Often appears with verbs like "fare" or "farsi": "Devo fare un taglio di capelli" / "Devo farmi un taglio di capelli" (I need to get a haircut). In a salon you might hear "Che taglio vuole?" (What cut would you like?).
target_language_example: Vorrei un taglio di capelli corto, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a short haircut, please.

additional_notes: Used to say that a situation is positive, or that something you’ve just heard makes things better. Often follows a clause introduced by se (“if”): “Se vieni, tanto meglio” = “If you come, even better.” Can also be said on its own as a reaction.
target_language_example: Se puoi venire domani, tanto meglio.
native_language_example: If you can come tomorrow, even better.

meaning: “as much as” / “as … as” (for quantity or degree).
additional_notes: Used to compare equality. With adjectives/adverbs: “tanto … quanto” = “as … as” (e.g., tanto grande quanto…). With verbs/amounts: “tanto quanto” = “as much as” (e.g., quanto posso/quanto vuoi). Often appears as a pair: “tanto … quanto …”.
target_language_example: Ho tanto sonno quanto te.
native_language_example: I’m as sleepy as you.

additional_notes: Used with a female listener to emphasize that you mean the person themselves (often after a preposition or for emphasis): “per te stessa” (for yourself), “da te stessa” (by yourself). It uses the stressed pronoun “te” + “stessa” (feminine). For a male listener, say “te stesso”.
target_language_example: Devi farlo per te stessa.
native_language_example: You have to do it for yourself.

additional_notes: Reflexive/emphatic pronoun used to stress that the subject and object are the same person (“you… yourself”). Often used after verbs like vedere, guardare, conoscere, ricordare: “Guarda te stesso.” For a woman, use “te stessa.” In informal speech you may also hear “te” alone, but “te stesso/a” adds emphasis.
target_language_example: Devi credere in te stesso.
native_language_example: You have to believe in yourself.

additional_notes: Common everyday way to refer to a mobile phone. Often shortened to just "cellulare" (very common) or "telefonino" (more casual, often meaning a small/older phone). In Italy, "cellulare" is frequently preferred over "mobile".
target_language_example: Scusa, ho dimenticato il telefono cellulare a casa.
native_language_example: Sorry, I forgot my cell phone at home.

additional_notes: Used to talk about time when you’re not working or studying. Common in everyday conversation and in phrases like "nel tempo libero" (in my free time) and "attività del tempo libero" (leisure activities).
target_language_example: Nel mio tempo libero mi piace leggere e fare sport.
native_language_example: In my free time I like to read and play sports.

meaning: to keep under control; to rein in.
additional_notes: Used for controlling something or someone that could get out of hand (emotions, spending, an animal, a situation). Often followed by what is being controlled: "tenere a freno la rabbia" (keep your anger under control), "tenere a freno le spese" (rein in expenses).
target_language_example: Devo tenere a freno la mia rabbia.
native_language_example: I have to keep my anger under control.

meaning: to hold your tongue; to stop yourself from speaking (especially saying something inappropriate).
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression meaning to control what you say, often when you’re angry, tempted to gossip, or about to say something rude. Used with different subjects: "Tieni a freno la lingua!" (Hold your tongue!), "Ho tenuto a freno la lingua" (I held my tongue).
target_language_example: Volevo rispondergli male, ma ho tenuto a freno la lingua.
native_language_example: I wanted to snap back at him, but I held my tongue.

meaning: to take into account; to consider.
additional_notes: Often used as "tenere conto di" + noun/pronoun ("take ... into account"). Common in advice, instructions, and formal or neutral speech. Example: "Tieni conto del traffico" = "Consider the traffic." Related idea: "tenerne conto" uses "ne" to mean "of it/of that".
target_language_example: Tieni conto del traffico prima di partire.
native_language_example: Take the traffic into account before leaving.

meaning: to hang in there; to keep going (despite difficulties).
additional_notes: Used to encourage someone to persevere or to say you’re resisting or enduring a tough situation. Common in everyday speech and can be used on its own as an encouragement (e.g., "Dai, tieni duro!"). It’s somewhat idiomatic: literally it’s like “hold hard/tight,” but in English you usually say “hang in there.”
target_language_example: So che è un periodo difficile, ma tieni duro: andrà meglio.
native_language_example: I know it’s a tough time, but hang in there: it will get better.

meaning: to keep in mind; to bear in mind.
additional_notes: Commonly used to remind someone of an important detail, often with a clause: "Tieni/tenete presente che..." (= "Keep in mind that..."). In the past: "Ho tenuto presente..." (= "I kept in mind..."). Slightly formal/neutral, typical in advice, instructions, and workplace/school contexts.
target_language_example: Tieni presente che domani i negozi sono chiusi.
native_language_example: Keep in mind that tomorrow the shops are closed.

meaning: to hold tight; to keep a firm grip on.
additional_notes: Used literally (holding something firmly) and figuratively (holding onto something you value, or keeping someone/something close). Often followed by a direct object: “Tieni stretto la borsa!” = “Hold your bag tight!” In the imperative, common forms are “tieni stretto” (you, informal) and “tenga stretto” (you, formal).
target_language_example: Tieni stretto il mio braccio, c’è troppa gente.
native_language_example: Hold my arm tight, there are too many people.

additional_notes: Common way to refer to the sport; literally “tennis (played) on a table.” You may also hear “ping-pong,” but “tennis da tavolo” is the standard, more neutral term.
target_language_example: Ti va di fare una partita a tennis da tavolo?
native_language_example: Do you feel like playing a game of table tennis?

meaning: a very vulgar insult meaning “dickhead” / “asshole” (a stupid, unpleasant person).
additional_notes: Strong profanity and highly offensive. Used to insult someone directly (e.g., “Sei un/una testa di cazzo”) or to talk about someone (“È una testa di cazzo”). Avoid in polite/company situations; it can easily start a fight. Literally means “head of dick,” but it’s used like English “dickhead.”
target_language_example: Non fare il testa di cazzo: ascoltami un attimo.
native_language_example: Don’t be a dickhead: listen to me for a second.

additional_notes: Used for a person who personally saw an event (often in news, police, or legal contexts). You may also see it as "un/una testimone oculare"; "testimone" can be masculine or feminine, and the article shows the gender.
target_language_example: La polizia sta cercando un testimone oculare dell’incidente.
native_language_example: The police are looking for an eyewitness to the accident.

additional_notes: Used to express romantic love. “Ti” = “you” (informal singular object pronoun), and “amo” = “I love.” For friends/family, Italians often use “ti voglio bene” instead, which is less romantic.
target_language_example: Ti amo tanto.
native_language_example: I love you so much.

meaning: I care about you / I love you (in a non-romantic way).
