additional_notes: A very common way to express affection toward family, close friends, or children. It’s warmer than “I like you,” but usually not used for romantic love (for that, Italians typically say “ti amo”). You can also say “voglio bene a…” (e.g., “Voglio bene a mia sorella”).
target_language_example: Mamma, ti voglio bene!
native_language_example: Mom, I love you!

meaning: I care about you a lot / I love you very much (affectionately, not necessarily romantically).
additional_notes: Very common way to express deep affection (to family, close friends, a partner). It’s often less romantic/sexual than "ti amo" and can feel warmer or more appropriate in everyday situations. You can change intensity: "ti voglio bene" (I care about you/I love you), "ti voglio un sacco di bene" (I care about you a ton).
target_language_example: Mamma, ti voglio tanto bene.
native_language_example: Mom, I love you so much.

meaning: to take/pull out; to bring up (a topic).
additional_notes: Literally “to pull out.” Used for physically taking something out of a bag/pocket, and also figuratively for introducing a topic or revealing information (e.g., tirare fuori un argomento / un segreto).
target_language_example: Puoi tirare fuori il portafoglio, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you take out your wallet, please?

meaning: to pull up; to raise; (also) to cheer up; to bring up (a child).
additional_notes: Very common, versatile phrasal verb. Literal uses: pull something upward (tirare su la zip/la serranda) or lift someone/something (tirare su i bambini in braccio). Figurative uses: tirare su qualcuno = cheer someone up; tirare su un figlio/una figlia = raise a child. The exact meaning depends heavily on context.
target_language_example: Dai, tirati su: andrà meglio domani.
native_language_example: Come on, cheer up: it’ll be better tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used both literally (reaching the bottom of something, like water) and very commonly figuratively (reaching the lowest point in a difficult situation, emotionally, financially, etc.). Often appears in past tenses: “ho toccato il fondo” (I hit rock bottom).
target_language_example: Dopo aver perso il lavoro, ho toccato il fondo, ma poi ho ricominciato da capo.
native_language_example: After losing my job, I hit rock bottom, but then I started over.

additional_notes: A common dessert you’ll see on menus and in bakeries. Literally “cake with chocolate”; you can also hear "torta di cioccolato" (chocolate cake).
target_language_example: Vorrei una fetta di torta al cioccolato, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a slice of chocolate cake, please.

additional_notes: A common dessert. In Italy, "torta di mele" often refers to an apple cake (a soft, baked cake with apples), while "apple pie" in American English can suggest a pie with a crust. You may also see "crostata di mele" for a more tart/pastry-style version.
target_language_example: Per dessert prendiamo una fetta di torta di mele.
native_language_example: For dessert, let’s have a slice of apple pie/apple cake.

meaning: daydreaming; distracted ("with your head in the clouds").
additional_notes: Common idiom used to say someone isn’t paying attention or seems absent-minded. Often used with the verb "essere": "Sei sempre tra le nuvole" (You’re always daydreaming). Literally it means "among the clouds".
target_language_example: Scusa, oggi sono un po' tra le nuvole.
native_language_example: Sorry, today I’m a bit distracted / I’ve got my head in the clouds.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "dire" or "pensare" to indicate something you say or think privately (not out loud). Commonly appears as "tra me e me" (“to myself”).
target_language_example: Tra me, pensavo che sarebbe arrivato in ritardo.
native_language_example: To myself, I thought he would arrive late.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen shortly (minutes, not hours). Often interchangeable with "fra poco". Can refer to the future ("Tra poco arrivo") or to something that happened shortly ago with the past tense ("L’ho visto tra poco" = I saw him a little while ago), though the future use is more common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Tra poco torno, devo solo prendere un caffè.
native_language_example: I’ll be back soon; I just need to grab a coffee.

meaning: all of them (feminine plural), every single one.
additional_notes: Emphatic form of “tutte” used to stress that you mean the whole group, without exceptions. Refers to a feminine plural noun (e.g., ragazze, cose); with masculine plural you’d use “tutti quanti.” Often used after the noun or pronoun: “le ragazze tutte quante,” “tutte quante.”
target_language_example: Le ho invitate tutte quante.
native_language_example: I invited all of them (every single one).

additional_notes: Used to include everyone/everything in a group when listing items or people: "tutti e + [noun/pronoun]" or "tutti e + [number]" (e.g., "tutti e tre" = “all three”). It’s masculine plural; use "tutte e" for an all-female group. Often followed by another element, so it may feel incomplete on its own.
target_language_example: Siete tutti e tre pronti?
native_language_example: Are all three of you ready?

additional_notes: Usually refers to the holiday on November 1st (Ognissanti), when Italians may visit cemeteries and remember the dead (often together with Nov 2, Giorno dei Morti). In everyday speech it can also appear in expressions like "Tutti i Santi!" to show annoyance or surprise (mild exclamation).
target_language_example: A Tutti i Santi andiamo al cimitero a trovare i nonni.
native_language_example: On All Saints’ Day we go to the cemetery to visit (the graves of) our grandparents.

additional_notes: Common time expression meaning something happens daily. Often placed at the end of the sentence (e.g., "Studio tutti i giorni") or near the verb for emphasis. "Tutti i giorni" is a set phrase; for singular masculine nouns you’ll often see the pattern "tutti i + plural noun" (e.g., "tutti i weekend").
target_language_example: Vado in palestra tutti i giorni.
native_language_example: I go to the gym every day.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize “all/everyone,” often meaning “every single one.” It can refer to people or things, and it often appears after the noun/pronoun it emphasizes (e.g., “voi tutti quanti”). Common in spoken Italian; “tutti” alone is also correct but less emphatic.
target_language_example: Venite tutti quanti a cena da noi stasera!
native_language_example: Come all of you to dinner at our place tonight!

additional_notes: Common, informal-feeling everyday phrase. Often used as a greeting question: “Tutto bene?” (“How are you?/Is everything okay?”). It can also be an answer meaning “Everything’s fine.” You may also hear the fuller version “Tutto va bene”.
target_language_example: Ciao! Tutto bene? — Sì, tutto bene, grazie.
native_language_example: Hi! All good? — Yes, everything’s fine, thanks.

additional_notes: Used to say there’s nothing more to add, or that something is simple and finished. Common in spoken Italian; often also said as "tutto qui" (same meaning).
target_language_example: Non c’è altro da fare, tutto qua.
native_language_example: There’s nothing else to do, that’s all.

additional_notes: Used to order or talk about green tea. In Italian, the accent in “tè” distinguishes it from “te” (“you”). You may also see it without the accent in casual writing ("te verde"), but “tè” is the standard spelling.
target_language_example: Vorrei un tè verde, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a green tea, please.

meaning: the final word; the last say.
additional_notes: Used for the definitive/decisive statement or decision in a discussion. Common in the expression “avere l’ultima parola” (“to have the last word” / “to have the final say”).
target_language_example: In questa decisione, il direttore ha l’ultima parola.
native_language_example: In this decision, the director has the final say.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that there is nothing (often in a slightly annoyed or ironic tone). Common after verbs like fare (“to do/make”) and sapere (“to know”): “non fare/sapere un bel niente.” Literally “a nice nothing,” but it means the opposite—emphatic “nothing.”
target_language_example: Ho studiato tutto il giorno, ma non ho capito un bel niente.
native_language_example: I studied all day, but I didn’t understand anything at all.

additional_notes: Literally “a world.” Common in everyday speech to emphasize a large quantity or a big difference, often with di + noun (e.g., un mondo di gente = lots of people). You can also use it with more/meno (un mondo più/meno) to mean “much more/less.”
target_language_example: C’era un mondo di gente alla festa.
native_language_example: There were loads of people at the party.

additional_notes: Used to soften a request, opinion, or quantity. Often appears with common verbs like aspettare (to wait), parlare (to speak), and volere (to want): “Aspetta un poco” = “Wait a bit.” In everyday speech you may also hear “un po’” (same meaning; spelling with apostrophe is very common).
target_language_example: Aspetta un poco, per favore.
native_language_example: Wait a bit, please.

additional_notes: Common in everyday Italian to mean “a lot,” often with verbs like avere (to have) or piacere (to like): “Ho un sacco di cose da fare” = “I have a lot of things to do.” You can use it as “un sacco di + noun” (a lot of + noun) or as an adverb without “di” (“Mi piace un sacco” = “I like it a lot”). More informal than “molto” but widely used.
target_language_example: Ho un sacco di lavoro oggi.
native_language_example: I have a lot of work today.

meaning: once; back then; in the past.
additional_notes: Common in storytelling and everyday speech to refer to an earlier time (often contrasted with now). Often used in phrases like “Un tempo… ma adesso…” (“Once… but now…”). It can also mean “at one time” in a more general sense.
target_language_example: Un tempo vivevo a Roma, ma adesso abito a Milano.
native_language_example: I used to live in Rome, but now I live in Milan.

meaning: “once” or “one time”; sometimes “once upon a time.”
additional_notes: Literally “one time.” Commonly used to talk about something that happened one time in the past (Una volta sono stato a Roma = I went to Rome once). Also used in stories as “Once upon a time…” (Una volta c’era…). In some contexts it can mean “once/when” in a general past sense, similar to “back when” (Una volta si faceva così = In the past, people did it this way).
target_language_example: Una volta ho mangiato sushi, ma non mi è piaciuto.
native_language_example: I ate sushi once, but I didn’t like it.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition in time: after one action/event is completed, the next one happens. Often followed by the subjunctive when referring to a future or uncertain event (e.g., “Una volta che sia/abbia…”), but the indicative is common when talking about something habitual or in the past.
target_language_example: Una volta che finisci i compiti, puoi uscire.
native_language_example: Once you finish your homework, you can go out.

additional_notes: Used to say you want to settle or finish something definitively, so it won’t come up again. Often paired with verbs like "decidere" (decide), "chiarire" (clear up), "finire" (finish), "risolvere" (solve). Can also be used with emphasis in complaints or requests (not slang, but can sound forceful).
target_language_example: Dobbiamo chiarire questa cosa una volta per tutte.
native_language_example: We have to clear this up once and for all.

meaning: “one of these days” (sometime soon, but not on a specific day).
additional_notes: Used to say you plan or expect to do something in the near future, without fixing a date. It can sound like a friendly intention (“We should meet up one of these days”) or like a mild warning (“One of these days you’ll get in trouble”). Often followed by the future tense (farò, ci vedremo, ecc.).
target_language_example: Uno di questi giorni ci vediamo per un caffè.
native_language_example: One of these days we’ll meet up for a coffee.

additional_notes: Common breakfast/meal item. You’ll hear it on menus or when ordering food. Singular: “un uovo strapazzato”; plural: “uova strapazzate”. Often used with “con” + ingredient (e.g., “con formaggio”, “con prosciutto”).
target_language_example: Per colazione vorrei delle uova strapazzate, per favore.
native_language_example: For breakfast I’d like some scrambled eggs, please.

additional_notes: Common food term. You can order it or describe how you want an egg cooked. Plural: uova sode. Often used in salads (insalata) or as a simple snack.
target_language_example: A colazione prendo un uovo sodo e un caffè.
native_language_example: For breakfast I have a hard-boiled egg and a coffee.

meaning: “OK / alright / fine,” often meaning “never mind / anyway.”
additional_notes: Very common in spoken Italian to show acceptance, resignation, or to move the conversation on. Often written as "vabbè" (also "va be'"), and it can sound like “well…” in English depending on tone. Used alone as an interjection or at the start of a sentence: "Va beh, andiamo" = “Alright, let’s go.”
target_language_example: Va beh, non importa: ne parliamo domani.
native_language_example: Alright, it doesn’t matter: we’ll talk about it tomorrow.

meaning: 'OK / all right / that's fine'; also 'it's going well'.
additional_notes: Very common everyday phrase. Use it to agree, accept a suggestion, or say something is fine (like “OK”). It can also describe how things are going, often as an answer to “Come va?” (“How’s it going?”).
target_language_example: Va bene, ci vediamo domani.
native_language_example: OK, see you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say something is self-evident or naturally follows from what was said. Often appears as: “Va da sé che …” (= “It goes without saying that …”). Typical in spoken and written Italian; slightly formal/neutral in tone.
target_language_example: Va da sé che domani ci vediamo alle otto.
native_language_example: It goes without saying that tomorrow we’ll see each other at eight.

additional_notes: Used to describe repeated movement in both directions (people, traffic, errands), often implying bustle or constant activity. It’s common in everyday speech, and can also be used figuratively for frequent changes or people coming and leaving a place. Often heard in: "un gran va e vieni" (a lot of comings and goings).
target_language_example: C’era un gran va e vieni di gente davanti alla stazione.
native_language_example: There were lots of people coming and going in front of the station.

additional_notes: A highly offensive, aggressive phrase used to tell someone off or express strong anger/contempt. It’s extremely vulgar (contains the verb "fottere") and should be avoided in polite conversation. Often used as an imperative directed at “you” (tu).
target_language_example: Se continui a insultarmi, vai a farti fottere.
native_language_example: If you keep insulting me, go fuck yourself.

additional_notes: Used to encourage someone or approve what they’re doing (“That’s right—continue like that”). Literally it means “you go like this/that,” and it can also be used more neutrally as an instruction (“go like this”). Often said on its own as a short, spoken comment.
target_language_example: Bravissimo, vai così!
native_language_example: Great job—keep it up!

meaning: coming and going; back-and-forth movement (constant traffic).
additional_notes: Literally “you go and you come.” Used to describe frequent movement of people or vehicles in a place (“a lot of coming and going”), or repeated trips back and forth. It’s common in everyday speech and can also be used figuratively for an unsettled situation with frequent changes.
target_language_example: In questa casa c’è sempre un vai e vieni di gente.
native_language_example: In this house there’s always people coming and going.

meaning: to be worth it; to be worthwhile.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is worth doing because the result/benefit justifies the effort, time, or cost. Often appears as "ne vale la pena" (it’s worth it) or in questions like "Vale la pena...?" (Is it worth it?). The subject is usually the thing you’re doing: "Vale la pena andare..." = “It’s worth going...”.
target_language_example: Vale la pena vedere questo film.
native_language_example: It’s worth seeing this movie.

additional_notes: Used for a bathtub (as opposed to a shower: "doccia"). In everyday speech you might also hear "vasca" alone when it’s clear you’re talking about the bathroom.
target_language_example: C’è una vasca da bagno in questo hotel?
native_language_example: Is there a bathtub in this hotel?

meaning: the old days; times long ago.
additional_notes: Usually used with an article (i vecchi tempi) and often in nostalgic expressions like "ai vecchi tempi" (like in the old days) or "bei vecchi tempi" (the good old days). Refers to the past in a general way, not a specific date.
target_language_example: Mi mancano i vecchi tempi, quando ci vedevamo ogni giorno.
native_language_example: I miss the old days, when we saw each other every day.

meaning: "my old friend" (a friendly, familiar way to address someone).
additional_notes: Used mainly when speaking to a man, often between friends, similar to “buddy,” “pal,” or “my man.” It’s affectionate and informal; it doesn’t necessarily mean the person is actually old. You can also hear the feminine version "vecchia mia" when addressing a woman.
target_language_example: Dai, vecchio mio, andiamo a prendere un caffè.
native_language_example: Come on, buddy, let’s go grab a coffee.

meaning: to see the light; to become clear; to be published/come out.
additional_notes: Used both literally (someone can see light) and figuratively. Figuratively it can mean (1) to finally understand something (“it clicked”), or (2) for a book, article, project, etc. to be released/published (“to see the light of day”). Often appears as “vedere la luce del giorno”.
target_language_example: Finalmente ho visto la luce: era un malinteso.
native_language_example: I finally saw the light: it was a misunderstanding.

meaning: to be born (to come into the world).
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s birth in a neutral or slightly literary way. It’s an intransitive expression; the person who is born is the subject (e.g., “Sono venuto/a al mondo…”). Often used with time/place: “nel 1990”, “a Roma”.
target_language_example: Mia sorella è venuta al mondo nel 2005.
native_language_example: My sister was born in 2005.

meaning: to come out; to emerge; to turn out.
additional_notes: Literally “to come out.” Used for something physically coming out (e.g., leaving a place), but very often figuratively for information or a problem emerging ("È venuto fuori un problema"), or for how something turns out / comes out after an effort ("Il dolce è venuto fuori bene" = the cake turned out well). In the negative, "non viene fuori" can mean "it won’t come out" or "it won’t work out / I can’t figure it out."
target_language_example: Alla fine è venuta fuori la verità.
native_language_example: In the end the truth came out.

meaning: to fail; to fall short; to give way (to weaken/collapse).
additional_notes: Used when something stops being valid or effective, or when someone/something weakens or collapses. Common with abstract nouns: "venire meno la fiducia" (trust fails), "venire meno l’accordo" (the agreement falls through), "venire meno un requisito" (a requirement is no longer met). Also used for a person fainting/losing strength: "è venuto meno". In the sense of "to fail to keep" a duty/promise, it can mean "to let someone down" (more formal).
target_language_example: Quando è venuta meno la corrente, l’ascensore si è fermato.
native_language_example: When the power went out, the elevator stopped.

meaning: to come up; to rise; to grow up (children/plants).
additional_notes: Common meanings include movement upward ("Come up!") and how someone/something is growing or turning out (especially children or plants): "Come viene su tuo figlio?" = "How is your son growing up?" It can also mean "to come back up" (e.g., stomach acid/food).
target_language_example: I pomodori stanno venendo su bene quest’anno.
native_language_example: The tomatoes are growing well this year.

meaning: to come away; to leave/go away (often with someone).
additional_notes: Used a lot as an invitation/urge to leave a place: “Vieni via!” = “Come on, let’s go!/Come away!” It can also mean something comes off/detaches: “È venuto via” = “It came off.”
target_language_example: Dai, vieni via con noi!
native_language_example: Come on, come with us!

meaning: real; actual; proper (in the true sense).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is genuine or fully qualifies as what you’re calling it (not just “sort of”). Often follows a noun (e.g., "un problema vero e proprio") or appears after the verb "essere" ("è un... vero e proprio"). It agrees in gender and number with the noun: vero e proprio (m. sg.), vera e propria (f. sg.), veri e propri (m. pl.), vere e proprie (f. pl.).
target_language_example: Non è una vacanza vera e propria, è solo un weekend fuori città.
native_language_example: It’s not a real vacation, it’s just a weekend out of town.

additional_notes: Used with a place or person to show moving away or being away from somewhere/someone. Often appears with verbs like andare (to go), stare (to stay), tenere (to keep), and with the command Vai via! ('Go away!').
target_language_example: Sono via da casa tutto il giorno.
native_language_example: I’m away from home all day.

additional_notes: Used to say that permission/authorization has been granted (often in official, work, or news contexts). Common with verbs like dare (to give) or avere (to have): "dare il via libera" = to give the go-ahead; "avere il via libera" = to get the go-ahead. Also used figuratively for green-lighting a project or plan.
target_language_example: Abbiamo avuto il via libera per iniziare i lavori.
native_language_example: We got the go-ahead to start the work.

meaning: dead end (street); also a dead end (no solution).
additional_notes: Literally “blind alley.” Used for a street with no exit, and figuratively for a situation with no way forward. With streets you may also hear “strada a fondo cieco.”
target_language_example: Siamo finiti in un vicolo cieco: dobbiamo tornare indietro.
native_language_example: We ended up in a dead end: we have to go back.

additional_notes: Mostly found in older, literary, or poetic Italian. It works like an intensifier meaning “even more” (similar to modern “ancor più” or “ancora di più”). In everyday speech you’ll usually use “ancora di più / ancor più” instead.
target_language_example: Più lo conoscevo, vie più lo stimavo.
native_language_example: The more I got to know him, the more I respected him.

additional_notes: In Italian, the singular is often used when referring to the profession in general; the plural is usually "vigili del fuoco" (firefighters). Used in emergencies or when talking about fire services. You may also hear "i Vigili del Fuoco" to mean the fire department/service as an institution.
target_language_example: Ho chiamato i vigili del fuoco perché c’era fumo in cucina.
native_language_example: I called the firefighters because there was smoke in the kitchen.

additional_notes: Used to refer to December 24th (the day/evening before Christmas Day). Often used when talking about dinner or celebrations that happen that night (e.g., "la cena della vigilia di Natale").
target_language_example: Che cosa fai la vigilia di Natale?
native_language_example: What are you doing on Christmas Eve?

additional_notes: Used when ordering or talking about wine. In Italian menus you may also see it contrasted with "vino rosso" (red wine) and "vino rosé" (rosé). You can specify quantity or preference, e.g., "Un bicchiere di vino bianco, per favore" (a glass of white wine) or "Preferisco il vino bianco" (I prefer white wine).
target_language_example: Vorrei un bicchiere di vino bianco, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a glass of white wine, please.

additional_notes: Common in restaurants and shops when ordering or choosing wine. It contrasts with "vino bianco" (white wine). You can use it with "un/una" (a glass/bottle) or with "del" (some): "un bicchiere di vino rosso", "una bottiglia di vino rosso", "Vorrei del vino rosso".
target_language_example: Vorrei un bicchiere di vino rosso, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a glass of red wine, please.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a reason or justification. Common in both speech and writing. It can refer to something already known/obvious ("given that...") or simply mean "since/because". Often followed by a verb clause (e.g., "visto che non hai tempo...").
target_language_example: Visto che piove, restiamo a casa.
native_language_example: Since it’s raining, let’s stay at home.

additional_notes: Used to refer to unofficial talk and speculation, often in workplaces, politics, or the media. It implies the information isn’t confirmed (“they’re saying…”), similar to “word on the street,” but more like “office/political rumors.” Literally it’s “corridor voices,” but you wouldn’t translate it word-for-word into English.
target_language_example: Secondo le voci di corridoio, l’azienda licenzierà alcuni dipendenti.
native_language_example: According to rumors, the company will lay off some employees.

meaning: "you yourselves" (addressing more than one female person).
additional_notes: Emphatic form used with the plural subject pronoun "voi" to stress that the people being addressed did the action personally (not someone else). "Stesse" agrees in gender/number with the group: feminine plural; for masculine or mixed groups, use "voi stessi". It often comes right after "voi" (e.g., "voi stesse"), or after a preposition (e.g., "da voi stesse" = "by yourselves").
target_language_example: Voi stesse potete decidere cosa fare.
native_language_example: You yourselves can decide what to do.

additional_notes: Reflexive/emphatic phrase for the 2nd-person plural (voi). It’s used either to emphasize the subject (“you yourselves”) or after a preposition like da/tra/fra/come (“by/among/like yourselves”). Masculine plural default; for an all-female group you can also say “voi stesse.”
target_language_example: Dovete farlo voi stessi, non qualcun altro.
native_language_example: You have to do it yourselves, not someone else.

meaning: to fly away; to blow away (figuratively: to disappear quickly).
additional_notes: Literally “to fly away.” Used for something that actually flies off (a bird, a hat, papers in the wind) and also figuratively for time, money, or opportunities “disappearing” quickly. Common structure: “è volato via” = “it flew away / it’s gone.”
target_language_example: Il cappello mi è volato via per il vento.
native_language_example: My hat blew away because of the wind.

meaning: (Roman dialect) “let’s love each other / let’s be kind to each other.”
additional_notes: Informal Roman (Rome) dialect for standard Italian “vogliamoci bene”. Used as a friendly, sometimes slightly ironic appeal to get along, stop arguing, or show goodwill. You may hear it in casual speech, movies, or jokes; in formal contexts use “vogliamoci bene” or “cerchiamo di andare d’accordo”.
target_language_example: Dai, su: volemose bene e non litighiamo.
native_language_example: Come on: let’s be kind to each other and not argue.

meaning: to care about; to love (in an affectionate, non-romantic way).
additional_notes: Used to express affection and fondness for family, friends, or even pets—more like “to care for” or “to be very fond of” than romantic “to be in love” (which is typically *amare*). Often appears as *ti voglio bene* (“I care about you / I love you”).
target_language_example: Ti voglio bene, mamma.
native_language_example: I love you, Mom.

additional_notes: Used to explain the meaning of a word, phrase, gesture, or situation. It can also be used in the past (e.g., "ha voluto dire") or with a question word (e.g., "Che cosa vuol dire?"). Often appears as "vuol dire" (short for "vuole dire").
target_language_example: Che cosa vuol dire questa parola?
native_language_example: What does this word mean?

meaning: 'to turn your back (on someone/something)'; figuratively, 'to abandon/ignore'.
additional_notes: Literally 'to turn the shoulders/back'. Used both physically (turning away) and figuratively (refusing to help, abandoning someone, ignoring a cause). Often followed by "a" + person/thing: "voltare le spalle a qualcuno/a qualcosa".
target_language_example: Non voltarmi le spalle proprio adesso.
native_language_example: Don’t turn your back on me right now.

meaning: a (usually immigrant) street vendor; often used in a derogatory way.
additional_notes: Slang term originally imitating the phrase "vuoi comprare?" (“do you want to buy?”), stereotypically associated with beach/street sellers. It’s widely considered offensive and disrespectful; in neutral speech prefer "venditore ambulante" (street vendor) or "venditore" (seller).
target_language_example: È un termine offensivo: meglio dire "venditore ambulante" invece di "vu cumprà".
native_language_example: It’s an offensive term: it’s better to say “street vendor” instead of “vu cumprà.”

additional_notes: Commonly written with a hyphen (week-end) or as one word (weekend). Often used with the verb "fare": "Cosa fai questo week-end?" (= What are you doing this weekend?). You can also say "nel week-end" (during the weekend) or "il week-end" (on the weekend).
target_language_example: Cosa fai questo week-end?
native_language_example: What are you doing this weekend?

additional_notes: Used as a polite, friendly reply when you meet someone, when someone thanks you, or when you’re happy to help. Common variants: “È stato un piacere” (“it was a pleasure”) and “Il piacere è mio” (“the pleasure is mine”).
target_language_example: Grazie per l’aiuto — è un piacere!
native_language_example: Thanks for the help — it’s a pleasure!
